Ehud is a left-handed man from the smallest tribe, which is why the guards do not find the blade strapped to his right thigh; he kills Eglon of Moab in a locked room and buys eighty years, the longest peace in the book. And Shamgar gets one verse, an oxgoad and six hundred Philistines.

A younger brother, a man whose sword arm did not work, and a farmer with a cattle prod. It is a fair summary of how God has always gone about it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Left to Teach Them War
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens by naming the nations God left and giving two reasons for it. The first is testing (v. 1, restated in v. 4): to find out whether Israel would obey. The second is stranger and is stated as the whole purpose — only in order that the generations of the people of Israel might know war, to teach war to those who had not known it before (v. 2). The nations are listed (v. 3), and then the result: Israel lived among them, married their sons and daughters, and served their gods (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The generation being tested had never fought. They were born into a country their parents had taken, and they had never once had to depend on God against an enemy. So the enemy is left standing, and the writer calls that an education.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 6 runs in a sequence and the last clause is where it was always going: they took their daughters, they gave their own daughters, and they served their gods. That is precisely the reason Moses gave for the prohibition — not race but worship: they would turn away your sons from following me (Deut. 7:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the nations that the LORD left, to test Israel by them, that is, all in Israel who had not experienced all the wars in Canaan. It was only in order that the generations of the people of Israel might know war, to teach war to those who had not known it before. These are the nations: the five lords of the Philistines and all the Canaanites and the Sidonians and the Hivites who lived on Mount Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon as far as Lebo-hamath. They were for the testing of Israel, to know whether Israel would obey the commandments of the LORD, which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now these are the nations that the LORD left, to test Israel by them, that is, all in Israel who had not experienced all the wars in Canaan. It was only in order that the generations of the people of Israel might know war, to teach war to those who had not known it before.'

Two purposes are given for the unfinished conquest, and the second is the surprising one.

The first is the testing already announced at the end of chapter 2. The second is put as though it were the whole point: only in order that the generations... might know war, to teach war to those who had not known it before.

Think about who is being described. This is the generation born after the fighting stopped. They grew up in houses their parents had taken, ate from vineyards somebody else had planted, and had never in their lives faced an enemy across a field. They had inherited the results of faith without ever having exercised any.

So God leaves the Philistines and the Canaanites in place, and the writer calls it a school. Not a punishment here, and not a mistake — a course of instruction for people who had grown up soft in a country won by other men's obedience.

Hold that against the instinct to read every remaining difficulty as a failure. A settled Christian who has never had to depend on God for anything is not in a stronger position than one who has; he is in a more dangerous one, and he has no way of knowing it until something is left standing in his way.

'They were for the testing of Israel, to know whether Israel would obey the commandments of the LORD, which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses.'

The test is not of their doctrine or their sincerity. It is of their obedience, and the syllabus is already written and already published. Nothing new will be asked of them.

verseByVerse.quote: So the people of Israel lived among the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. And their daughters they took to themselves for wives, and their own daughters they gave to their sons, and they served their gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So the people of Israel lived among the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.'

The result of the test is reported in one sentence, and it uses the wording that chapter 1 introduced at Asher: Israel lived among them. Six nations are named, and Israel is listed as the population living in their country rather than the other way round.

'And their daughters they took to themselves for wives, and their own daughters they gave to their sons, and they served their gods.'

Then the sequence, and it runs in one direction with no pause in it. They took wives. They gave daughters. They served their gods.

Read those three clauses as a single motion, because that is how the verse is built. Nobody married a Canaanite in order to worship Baal. The worship arrived at the end of a chain that began with an entirely ordinary decision about a wedding.

That is exactly the reason God had given for the prohibition in the first place. It was never about ancestry — Rahab married into Judah, Ruth the Moabite is in the same family tree, and a Kenite clan is settled among them in chapter 1. Moses stated the ground plainly: they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut. 7:4). The rule was about what happens to worship in a household, not about blood.

Paul reasons the same way about being unequally yoked (2 Cor. 6:14), and for the same reason: the heart does not stay independent of what it has bound itself to. Israel proves it in a single verse. They married the families and ended up at the family altars.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first full turn of the cycle, told in textbook form. Israel did evil, forgot the LORD and served the Baals and the Asheroth (v. 7); God sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim of Mesopotamia for eight years (v. 8); they cried out, and the LORD raised up Othniel, Caleb's younger brother (v. 9). The Spirit of the LORD came on him, he judged Israel and went out to war, and God gave the king into his hand (v. 10). Then verse 11, which contains both the reward and the flaw: the land had rest forty years, and then Othniel died.
verseByVerse.theology: Othniel is the model, and the writer gives him no faults. He is from Caleb's family, the Spirit rests on him, he wins, and the land is quiet for a generation. Every judge after this is measured against him, and every one falls short.
verseByVerse.examples: The oppressor's name is almost certainly a joke at his expense. Cushan-rishathaim reads as something like Cushan of double wickedness, which is not the sort of thing a man calls himself. Israel is groaning under a king the narrator will not dignify with his real name.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. They forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asheroth. Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia. And the people of Israel served Cushan-rishathaim eight years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. They forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asheroth.'

One verb in that sentence explains the whole book, and it is not a dramatic one. They forgot.

Not rejected. Not renounced. Not argued with. There is no record anywhere in Judges of Israel deciding that the God of the exodus was untrue; what the writer keeps describing is a nation mislaying him. Chapter 2 said the generation did not know him. This one says they forgot him.

Forgetting is the most ordinary thing a person does, and it takes no effort at all. It is what happens to anything that is not deliberately kept in front of the mind, and Moses had spent a whole book warning about it: take care lest you forget the LORD, when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses and live in them (Deut. 8:11-12).

'Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia. And the people of Israel served Cushan-rishathaim eight years.'

Say the name of the oppressor out loud. Cushan-rishathaim reads in Hebrew as something like Cushan of double wickedness, and no king ever called himself that. The narrator is refusing to use the man's real name.

Eight years under a tyrant, and the writer will not even grant him the dignity of accurate titles. It is a small act of defiance in a sentence about defeat.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer for the people of Israel, who saved them, Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother. The Spirit of the LORD was upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to war, and the LORD gave Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand. And his hand prevailed over Cushan-rishathaim. So the land had rest for forty years. Then Othniel the son of Kenaz died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But when the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer for the people of Israel, who saved them, Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother.'

They cry out. It is not called repentance and nothing is said about their turning from the Baals; they are simply in pain and they make a noise about it, which is the groaning God was described as unable to bear in 2:18.

The man raised up is already known to the reader. Othniel took Kiriath-sepher and married Achsah back in chapter 1, in the passage lifted out of Joshua. He belongs to the last good family in the book: Caleb's.

'The Spirit of the LORD was upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to war, and the LORD gave Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand.'

Here is the sentence that will explain every deliverance in this book: the Spirit of the LORD was upon him.

Not his lineage, though it was good. Not his record, though he had one. The book will go on to prove the point by putting the same words over men with far worse credentials — a frightened farmer hiding in a winepress, a rejected son of a prostitute, a man who could not keep away from Philistine women. The one qualification is the Spirit, and it is given rather than earned.

'So the land had rest for forty years. Then Othniel the son of Kenaz died.'

One verse, two facts, and the second cancels the first.

Forty years is a full generation of peace, and it is real. Then the sentence turns on a word this book will use again and again as a hinge: died.

Othniel is the model judge. There is not a single criticism of him anywhere in Scripture, the Spirit rested on him, and he handed his people a working lifetime of quiet. He was also mortal, and the rest he won was buried with him. The best available deliverer, doing everything right, could not give Israel anything that outlasted his own funeral.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wheel turns on the word again (v. 12), and this time God strengthened the oppressor: Eglon of Moab, with Ammon and Amalek, takes the city of palms and holds Israel eighteen years (vv. 13-14). Israel cries out and God raises up Ehud, a left-handed Benjaminite, who makes a short two-edged sword and straps it to his right thigh (vv. 15-16). He delivers the tribute, sends the carriers away, comes back with a secret message, and kills the king alone in his roof chamber (vv. 17-22). He locks the doors and walks out; the servants stand outside waiting until they are embarrassed (vv. 23-25). Ehud escapes, sounds the trumpet, takes the fords of the Jordan, and ten thousand Moabites fall — and the land has rest for eighty years (vv. 26-30).
verseByVerse.theology: God's deliverer is a man from the smallest tribe with a disqualified sword arm, carrying a homemade blade to a tribute ceremony. The whole plan depends on the thing about him that a guard would have written off.
verseByVerse.examples: Eighty years is the longest rest recorded in the book, twice Othniel's forty. It is also, like every other rest here, measured in the lifetime of one man.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel, because they had done what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He gathered to himself the Ammonites and the Amalekites, and went and defeated Israel. And they took possession of the city of palms. And the people of Israel served Eglon the king of Moab eighteen years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel, because they had done what was evil in the sight of the LORD.'

The word that drives the whole book is here: again. Othniel is barely in the ground and the wheel has come round.

Then a verb worth stopping on. The LORD strengthened Eglon. God does not merely allow the oppressor; he equips him. The rod that beats Israel is put into a Moabite hand by the God who is being disobeyed.

That is uncomfortable and it is consistent. This book will not let its readers imagine that Israel's troubles come from God's absence. They come from his attention.

'He gathered to himself the Ammonites and the Amalekites, and went and defeated Israel. And they took possession of the city of palms. And the people of Israel served Eglon the king of Moab eighteen years.'

The city of palms is Jericho. The first city God gave them, whose walls fell flat at a shout, is now a Moabite forward base.

Count the years. Cushan held them eight; Eglon holds them eighteen. The oppressions are getting longer, exactly as chapter 2 said the spiral would run.

There is one more sting in the choice of oppressor. Moab was family — descended from Lot, Abraham's nephew — and Israel had been forbidden to attack them in the wilderness because of it (Deut. 2:9). The people God brought out of the greatest empire on earth are now paying tribute to their second cousins.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, and the LORD raised up for them a deliverer, Ehud, the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, a left-handed man. The people of Israel sent tribute by him to Eglon the king of Moab. And Ehud made for himself a sword with two edges, a cubit in length, and he bound it on his right thigh under his clothes. And he presented the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Now Eglon was a very fat man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, and the LORD raised up for them a deliverer, Ehud, the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, a left-handed man.'

The narrator gives one physical detail about this man and it is the one the whole story turns on.

The Hebrew does not simply say left-handed. It says something like bound or restricted as to his right hand — a man whose sword arm does not work as a sword arm should. In a world where every soldier drew from the left hip with his right hand, that is a defect on a military record.

He is also a Benjaminite, and the name Benjamin means son of the right hand. The son of the right hand cannot use his right hand.

The trait ran in that tribe. Later in this same book, Benjamin fields seven hundred picked left-handed men who could sling a stone at a hair and not miss (20:16). What looks like an individual peculiarity is a tribal specialty, and the enemy has not thought about it.

'And Ehud made for himself a sword with two edges, a cubit in length, and he bound it on his right thigh under his clothes. And he presented the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Now Eglon was a very fat man.'

He makes the weapon himself: short, about eighteen inches, sharpened on both edges, and small enough to hide under a cloak. Then he straps it to his right thigh.

That is the detail on which a nation's freedom turns. A guard searching a man for weapons runs his hands down the left side, because that is where a right-handed man carries. Ehud is not searched on the right, and the blade goes in through the front door of the palace on the body of a man who has been officially disarmed.

The last sentence of verse 17 looks like an aside and it is loading a gun: now Eglon was a very fat man. The narrator wants that fact in the reader's mind before the roof chamber, and his name is probably part of the joke — Eglon is close to the Hebrew for a calf. A king who has grown heavy on eighteen years of another nation's tribute is about to be dealt with like livestock.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he sent away the people who carried the tribute. But he himself turned back at the idols near Gilgal and said, "I have a secret message for you, O king." And he commanded, "Silence." And all his attendants went out from his presence. And Ehud came to him as he was sitting alone in his cool roof chamber. And Ehud said, "I have a message from God for you." And he arose from his seat. And Ehud reached with his left hand, took the sword from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly. And the hilt also went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade, for he did not pull the sword out of his belly; and the dung came out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And when Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he sent away the people who carried the tribute. But he himself turned back at the idols near Gilgal and said, "I have a secret message for you, O king." And he commanded, "Silence." And all his attendants went out from his presence.'

He sends the delegation home first, so that no Israelite but himself is anywhere near the palace when it happens. Then he turns back, and the place where he turns is noted: at the idols near Gilgal.

Gilgal, of all places. The ground where the twelve stones from the Jordan were set up now has carved images standing on it, and the man who is about to deliver Israel turns round at them.

The king's response is the give-away. Ehud says he has a secret, and Eglon empties the room. The one thing an oppressor cannot resist is intelligence, and he dismisses his own bodyguard to get it.

'And Ehud came to him as he was sitting alone in his cool roof chamber. And Ehud said, "I have a message from God for you." And he arose from his seat.'

Now the sentence the whole scene has been built for: I have a message from God for you.

Eglon stands up to receive it. Whatever he believed about the God of Israel, he stood.

'And Ehud reached with his left hand, took the sword from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly. And the hilt also went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade, for he did not pull the sword out of his belly; and the dung came out.'

The message from God is eighteen inches of iron, and the narrator describes what happens to it with a bluntness that has embarrassed readers for centuries.

He does not look away. The hilt goes in after the blade. The fat closes over it. Ehud leaves the weapon where it is, and the last clause is exactly as undignified as it sounds.

This is deliberate. Scripture is capable of writing an oppressor's death with dignity, and it declines to do it here. Eighteen years of a nation's grain went into that body, and the writer lets the reader see what became of it. There is a strand running through the Bible that laughs at tyrants — he who sits in the heavens laughs (Ps. 2:4) — and this is the crudest page of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ehud went out into the porch and closed the doors of the roof chamber behind him and locked them. When he had gone, the servants came, and when they saw that the doors of the roof chamber were locked, they thought, "Surely he is relieving himself in the closet of the cool chamber." And they waited till they were embarrassed. But when he still did not open the doors of the roof chamber, they took the key and opened them, and there lay their lord dead on the floor. Ehud escaped while they delayed, and he passed beyond the idols and escaped to Seirah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Ehud went out into the porch and closed the doors of the roof chamber behind him and locked them.'

He locks up. A man who has just killed a head of state in his own palace stops, pulls the doors to, turns the key, and walks out through the household.

'When he had gone, the servants came, and when they saw that the doors of the roof chamber were locked, they thought, "Surely he is relieving himself in the closet of the cool chamber."'

The servants arrive, find the doors locked, and reach the obvious conclusion. Their king is using the lavatory.

'And they waited till they were embarrassed. But when he still did not open the doors of the roof chamber, they took the key and opened them, and there lay their lord dead on the floor.'

They wait. And the writer, who could have moved straight to the discovery, stops to record their state of mind: they waited till they were embarrassed.

Picture it, because the scene is staged to be pictured. A corridor full of courtiers standing outside a locked door, too well-bred to knock, growing steadily more uncomfortable, while the assassin gets further away by the minute and the man they are protecting has been dead for some time.

'Ehud escaped while they delayed, and he passed beyond the idols and escaped to Seirah.'

The delay is the escape route. What saves the deliverer is not his speed but the manners of his enemies, and the writer's point is not subtle: when God moves against an oppressor, the oppressor's own household becomes part of the arrangement.

Whatever else the court of Moab was that afternoon, it was not formidable. Eighteen years of domination ends with a locked door and a group of embarrassed men who cannot bring themselves to interrupt.

verseByVerse.quote: When he arrived, he sounded the trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim. Then the people of Israel went down with him from the hill country, and he was their leader. And he said to them, "Follow after me, for the LORD has given your enemies the Moabites into your hand." So they went down after him and seized the fords of the Jordan against the Moabites and did not allow anyone to pass over. And they killed at that time about 10,000 of the Moabites, all strong, able-bodied men; not a man escaped. So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. And the land had rest for eighty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When he arrived, he sounded the trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim. Then the people of Israel went down with him from the hill country, and he was their leader.'

The assassination was not the deliverance; it was the opening. Ehud blows a trumpet in the hills and a nation comes down after him.

See what has changed in the people. These are the same Israelites who have been paying tribute for eighteen years, and one man with a horn is enough. The oppression was never quite as solid as it looked; what was missing was somebody to move first.

'And he said to them, "Follow after me, for the LORD has given your enemies the Moabites into your hand." So they went down after him and seized the fords of the Jordan against the Moabites and did not allow anyone to pass over.'

His speech is two clauses long and the second is the whole theology of the book: the LORD has given. Perfect tense again, exactly as at Jericho and exactly as in 1:2. The killing of Eglon did not create the victory; it acted on one already granted.

The tactics are sound, too. The fords of the Jordan are the only way home for a Moabite army on the wrong side of the river, and Israel takes them first. The occupying force is cut off in a country that hates it.

'And they killed at that time about 10,000 of the Moabites, all strong, able-bodied men; not a man escaped. So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. And the land had rest for eighty years.'

Eighty years. It is the longest peace recorded in the book, twice what Othniel achieved, and it is the high-water mark of the whole period.

Two full generations of quiet came out of one afternoon in a locked room, and the man God used to buy them was a member of the smallest tribe whose sword arm did not work. The Moabites had searched him at the door.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One verse, and it is all we are told: Shamgar the son of Anath killed six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad, and he also saved Israel (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: No cycle, no years, no oppression narrated and no rest recorded. He is given a name, a farm implement, a number, and the same verb used of every other deliverer in the book.
verseByVerse.examples: An oxgoad is a long pole with an iron tip for prodding cattle and scraping a plough. The gallery of chapter 3 is now complete: a younger brother, a man who could not use his right hand, and a farmer with the tool that happened to be in his hand.

verseByVerse.quote: After him was Shamgar the son of Anath, who killed 600 of the Philistines with an oxgoad, and he also saved Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After him was Shamgar the son of Anath, who killed 600 of the Philistines with an oxgoad, and he also saved Israel.'

One verse, and then the chapter is over.

There is no cycle here. No apostasy is recorded, no oppression described, no crying out, no years of rest. Shamgar gets a name, a weapon, a number and a verb.

The weapon is the point. An oxgoad is a farm tool: a wooden pole eight feet long or so, with an iron spike at one end for driving cattle and a flat blade at the other for scraping mud off a ploughshare. It is what a man has in his hand when he is working, and it is not a sword.

Six hundred Philistines, with an implement for prodding oxen. This is also the first time the Philistines appear in this book as an enemy, and they will be the last one it deals with; the whole Samson cycle is against them, and they are still there when Saul dies.

Set the three deliverers of this chapter side by side, because the writer has arranged them that way. A younger brother from a good family. A man whose right hand did not work. And a farmer with a cattle prod.

Nothing in that list is what a nation would choose. It is a fair summary of how God has always gone about it — God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong, and what is low and despised, so that no human being might boast in his presence (1 Cor. 1:27-29).

The last four words are the ones to keep: and he also saved Israel. It is the same verb used of Othniel and of Ehud, the word behind the name of Joshua and the name of Jesus. A man with a stick is entered in the record with the same word as everybody else, and God did not need better equipment than what was already in his hand.

3.theology:
The enemy as curriculum. Verse 2 says the nations were left to teach war to a generation that had never fought. A settled believer who has never had to depend on God is not in a safer position than one who has, and has no way of discovering it until something is left standing in his way. The remaining difficulty in a Christian life is not automatically evidence of a battle lost.

They forgot. The verb in verse 7 is the ordinary one, and it takes no effort at all. Judges never once records Israel deciding that the God of the exodus was untrue; chapter 2 said they did not know him, and this chapter says they forgot him. Moses had spent a book warning about exactly this, and located the danger in prosperity rather than persecution — when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses and live in them (Deut. 8:11-12).

The one qualification. What explains Othniel is not his family, though it was the best in the book, but four words: the Spirit of the LORD was upon him (v. 10). The book will put those same words over a frightened farmer hiding in a winepress, the rejected son of a prostitute, and a man who could not keep away from Philistine women. The qualification is given, not earned.

Improbable instruments. Ehud's deliverance turns entirely on the trait a recruiting officer would have written off: a Benjaminite — a son of the right hand — whose right hand did not work, which is why nobody searched the right side. Shamgar's weapon is what happened to be in his hand at work. It is the pattern Paul states outright: God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong, so that no human being might boast (1 Cor. 1:27-29).
3.examples:
Then: A generation that had never fought a battle married into the neighbours and ended up at their altars. Then God raised up a model judge who died, an assassin whose disability was the plan, and a farmer with a stick — and every deliverance was real and every one of them wore off.

Now: Two things. Verse 6 is the sequence to watch, because nobody in it chose to change gods; they chose relationships, and the worship followed. And verse 7 is the honest description of most spiritual decline: not rejection but forgetting, which requires no decision and happens to anything not deliberately kept in front of the mind. Moses put the danger in the good years, not the hard ones.

4.title: Deborah and Barak
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD after Ehud died.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim.<sup>3</sup>Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD for help, for he had 900 chariots of iron and he oppressed the people of Israel cruelly for twenty years.<sup>4</sup>Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time.<sup>5</sup>She used to sit under the palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the people of Israel came up to her for judgment.<sup>6</sup>She sent and summoned Barak the son of Abinoam from Kedesh-naphtali and said to him, "Has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you, 'Go, gather your men at Mount Tabor, taking 10,000 from the people of Naphtali and the people of Zebulun.<sup>7</sup>And I will draw out Sisera, the general of Jabin's army, to meet you by the river Kishon with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand'?"<sup>8</sup>Barak said to her, "If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go."<sup>9</sup>And she said, "I will surely go with you. Nevertheless, the road on which you are going will not lead to your glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman." Then Deborah arose and went with Barak to Kedesh.<sup>10</sup>And Barak called out Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh. And 10,000 men went up at his heels, and Deborah went up with him.<sup>11</sup>Now Heber the Kenite had separated from the Kenites, the descendants of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses, and had pitched his tent as far away as the oak in Zaanannim, which is near Kedesh.<sup>12</sup>When Sisera was told that Barak the son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor,<sup>13</sup>Sisera called out all his chariots, 900 chariots of iron, and all the men who were with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the river Kishon.<sup>14</sup>And Deborah said to Barak, "Up! For this is the day in which the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Does not the LORD go out before you?" So Barak went down from Mount Tabor with 10,000 men following him.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD routed Sisera and all his chariots and all his army before Barak by the edge of the sword. And Sisera got down from his chariot and fled away on foot.<sup>16</sup>And Barak pursued the chariots and the army to Harosheth-hagoyim, and all the army of Sisera fell by the edge of the sword; not a man was left.<sup>17</sup>But Sisera fled away on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.<sup>18</sup>And Jael came out to meet Sisera and said to him, "Turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not be afraid." So he turned aside to her into the tent, and she covered him with a rug.<sup>19</sup>And he said to her, "Please give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty." So she opened a skin of milk and gave him a drink and covered him.<sup>20</sup>And he said to her, "Stand at the opening of the tent, and if any man comes and asks you, 'Is anyone here?' say, 'No.'"<sup>21</sup>But Jael the wife of Heber took a tent peg, and took a hammer in her hand. Then she went softly to him and drove the peg into his temple until it went down into the ground while he was lying fast asleep from weariness. So he died.<sup>22</sup>And behold, as Barak was pursuing Sisera, Jael went out to meet him and said to him, "Come, and I will show you the man whom you are seeking." So he went in to her tent, and there lay Sisera dead, with the tent peg in his temple.<sup>23</sup>So on that day God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan before the people of Israel.<sup>24</sup>And the hand of the people of Israel pressed harder and harder against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.
4.overview:
Ehud dies, the cycle turns, and the oppressor this time is Jabin king of Canaan, reigning in Hazor. That should stop a reader who has just finished Joshua: Hazor was burned to the ground and its king killed, the one city in the whole northern campaign Joshua burned, because it had been the head of all those kingdoms (Josh. 11:10-11). Nothing had to be reconquered for a Jabin to be there again. The site was left empty and somebody moved back in.

His commander has nine hundred chariots of iron, and that number has a history too. Iron chariots entered this book at 1:19 as the reason Judah could not take the plain. The thing a generation declined to face has multiplied into nine hundred of them and twenty years of cruelty.

Deborah is already in place before the rescue begins — a prophetess, settling disputes under a palm tree while a foreign general runs the north. And her word to Barak is a question, not a commission: has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you? He already had his orders. She sends for him to ask why he is still at home.

He will go if she goes. She goes, without a lecture, and tells him what it costs — the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman, which is the same verb used two verses in of God selling Israel into Jabin's hand. Then a flooded river, an abandoned chariot, a tent pitched near Kedesh for no stated reason, and a woman with the tools of her own trade.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Nine Hundred Chariots, and a Woman Under a Palm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel does evil again after Ehud died (v. 1), and God sells them to Jabin king of Canaan, who reigns in Hazor, with Sisera commanding his army (v. 2). Sisera has nine hundred chariots of iron, and he oppresses Israel cruelly for twenty years (v. 3). Then the narrator introduces the person God has already put in place: Deborah, a prophetess, judging Israel, sitting under a palm between Ramah and Bethel while the people come up to her for judgment (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The chariots are not new. In 1:19 iron chariots were the reason Judah could not drive out the plain. That excuse has now multiplied into nine hundred of them and twenty years of cruelty. What a generation declines to face does not stay the same size.
verseByVerse.examples: Hazor should not have a king. Joshua burned Hazor to the ground and killed its king — the one city in the whole northern campaign he burned, because it had been the head of all those kingdoms (Josh. 11:10-11). A century later there is a Jabin in Hazor with nine hundred chariots. What Israel did not hold rebuilt itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD after Ehud died. And the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim. Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD for help, for he had 900 chariots of iron and he oppressed the people of Israel cruelly for twenty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD after Ehud died. And the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor.'

The formula runs as before, and the trigger is named without comment: after Ehud died. Eighty years of rest ended at a funeral, exactly as chapter 2 said it would.

Then a detail that should stop a reader who has just come through Joshua. There is a king in Hazor.

Hazor was burned. Joshua took it, killed its king, and set fire to the city — the only town in the entire northern campaign he burned, and the writer of Joshua explained why: it had been the head of all those kingdoms (Josh. 11:10-11). It was the capital of the opposition, and Israel destroyed it on purpose.

A century or so later, there is a Jabin reigning in Hazor with a standing army. Nothing had to be conquered for that to happen; the site was simply left empty and somebody moved back in. What God's people do not occupy does not stay unoccupied.

'The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim. Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD for help, for he had 900 chariots of iron and he oppressed the people of Israel cruelly for twenty years.'

Nine hundred chariots of iron.

Go back to 1:19, where the phrase entered the book: the LORD was with Judah, and he could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain because they had chariots of iron. That was the excuse, and it sounded practical at the time.

The thing Judah declined to face has now multiplied into nine hundred and become a twenty-year occupation described as cruel. This is the longest oppression yet — eight years under Cushan, eighteen under Eglon, twenty now — and it is the direct descendant of a sentence about iron in chapter 1.

What a generation will not face does not stay the size it was when they decided not to face it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time. She used to sit under the palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the people of Israel came up to her for judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time. She used to sit under the palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the people of Israel came up to her for judgment.'

Before the deliverer is raised up, the narrator introduces someone who is already there.

Three things are said about her and each one is unusual. She is a prophetess, and she is the only judge in the book who is also called that — the others are given the Spirit for a campaign; she is given words. She is the wife of Lappidoth, which locates her in an ordinary household. And she was judging Israel, in the plain sense of the word: people brought disputes to her and she settled them.

Hold that last point, because it is not what the other judges do. Othniel, Ehud, Gideon and Samson are military deliverers; the word judge in this book usually means rescuer rather than magistrate. Deborah is the one who actually judges, and she is doing it before any of this starts, sitting under a named tree in the hill country while a foreign general runs the north.

The picture is quietly remarkable. Israel is under occupation, the tribes are scattered and frightened, and there is one fixed point in the country where the word of God is being applied to ordinary disputes, day after day, by a woman under a palm tree. The nation has no army worth the name and no king. It has a court.

Nothing in the chapter treats her prominence as a scandal, and the song in the next chapter tells us how she read it herself: the villages ceased in Israel, they ceased, until I arose as a mother in Israel (5:7). When the men who should have led did not, God did not stop governing his people. He put somebody else under the tree.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — Has Not the LORD Commanded You?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deborah summons Barak and puts the whole thing to him as a question: has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor (v. 6)? The promise comes with it — I will draw out Sisera to the Kishon with his chariots, and I will give him into your hand (v. 7). Barak's answer sets a condition: if you go with me I will go, and if not, I will not (v. 8). Deborah agrees and names the price — the road you are going on will not lead to your glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman (v. 9). Ten thousand men go up at his heels, and Deborah goes with him (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 6 is a question, not a commission. Barak already had his orders; what Deborah sends for him to ask is why he is still at home. That changes the scene entirely: this is not a man being called but a man being reminded.
verseByVerse.examples: The word in verse 9 is the same word as in verse 2. God sold Israel into Jabin's hand; now God will sell Sisera into a woman's hand. The transaction is simply being reversed, and by the same seller.

verseByVerse.quote: She sent and summoned Barak the son of Abinoam from Kedesh-naphtali and said to him, "Has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you, 'Go, gather your men at Mount Tabor, taking 10,000 from the people of Naphtali and the people of Zebulun. And I will draw out Sisera, the general of Jabin's army, to meet you by the river Kishon with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'She sent and summoned Barak the son of Abinoam from Kedesh-naphtali and said to him, "Has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you, 'Go, gather your men at Mount Tabor, taking 10,000 from the people of Naphtali and the people of Zebulun'?"'

Read the first clause of what she says as the question it is. Has not the LORD... commanded you?

This is not Deborah handing Barak a new commission. It is Deborah sending for a man who already has one, and asking him why nothing has happened. God had spoken to Barak; the muster point was chosen; the tribes were named; the numbers were given. Barak was at home in Kedesh-naphtali with his orders in his pocket.

That changes the scene considerably. The problem in the north is not that God has been silent. It is that a man has heard him and stayed where he was.

'"And I will draw out Sisera, the general of Jabin's army, to meet you by the river Kishon with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand."'

The command comes wrapped in a promise, and the promise does the harder half of the work. God will draw out Sisera — Israel does not have to find him or provoke him; the enemy will be brought to the chosen ground. And I will give him into your hand, the perfect grammar of this whole history, said before anybody has marched.

Look at the ground God names, because it is the last place a sensible commander would pick. The Kishon runs through the plain of Jezreel, which is flat, open and exactly the country chariots were built for. God proposes to fight nine hundred iron chariots on their own terrain, and says he will personally arrange the enemy's attendance.

verseByVerse.quote: Barak said to her, "If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go." And she said, "I will surely go with you. Nevertheless, the road on which you are going will not lead to your glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman." Then Deborah arose and went with Barak to Kedesh. And Barak called out Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh. And 10,000 men went up at his heels, and Deborah went up with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Barak said to her, "If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go."'

Barak's answer is not a refusal, and it is not obedience either. It is a condition.

Be fair to him first. He does not deny the word, argue with the plan or dispute the odds, and Hebrews will list him among the people who conquered kingdoms by faith (Heb. 11:32). Something in him believes this.

But look at what his faith is resting on. He has the command of God, delivered by a prophetess whose word the whole country trusts. What he wants in addition is a person he can see standing next to him. He will act on the word of God provided the woman who carries it comes within arm's reach and stays there.

'And she said, "I will surely go with you. Nevertheless, the road on which you are going will not lead to your glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman."'

She agrees at once, without a lecture, and then tells him what it will cost. Not the victory — the victory is not in question. The glory.

Catch the verb she uses. God will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman, and it is the same word used two verses into the chapter, where the LORD sold Israel into the hand of Jabin. The same seller, the opposite direction. What was done to Israel is about to be done to Sisera, and by the same hand.

'Then Deborah arose and went with Barak to Kedesh. And Barak called out Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh. And 10,000 men went up at his heels, and Deborah went up with him.'

She goes. There is no sulking and no bargaining; a man who needed her presence in order to obey is given her presence, and the ten thousand assemble.

God does not withdraw the commission from a man who asked for a crutch. He gives him the crutch and the commission, and quietly moves the honour somewhere else.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A parenthesis drops in a fact that will matter later: Heber the Kenite has separated from his people and pitched his tent near Kedesh (v. 11). Sisera hears that Barak is on Tabor and brings out all nine hundred chariots to the river Kishon (vv. 12-13). Deborah gives the order — Up! For this is the day in which the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Does not the LORD go out before you? — and ten thousand men come down off the mountain (v. 14). The LORD routs Sisera and his chariots; Sisera gets down and runs away on foot; not a man of his army is left (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The verb in verse 15 belongs to God: the LORD routed Sisera. Israel has infantry on a hill facing armour in a plain, and the plain is where chariots are supposed to win. Chapter 5 will say what happened — the Kishon came down in flood and took them (5:21).
verseByVerse.examples: Sisera got down from his chariot. Nine hundred iron chariots had made a nation afraid for twenty years, and the man who commanded them finishes the afternoon running across country on foot like anybody else.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Heber the Kenite had separated from the Kenites, the descendants of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses, and had pitched his tent as far away as the oak in Zaanannim, which is near Kedesh. When Sisera was told that Barak the son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor, Sisera called out all his chariots, 900 chariots of iron, and all the men who were with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the river Kishon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Heber the Kenite had separated from the Kenites, the descendants of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses, and had pitched his tent as far away as the oak in Zaanannim, which is near Kedesh.'

A parenthesis, dropped into the middle of a military narrative, about a man moving house.

The Kenites entered this book in 1:16, coming up with Judah into the wilderness of the south and settling among the people. Heber has left them and come north, and pitched his tent near Kedesh — which is precisely where Barak is mustering.

Nothing in the verse explains why it is here. It reads like an aside a careful writer could have left out. Eight verses later it will be the most important sentence in the chapter.

'When Sisera was told that Barak the son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor, Sisera called out all his chariots, 900 chariots of iron, and all the men who were with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the river Kishon.'

Sisera hears about the muster and does exactly what God said he would do.

Verse 7 had promised: I will draw out Sisera... to the river Kishon. Here he comes, of his own initiative, at speed, with everything he has, to the exact spot named in advance. He believes he is responding to a piece of military intelligence about a badly outnumbered enemy sitting on a hill.

He is right about all of it. Barak's men are outnumbered and outmatched, and the ground Sisera is racing towards is level plain that will let him deploy nine hundred chariots at once. Everything Sisera concludes is correct, and it takes him to the place God chose.

verseByVerse.quote: And Deborah said to Barak, "Up! For this is the day in which the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Does not the LORD go out before you?" So Barak went down from Mount Tabor with 10,000 men following him. And the LORD routed Sisera and all his chariots and all his army before Barak by the edge of the sword. And Sisera got down from his chariot and fled away on foot. And Barak pursued the chariots and the army to Harosheth-hagoyim, and all the army of Sisera fell by the edge of the sword; not a man was left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Deborah said to Barak, "Up! For this is the day in which the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Does not the LORD go out before you?" So Barak went down from Mount Tabor with 10,000 men following him.'

The order to attack is one word, and the reasons attached to it are both in the past tense.

This is the day in which the LORD has given. Not will give. And then a question that is really the whole argument: does not the LORD go out before you? Barak is not being sent to win a battle. He is being told that somebody has already gone ahead of him into it.

He goes down. That is the moment of the chapter for him, and it should not be undersold: ten thousand men with no armour walk off a defensible hill onto flat ground towards massed chariots, because a woman told them the LORD had gone in front.

'And the LORD routed Sisera and all his chariots and all his army before Barak by the edge of the sword. And Sisera got down from his chariot and fled away on foot.'

The subject of the sentence is God. The LORD routed Sisera. The swords in Israelite hands are mentioned, and they are not the explanation.

The next chapter says what happened, in one line of poetry: the torrent Kishon swept them away (5:21). The river came down, the plain turned to mud, and nine hundred iron chariots became nine hundred very heavy objects stuck in a floodplain. The thing that made them unstoppable on dry ground is what fixed them in place when the ground changed.

Then the detail the writer clearly enjoys: Sisera got down from his chariot and fled away on foot. The chariot was the man's whole identity, the reason a nation had lain down for twenty years, and he abandons it in a field and runs.

'And Barak pursued the chariots and the army to Harosheth-hagoyim, and all the army of Sisera fell by the edge of the sword; not a man was left.'

Barak does his part properly. Whatever was wrong with his faith in verse 8, there is nothing wrong with his pursuit; he chases them the whole way back to their own base and finishes it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sisera runs to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber, because there is peace between Jabin and that household (v. 17). She comes out to meet him — turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not be afraid — and covers him with a rug (v. 18). He asks for water and she gives him milk (v. 19), then posts him a sentry: if anyone asks, say no one is here (v. 20). While he lies fast asleep from weariness she takes a tent peg and a hammer, goes softly to him, and drives it through his temple into the ground (v. 21). When Barak arrives she goes out to meet him with the words the whole chapter has been building to (v. 22). God subdues Jabin, and Israel presses harder and harder until he is destroyed (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: Pitching tents was women's work in a nomadic household. Jael is not improvising with a strange object; she is using the tools of her own trade, which she handled every day and knew exactly how to swing.
verseByVerse.examples: The last two verses record something that has not happened anywhere else in this book: a job finished. Israel pressed harder and harder until they destroyed Jabin. Chapter 1 is a list of things left standing; this is the one enemy who is not left standing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: But Sisera fled away on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite. And Jael came out to meet Sisera and said to him, "Turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not be afraid." So he turned aside to her into the tent, and she covered him with a rug. And he said to her, "Please give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty." So she opened a skin of milk and gave him a drink and covered him. And he said to her, "Stand at the opening of the tent, and if any man comes and asks you, 'Is anyone here?' say, 'No.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But Sisera fled away on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.'

Now the parenthesis from verse 11 pays.

Sisera runs for the one place in the district where he has a treaty. Heber's household is at peace with Jabin, and a man on foot with an army behind him goes where he will not be handed over. His reasoning is sound and his information is correct.

'And Jael came out to meet Sisera and said to him, "Turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not be afraid." So he turned aside to her into the tent, and she covered him with a rug.'

She comes out to him. Everything she says is what an exhausted fugitive most wants to hear — my lord, twice turn aside, and do not be afraid — and the first thing she does is cover him up.

'And he said to her, "Please give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty." So she opened a skin of milk and gave him a drink and covered him.'

He asks for water. She gives him milk, which is warmer, heavier and more likely to send a worn-out man to sleep, and covers him a second time.

Every detail is more hospitable than what was asked for, and the hospitality is the trap. In that world a guest under a tent roof was under the host's protection absolutely; that is what Sisera is counting on and it is exactly why he does not watch her.

'And he said to her, "Stand at the opening of the tent, and if any man comes and asks you, 'Is anyone here?' say, 'No.'"'

His last recorded words are an order to lie for him, and they are the final proof of how completely he has misjudged the room. He posts her as his sentry. He puts the woman who is about to kill him between himself and the door, and goes to sleep.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jael the wife of Heber took a tent peg, and took a hammer in her hand. Then she went softly to him and drove the peg into his temple until it went down into the ground while he was lying fast asleep from weariness. So he died. And behold, as Barak was pursuing Sisera, Jael went out to meet him and said to him, "Come, and I will show you the man whom you are seeking." So he went in to her tent, and there lay Sisera dead, with the tent peg in his temple. So on that day God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan before the people of Israel. And the hand of the people of Israel pressed harder and harder against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But Jael the wife of Heber took a tent peg, and took a hammer in her hand. Then she went softly to him and drove the peg into his temple until it went down into the ground while he was lying fast asleep from weariness. So he died.'

Consider what is in her hands. A tent peg and a mallet are not weapons she has improvised; they are the tools of her trade. In a nomadic household the tents were pitched and struck by the women, and Jael had driven pegs into hard ground several times a month for her whole adult life.

She knows the weight of that hammer and how many strokes a peg takes. It is the most ordinary object in the camp, and she crosses the floor with it quietly and does what she has done a thousand times.

The commander of nine hundred chariots is killed in his sleep, in a tent, by a woman using domestic equipment, and the writer does not soften a syllable of it.

'And behold, as Barak was pursuing Sisera, Jael went out to meet him and said to him, "Come, and I will show you the man whom you are seeking." So he went in to her tent, and there lay Sisera dead, with the tent peg in his temple.'

Barak arrives at a run, still chasing, and a woman steps out of a tent and offers to show him what he is looking for.

Deborah's word in verse 9 is fulfilled in that sentence and Barak hears it land. He will get the victory in the record and the credit in Hebrews, and he will not get this. The general walks into a tent to find the war already over and somebody else's tools in the corpse.

'So on that day God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan before the people of Israel. And the hand of the people of Israel pressed harder and harder against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.'

The chapter signs off by naming the author of the whole thing, and it is not Barak, Deborah or Jael. God subdued Jabin.

Then a last sentence that is unlike anything else in this book. Israel pressed harder and harder until they destroyed Jabin.

Set that against chapter 1, where the refrain was did not drive out, seven times over, and against every other victory in Judges, which ends in a rest that wears off. Here, once, the work is carried through to the end. The king in the rebuilt city that Joshua had burned is finished, and Hazor is not mentioned again.

It took a woman under a palm tree who was already doing her job, a man who had to be sent for and asked why he was still at home, ten thousand men who walked off a hill onto chariot ground, a river that came down at the right hour, and a housewife with a mallet. God arranged every piece of it, including the tent that had been pitched near Kedesh for no stated reason eight verses earlier, and then took the credit in a single sentence at the end.

4.theology:
What is not faced grows. The iron chariots of 1:19 were an excuse that sounded practical at the time. Twenty years of cruelty and nine hundred chariots later, they are the thing the whole chapter is about — and the burned-out capital Israel did not occupy has a king in it again. Neither of those required a new decision by anybody. They are what happens to ground that is left.

A question, not a call. Barak is not being commissioned in verse 6; he is being asked why nothing has happened since he was. The problem in the north was never divine silence. And when he answers with a condition — I will go if you go — God does not withdraw the commission from a man who wants a crutch. He gives him the crutch, and quietly moves the honour.

The transaction reversed. In verse 2 the LORD sold Israel into Jabin's hand; in verse 9 the LORD will sell Sisera into a woman's hand. The same verb and the same seller. Israel's oppression and Israel's deliverance are two entries in one ledger kept by one person.

Ordinary equipment. The chapter's deliverance is carried by a woman already doing her job under a tree, a river doing what rivers do in spring, and a housewife with a mallet and a peg she had driven into hard ground a thousand times. Nothing in it was fetched in specially. And the last two verses record what happens nowhere else in Judges: Israel pressed harder and harder until they destroyed the enemy. One job, in the whole book, finished.
4.examples:
Then: A general sat at home with his orders while a woman held court under a palm tree and a foreign army ran the north. When he finally moved, he moved on condition, walked ten thousand men off a hill onto chariot ground, and arrived at the end of the chase to find the war already finished by somebody with a tent peg.

Now: Two questions. The first is Deborah's, and it is aimed at people who have already been told what to do: has not the LORD commanded you? A great deal of Christian paralysis is not waiting for guidance but sitting on it. The second is about the iron chariots — the thing you decided years ago was beyond reach. It has not stayed the size it was when you decided.

5.title: The Song of Deborah
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day:<sup>2</sup>"That the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly, bless the LORD!<sup>3</sup>"Hear, O kings; give ear, O princes; to the LORD I will sing; I will make melody to the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>4</sup>"LORD, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the region of Edom, the earth trembled and the heavens dropped, yes, the clouds dropped water.<sup>5</sup>The mountains quaked before the LORD, even Sinai before the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>6</sup>"In the days of Shamgar, son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were abandoned, and travelers kept to the byways.<sup>7</sup>The villagers ceased in Israel; they ceased to be until I arose; I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel.<sup>8</sup>When new gods were chosen, then war was in the gates. Was shield or spear to be seen among forty thousand in Israel?<sup>9</sup>My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless the LORD.<sup>10</sup>"Tell of it, you who ride on white donkeys, you who sit on rich carpets and you who walk by the way.<sup>11</sup>To the sound of musicians at the watering places, there they repeat the righteous triumphs of the LORD, the righteous triumphs of his villagers in Israel. "Then down to the gates marched the people of the LORD.<sup>12</sup>"Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, break out in a song! Arise, Barak, lead away your captives, O son of Abinoam.<sup>13</sup>Then down marched the remnant of the noble; the people of the LORD marched down for me against the mighty.<sup>14</sup>From Ephraim their root they marched down into the valley, following you, Benjamin, with your kinsmen; from Machir marched down the commanders, and from Zebulun those who bear the lieutenant's staff;<sup>15</sup>the princes of Issachar came with Deborah, and Issachar faithful to Barak; into the valley they rushed at his heels. Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.<sup>16</sup>Why did you sit still among the sheepfolds, to hear the whistling for the flocks? Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.<sup>17</sup>Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan; and Dan, why did he stay with the ships? Asher sat still at the coast of the sea, staying by his landings.<sup>18</sup>Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the field.<sup>19</sup>"The kings came, they fought; then fought the kings of Canaan, at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo; they got no spoils of silver.<sup>20</sup>From heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera.<sup>21</sup>The torrent Kishon swept them away, the ancient torrent, the torrent Kishon. March on, my soul, with might!<sup>22</sup>"Then loud beat the horses' hoofs with the galloping, galloping of his steeds.<sup>23</sup>"Curse Meroz, says the angel of the LORD, curse its inhabitants thoroughly, because they did not come to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty.<sup>24</sup>"Most blessed of women be Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, of tent-dwelling women most blessed.<sup>25</sup>He asked for water and she gave him milk; she brought him curds in a noble's bowl.<sup>26</sup>She sent her hand to the tent peg and her right hand to the workmen's mallet; she struck Sisera; she crushed his head; she shattered and pierced his temple.<sup>27</sup>Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still; between her feet he sank, he fell; where he sank, there he fell—dead.<sup>28</sup>"Out of the window she peered, the mother of Sisera wailed through the lattice: 'Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why tarry the hoofbeats of his chariots?'<sup>29</sup>Her wisest princesses answer, indeed, she answers herself,<sup>30</sup>'Have they not found and divided the spoil?— A womb or two for every man; spoil of dyed materials for Sisera, spoil of dyed materials embroidered, two pieces of dyed work embroidered for the neck as spoil?'<sup>31</sup>"So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might." And the land had rest for forty years.
5.overview:
They sang it on the day, with the bodies still in the valley — and the first thing the song blesses God for is not the victory but the volunteering: the leaders took the lead, the people offered themselves willingly (v. 2). After a chapter in which the general had to be sent for and asked why he was still at home, that is where the gratitude starts.

The poem then reaches back four hundred years, to the LORD marching north out of Seir with the earth trembling and the clouds dropping water (vv. 4-5), so that a skirmish in Galilee is filed as one more episode in the march from Sinai. And it describes the occupation in terms of roads: the highways empty, travellers on back lanes, the unwalled villages abandoned. Tyranny does not usually announce itself in massacres. It shrinks ordinary life until people stop going out.

The longest section is a muster roll, and it is uncomfortable reading. Six tribes marched down; Issachar rushed into the valley at Barak's heels. Reuben had great searchings of heart — said twice, before and after the picture of him sitting among the sheepfolds listening to the whistling for the flocks. Gilead had a river in the way, Dan had shipping, Asher had harbours. Not one of those is a wicked excuse.

Then the song says what chapter 4 left out: from heaven the stars fought... the torrent Kishon swept them away. And its harshest word is not for Canaan but for Meroz, cursed by the angel of the LORD for not coming — a place never mentioned again anywhere in Scripture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The God Who Marched from Seir
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deborah and Barak sing on the day itself (v. 1), and the first thing they bless God for is not the victory but the volunteering: the leaders took the lead, the people offered themselves willingly (v. 2). The song then reaches back past this battle to Sinai — the LORD going out from Seir, the earth trembling, the clouds dropping water, the mountains quaking (vv. 4-5). Verses 6-8 paint what the occupation had been like: empty highways, travellers on the back roads, villages abandoned, and no shield or spear to be seen among forty thousand. Then the turn — until I arose as a mother in Israel (v. 7) — and a summons to every class in the country, rich on their white donkeys and poor on foot, to repeat the righteous triumphs of the LORD (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The song frames a local skirmish in Galilee as one more episode in the march that began at Sinai. Whatever happened by the Kishon that afternoon, the poem says it was the same God arriving, and the mountains have shaken before.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 states the causation the narrative left implicit: when new gods were chosen, then war was in the gates. The disarmament and the empty roads are not bad luck and not merely politics. Something was chosen, and this followed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day: "That the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly, bless the LORD! "Hear, O kings; give ear, O princes; to the LORD I will sing; I will make melody to the LORD, the God of Israel. "LORD, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the region of Edom, the earth trembled and the heavens dropped, yes, the clouds dropped water. The mountains quaked before the LORD, even Sinai before the LORD, the God of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day: "That the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly, bless the LORD!"'

They sing on the day. Not at the anniversary, not once the dust settled and somebody had time to compose properly — on the day itself, with the bodies still in the valley.

The first thing the song blesses God for is not the victory. It is the volunteering: the leaders took the lead, the people offered themselves willingly. After a chapter in which a general had to be sent for and asked why he was still at home, the poem's opening note of gratitude is that people finally came.

That theme brackets the whole song. It is here in verse 2 and again in verse 9, and everything between is a list of who did and who did not.

'"Hear, O kings; give ear, O princes; to the LORD I will sing; I will make melody to the LORD, the God of Israel."'

The audience summoned is not Israel. It is kings and princes — the class of person who has just been beaten. Deborah sings this at the rulers of the region, and the content is a description of what happens to armies that come against her God.

'"LORD, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the region of Edom, the earth trembled and the heavens dropped, yes, the clouds dropped water. The mountains quaked before the LORD, even Sinai before the LORD, the God of Israel."'

Before saying a word about Sisera, the song goes back four hundred years.

Seir and Edom are the country south of the Dead Sea, on the road up from Sinai. What is being described is the LORD marching north out of the desert with the earth shaking under him — the language of the exodus generation, of the mountain that smoked and the ground that could not hold still.

The poetic move is the whole argument of the song. A skirmish in Galilee is not being reported as a local success. It is being filed as one more episode in a march that started at Sinai, and the same weather is mentioned in both: the clouds dropped water. What is about to destroy Sisera's chariots is a storm, and the song has already told the reader who is walking in it.

verseByVerse.quote: "In the days of Shamgar, son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were abandoned, and travelers kept to the byways. The villagers ceased in Israel; they ceased to be until I arose; I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel. When new gods were chosen, then war was in the gates. Was shield or spear to be seen among forty thousand in Israel? My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless the LORD. "Tell of it, you who ride on white donkeys, you who sit on rich carpets and you who walk by the way. To the sound of musicians at the watering places, there they repeat the righteous triumphs of the LORD, the righteous triumphs of his villagers in Israel. "Then down to the gates marched the people of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"In the days of Shamgar, son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were abandoned, and travelers kept to the byways. The villagers ceased in Israel; they ceased to be."'

Here is what twenty years of occupation looked like from ground level, and the song describes it in terms of roads.

The highways were empty. Nobody used the main routes, because the main routes were where you were robbed, so traffic moved on tracks and back lanes. Trade slowed to the pace of people travelling scared.

Then the second detail, and it is worse: the villagers ceased. The unwalled settlements emptied. Farming families gave up the open country and moved into towns with gates, which meant the fields went out of cultivation and the nation began quietly starving in its own land.

That is what tyranny does. It does not usually announce itself in massacres; it shrinks ordinary life until people stop going out.

'"until I arose; I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel."'

The turn comes in four words, and the title she gives herself is not judge, prophetess or commander. A mother in Israel.

It is exactly right for what she did. She did not lead an army; she sent for a man who should have gone already, went with him when he would not go alone, and told him when to move. The country was rescued by somebody behaving like a mother to it.

'"When new gods were chosen, then war was in the gates. Was shield or spear to be seen among forty thousand in Israel?"'

Verse 8 states the causation the prose never quite spelled out. New gods were chosen, and then war came to the gates. The idolatry was not a religious matter running alongside a political one; it was the reason the roads emptied.

And the second half is a rhetorical question with a terrible answer. Forty thousand men in Israel, and not a shield or a spear among them — a nation systematically disarmed by its occupiers, exactly as the Philistines will later keep Israel without a blacksmith (1 Sam. 13:19-22).

'"Tell of it, you who ride on white donkeys, you who sit on rich carpets and you who walk by the way... there they repeat the righteous triumphs of the LORD."'

Then the summons to remember, and it is aimed at everybody. The people on white donkeys are the wealthy; the people walking are everyone else; and both are told to talk about this at the watering places, where villagers meet every day.

The song is arranging its own retelling. Verse 11 is what chapter 2 said had stopped happening.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song rouses itself — awake, awake, Deborah — and turns to the roll call (v. 12). Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir and Zebulun march down; the princes of Issachar come with Deborah and rush into the valley at Barak's heels (vv. 13-15a). Then the absentees, each with a reason: Reuben sat among the sheepfolds with great searchings of heart, twice repeated (vv. 15b-16); Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan; Dan stayed with the ships; Asher sat still at his landings (v. 17). And then the summit of the praise: Zebulun and Naphtali risked their lives to the death on the heights of the field (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Every excuse in the list is a livelihood. Sheep, distance, shipping, harbours — none of it is cowardice on the face of it, and all of it amounts to the same thing. The song does not accuse the absent tribes of treachery. It simply names what they were doing instead.
verseByVerse.examples: Reuben's phrase is repeated because it deserves to be. Great searchings of heart is not indifference; it is earnest, prolonged, agonised deliberation. Reuben took the matter extremely seriously and stayed at home.

verseByVerse.quote: "Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, break out in a song! Arise, Barak, lead away your captives, O son of Abinoam. Then down marched the remnant of the noble; the people of the LORD marched down for me against the mighty. From Ephraim their root they marched down into the valley, following you, Benjamin, with your kinsmen; from Machir marched down the commanders, and from Zebulun those who bear the lieutenant's staff; the princes of Issachar came with Deborah, and Issachar faithful to Barak; into the valley they rushed at his heels. Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart. Why did you sit still among the sheepfolds, to hear the whistling for the flocks? Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart. Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan; and Dan, why did he stay with the ships? Asher sat still at the coast of the sea, staying by his landings. Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, break out in a song! Arise, Barak, lead away your captives, O son of Abinoam."'

The song shakes itself and turns to the muster roll, which is the longest section of the poem and the most uncomfortable.

'"From Ephraim their root they marched down into the valley, following you, Benjamin, with your kinsmen; from Machir marched down the commanders, and from Zebulun those who bear the lieutenant's staff; the princes of Issachar came with Deborah."'

Six names come first, and the verbs are all of movement: marched down, came, rushed at his heels. Issachar is described as rushing into the valley — not summoned, not dragged, but running downhill towards nine hundred chariots.

'"Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart. Why did you sit still among the sheepfolds, to hear the whistling for the flocks? Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart."'

Then the absentees, and the song's treatment of Reuben is the sharpest thing in it.

He is not accused of cowardice, treachery or indifference. What he is charged with is great searchings of heart — and the phrase is repeated, before and after the question, so that the reader cannot miss it.

Reuben thought about it. Seriously, at length, with real feeling. There were meetings. The matter was weighed from every side, and there is no suggestion that the deliberation was insincere.

The picture between the two repetitions is devastating in its ordinariness: sitting among the sheepfolds, listening to the whistling for the flocks. That is a man staying within earshot of his own livelihood while the decision goes on inside him.

'"Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan; and Dan, why did he stay with the ships? Asher sat still at the coast of the sea, staying by his landings."'

The other three are given no motive at all beyond their occupations. Gilead has a river in the way. Dan has shipping. Asher has harbours and stays by his landings.

Not one of these is a wicked excuse. They are the reasons anybody would give: distance, business, responsibilities that do not pause because somebody else is in trouble. The song simply records what each tribe was doing at the time, and lets the list stand next to the next verse.

'"Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the field."'

These are the two tribes Barak mustered in 4:6, and they are given the highest line in the song. Risked their lives to the death, on the exposed high ground where the chariots could reach them.

Set the two halves of the roll call side by side, because that is what the poem is for. Reuben, deliberating within earshot of the sheep. Zebulun, on the heights of the field.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–23 — From Heaven the Stars Fought
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kings of Canaan came and fought at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo, and they got no spoils of silver (v. 19). Then the two lines that explain chapter 4: from heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera, and the torrent Kishon swept them away, the ancient torrent (vv. 20-21). The horses' hooves beat in flight (v. 22). And the song's harshest word is not for the Canaanites at all: the angel of the LORD curses Meroz, thoroughly, because they did not come to the help of the LORD (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Chapter 4 said only that the LORD routed Sisera. The song says how: the river came down. Nine hundred iron chariots on a flooded plain stopped being the reason Israel was afraid and became nine hundred very heavy objects that could not move.
