Three hundred trumpets in the night sound like three hundred companies, because a trumpet belonged to a unit commander; three hundred torches appearing at once look like an army that has already surrounded the camp. The Midianites are not defeated by the three hundred. They are defeated by what they concluded about them.

verseByVerse.quote: And he divided the 300 men into three companies and put trumpets into the hands of all of them and empty jars, with torches inside the jars. And he said to them, "Look at me, and do likewise. When I come to the outskirts of the camp, do as I do. When I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me, then blow the trumpets also on every side of all the camp and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And he divided the 300 men into three companies and put trumpets into the hands of all of them and empty jars, with torches inside the jars.'

Now the equipment, and it repays counting on the fingers.

Each man gets a trumpet. Each man gets an empty jar. Inside each jar, a lit torch, which is what the jar is for — a clay pot over a flame hides it completely until the pot is broken.

That is two hands, and there is nothing in either of them that can hurt anybody. No sword is issued to the three hundred. The men are going into a night attack on a valley full of raiders carrying a musical instrument and a pot.

'And he said to them, "Look at me, and do likewise. When I come to the outskirts of the camp, do as I do. When I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me, then blow the trumpets also on every side of all the camp and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon.'"'

The whole battle order is four words long: look at me, and do likewise.

There is no strategy to memorise and no contingency. Three companies take up positions on three sides of a sleeping army in the dark, and every man watches one man on a hillside and copies him.

Hear the shout as it stands, because it names the arrangement exactly: for the LORD and for Gideon. Not for Israel, not for the tribes, and not for freedom. A God and a farmer, in that order.

verseByVerse.quote: So Gideon and the hundred men who were with him came to the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, when they had just set the watch. And they blew the trumpets and smashed the jars that were in their hands. Then the three companies blew the trumpets and broke the jars. They held in their left hands the torches, and in their right hands the trumpets to blow. And they cried out, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!" Every man stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran. They cried out and fled. When they blew the 300 trumpets, the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade and against all the army. And the army fled as far as Beth-shittah toward Zererah, as far as the border of Abel-meholah, by Tabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Gideon and the hundred men who were with him came to the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, when they had just set the watch. And they blew the trumpets and smashed the jars that were in their hands.'

The timing is professional. The middle watch begins around ten at night, and Gideon moves at the changeover — the moment when the new sentries are settling in, their eyes are not yet adjusted, and the men coming off duty are heading for their blankets.

Then three hundred trumpets, and three hundred clay pots smashed at once.

'Then the three companies blew the trumpets and broke the jars. They held in their left hands the torches, and in their right hands the trumpets to blow. And they cried out, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!"'

The writer takes the trouble to tell us what is in each hand, and the arithmetic of it is the point: torches on the left, trumpets on the right, and no third hand for the sword they are shouting about.

Consider what this looks like from inside the camp. A man wakes in the dark to trumpets on three sides at once — and in that world a trumpet belonged to the commander of a unit, so three hundred horns means three hundred companies. At the same instant, three hundred flames appear in a ring where a moment ago there was nothing. And a war cry announcing a sword.

Nobody in that valley sees three hundred men. Everybody in it hears an army that has already surrounded them.

'Every man stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran. They cried out and fled.'

Verse 21 is the sentence to hold on to. Every man stood in his place around the camp. The three hundred do not charge, do not advance, do not engage. They stand still, holding a light and making a noise, and the enemy disintegrates in front of them.

'When they blew the 300 trumpets, the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade and against all the army.'

Here is what actually killed the Midianites: each other, in the dark, in a panic, unable to tell friend from enemy.

The subject of the verb is God. The LORD set every man's sword against his comrade. Verse 2 said the army had to be small enough that Israel could not claim the credit, and the final arrangement removes even the sword. Three hundred men with pots and horns stood still, and the enemy destroyed itself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the tribes are called out — Naphtali, Asher and all Manasseh — and they pursue (v. 23). Gideon sends to Ephraim to seize the water crossings as far as the Jordan, cutting the retreat (v. 24). Two princes of Midian are taken and killed at places that keep their names, the rock of Oreb and the winepress of Zeeb, and their heads are brought to Gideon across the Jordan (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The men who were sent home get the pursuit. The three hundred did the part that could only be credited to God, and the rest of Israel does the ordinary work of finishing a rout — which is real work, and is not despised.
verseByVerse.examples: Zeeb dies at a winepress. Gideon met the angel of the LORD threshing wheat in one, hiding from these very people. The book does not comment on it and does not need to.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali and from Asher and from all Manasseh, and they pursued after Midian. Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, "Come down against the Midianites and capture the waters against them, as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan." So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they captured the waters as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan. And they captured the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the winepress of Zeeb. Then they pursued Midian, and they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon across the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali and from Asher and from all Manasseh, and they pursued after Midian.'

Now the rest of Israel is recalled — including, presumably, a good many of the twenty-two thousand who had gone home admitting they were afraid.

There is something generous in the arrangement. The part of the work that could only ever be credited to God was done by three hundred men holding crockery. The pursuit, which is ordinary soldiering and takes days, is given back to the tribes.

God arranged an unmistakable miracle and then handed the follow-up to normal people doing normal work, and the second half is not despised in the telling.

'Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, "Come down against the Midianites and capture the waters against them, as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan."'

Gideon's own generalship is sound. He sends to Ephraim to seize the fords before the fleeing army reaches them, exactly as Ehud had done at the same river, and the retreat is closed.

'And they captured the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the winepress of Zeeb.'

Two enemy princes are taken and killed, and the places keep their names afterwards, which is how a country remembers a night like this.

The second location is worth a moment. Zeeb dies at a winepress.

The last winepress in this story had a young man crouched in it, threshing wheat where the wind could not reach, hiding a few bushels from the very people this prince commanded. The Midianites are now dying in one.

The book makes nothing of it, and there is nothing to make. God took a man out of a pit, gave him back his own name as a nickname daring a dead god to answer, reduced his army by ninety-nine per cent so that nobody could get the story wrong, sent him to overhear a stranger's dream about a barley loaf, and had him stand still in the dark holding a jar while the valley emptied.

Isaiah, seven hundred years later, was still using this night as shorthand for what God does to an oppressor: the rod of his oppressor you have broken as on the day of Midian (Isa. 9:4) — and the verses on either side of it are about a light shining on people who walked in darkness, and a child who is born.

7.theology:
An explanation, not just a victory. Verse 2 gives the reason for every reduction that follows, and it is theological rather than military. God will not win this in a way that leaves room for my own hand has saved me. The arithmetic runs from thirty-two thousand to three hundred to a battle in which nobody on Israel's side draws a sword at all.

God works with the fear rather than against it. The offer in verse 10 is unprompted and conditional: if you are afraid, take Purah. There is no rebuke in it and no requirement to pretend. Gideon accepts, goes down, hears what he needs and worships in the dark. What finally strengthened him was not another sign from heaven but a stranger's nightmare, and God had it waiting.

Standing still. The three hundred hold a torch in the left hand and a trumpet in the right, and verse 21 says every man stood in his place around the camp. They do not charge. The enemy is destroyed by what it concludes in the dark, and the writer names the agent: the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade.

The night of Midian. Seven centuries later Isaiah is still using this as the standard picture of God breaking an oppressor — the rod of his oppressor you have broken as on the day of Midian (Isa. 9:4) — and the verses around it are about light shining on people who walked in darkness, and a child who is born to us.
7.examples:
Then: An army of thirty-two thousand was cut to three hundred on purpose, and the three hundred were sent into a night attack carrying a pot and a horn. They stood still in a ring around a sleeping valley, broke the pots, and watched an army kill itself in the dark.

Now: Verse 10 is the one to keep. Notice what God does with a frightened man who has already been given more assurance than most people get in a lifetime: he does not shame him, does not withdraw the commission, and does not tell him to feel differently. He offers him a companion for the walk down. If you are waiting to stop being afraid before you go, this is a chapter about a man who went with somebody else beside him.

8.title: Gideon's Failure
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the men of Ephraim said to him, "What is this that you have done to us, not to call us when you went to fight against Midian?" And they accused him fiercely.<sup>2</sup>And he said to them, "What have I done now in comparison with you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer?<sup>3</sup>God has given into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. What have I been able to do in comparison with you?" Then their anger against him subsided when he said this.<sup>4</sup>And Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the 300 men who were with him, exhausted yet pursuing.<sup>5</sup>So he said to the men of Succoth, "Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me, for they are exhausted, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian."<sup>6</sup>And the officials of Succoth said, "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?"<sup>7</sup>So Gideon said, "Well then, when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will flail your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers."<sup>8</sup>And from there he went up to Penuel, and spoke to them in the same way, and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered.<sup>9</sup>And he said to the men of Penuel, "When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower."<sup>10</sup>Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their army, about 15,000 men, all who were left of all the army of the people of the East, for there had fallen 120,000 men who drew the sword.<sup>11</sup>And Gideon went up by the way of the tent dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah and attacked the army, for the army felt secure.<sup>12</sup>And Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and he pursued them and captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and he threw all the army into a panic.<sup>13</sup>Then Gideon the son of Joash returned from the battle by the ascent of Heres.<sup>14</sup>And he captured a young man of Succoth and questioned him. And he wrote down for him the officials and elders of Succoth, seventy-seven men.<sup>15</sup>And he came to the men of Succoth and said, "Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, 'Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your men who are exhausted?'"<sup>16</sup>And he took the elders of the city, and he took thorns of the wilderness and briers and with them taught the men of Succoth a lesson.<sup>17</sup>And he broke down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.<sup>18</sup>Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, "Where are the men whom you killed at Tabor?" They answered, "As you are, so were they. Every one of them resembled the son of a king."<sup>19</sup>And he said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the LORD lives, if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you."<sup>20</sup>So he said to Jether his firstborn, "Rise and kill them!" But the young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a young man.<sup>21</sup>Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, "Rise yourself and fall upon us, for as the man is, so is his strength." And Gideon arose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and he took the crescent ornaments that were on the necks of their camels.<sup>22</sup>Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian."<sup>23</sup>Gideon said to them, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you."<sup>24</sup>And Gideon said to them, "Let me make a request of you: every one of you give me the earrings from his spoil." (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.)<sup>25</sup>And they answered, "We will willingly give them." And they spread a cloak, and every man threw in it the earrings of his spoil.<sup>26</sup>And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was 1,700 shekels of gold, besides the crescent ornaments and the pendants and the purple garments worn by the kings of Midian, and besides the collars that were around the necks of their camels.<sup>27</sup>And Gideon made an ephod of it and put it in his city, in Ophrah. And all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.<sup>28</sup>So Midian was subdued before the people of Israel, and they raised their heads no more. And the land had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon.<sup>29</sup>Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and lived in his own house.<sup>30</sup>Now Gideon had seventy sons, his own offspring, for he had many wives.<sup>31</sup>And his concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he called his name Abimelech.<sup>32</sup>And Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age and was buried in the tomb of Joash his father, at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.<sup>33</sup>As soon as Gideon died, the people of Israel turned again and whored after the Baals and made Baal-berith their god.<sup>34</sup>And the people of Israel did not remember the LORD their God, who had delivered them from the hand of all their enemies on every side,<sup>35</sup>and they did not show steadfast love to the family of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) in return for all the good that he had done to Israel.
8.overview:
The victory is won and the chapter that follows is about what winning did to the man. It opens with Ephraim furious about credit rather than about Midian, and Gideon handling them with skilled flattery — and the scene stays with you, because the same tribe brings the identical complaint to Jephthah in chapter 12, and that time forty-two thousand men die.

Then four words that describe the Christian life better than most sermons: the three hundred cross the Jordan exhausted yet pursuing. Two Israelite towns refuse them bread, for a perfectly rational reason — if this fails, Midian will be back and will know who fed the raiders. Gideon promises to come back and flail them with thorns, and does: seventy-seven names written out by a frightened boy, and a town's men killed at Penuel, over a meal.

Verse 19 then reorganises the whole pursuit. The kings had killed his brothers at Tabor, and he says so: if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you. There has been a private account running under the national deliverance.

And the chapter's spine is two consecutive sentences. I will not rule over you... the LORD will rule over you (v. 23) — the finest thing he ever says. And then: let me make a request of you: give me the gold (v. 24). He refuses the crown and takes the treasury, makes a priestly ephod out of it, sets it up in his own town, and Israel whores after it. Then seventy sons, many wives, and a boy in Shechem named Abimelech — my father is king.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim arrives furious, and the grievance is not that Midian oppressed them but that they were not called to the fight: what is this that you have done to us, not to call us? (v. 1). Gideon answers with flattery — is not the gleaning of Ephraim's grapes better than the whole vintage of my clan? — and credits them with capturing Oreb and Zeeb (vv. 2-3). Their anger subsides.
verseByVerse.theology: The quarrel is about credit, arriving after the danger has passed. Nobody from Ephraim was at the spring of Harod when there were thirty-two thousand men and God said there were too many.
verseByVerse.examples: Keep this scene. The same tribe will bring the identical complaint to Jephthah in chapter 12, almost word for word — and that time nobody answers softly, and forty-two thousand Ephraimites die at the fords of the Jordan (12:1-6).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men of Ephraim said to him, "What is this that you have done to us, not to call us when you went to fight against Midian?" And they accused him fiercely. And he said to them, "What have I done now in comparison with you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer? God has given into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. What have I been able to do in comparison with you?" Then their anger against him subsided when he said this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the men of Ephraim said to him, "What is this that you have done to us, not to call us when you went to fight against Midian?" And they accused him fiercely.'

The fighting is over and the first thing that happens is a row about credit.

Look at the grievance carefully, because it is not what it pretends to be. Ephraim is not angry that Midian ate the harvest for seven years, or that nobody stopped it. They are angry that they were not invited to the part with the glory in it.

Their timing is exact. They arrive after the battle, after the rout, after the two princes are dead — and nobody from Ephraim was at the spring of Harod on the morning when there were thirty-two thousand men on the hill and God said there were too many.

'And he said to them, "What have I done now in comparison with you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer? God has given into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb."'

Gideon's answer is a piece of skilled flattery, and it works.

The image is from the vineyard. What Ephraim picked up off the ground after the harvest — the gleanings, the leftovers — is worth more than my whole clan's vintage. He is saying that their share of the mopping-up was greater than his share of the victory, which is not true and is exactly what they want to hear.

'Then their anger against him subsided when he said this.'

Six words, and they are the reason to keep this scene in mind.

The proverb says that a soft answer turns away wrath, and a harsh word stirs up anger (Prov. 15:1). Here is the soft answer, doing its work on men who came looking for a fight over nothing.

Mark it now, because the identical scene happens again four chapters later. Ephraim comes to Jephthah with the same complaint in almost the same words — why did you cross over to fight against the Ammonites and did not call us? — and that time there is no soft answer, and forty-two thousand men of Ephraim die at the fords of the Jordan (12:1-6).

The same tribe, the same grudge, the same wounded pride about not being asked. The difference between a quarrel and a massacre was one man's willingness to let somebody else be flattered.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gideon crosses the Jordan with his three hundred, exhausted yet pursuing (v. 4), and asks the Israelite town of Succoth for bread. They refuse, and their reason is a sneer with arithmetic in it: are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand (vv. 5-6)? Gideon promises to come back and flail them with thorns (v. 7). Penuel answers the same way and is promised a demolished tower (vv. 8-9). Then the raid: fifteen thousand are left of a hundred and thirty-five thousand, camped and feeling secure, and Gideon comes in by the desert road and takes both kings (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Succoth and Penuel are not Midianite towns. They are Israel, on the east bank, refusing food to Israelite soldiers chasing Israel's enemy — and their calculation is perfectly rational: if this fails, Midian will still be here and we will have fed the losing side.
verseByVerse.examples: The four words in verse 4 are the best description of the Christian life in the book. Exhausted yet pursuing. Not fresh, not confident, not winning gloriously; worn out, and still going after it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the 300 men who were with him, exhausted yet pursuing. So he said to the men of Succoth, "Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me, for they are exhausted, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian." And the officials of Succoth said, "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?" So Gideon said, "Well then, when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will flail your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers." And from there he went up to Penuel, and spoke to them in the same way, and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered. And he said to the men of Penuel, "When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the 300 men who were with him, exhausted yet pursuing.'

Carry four words of that verse about with you: exhausted yet pursuing.

The night attack is over and the three hundred are still going. They have been awake since before the middle watch, they have run a valley, crossed a river, and they are following two kings into the desert on empty stomachs.

It is as good a description of ordinary Christian perseverance as the Bible contains. Not fresh, not visibly winning, not enjoying it — worn out, and not stopping.

'So he said to the men of Succoth, "Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me, for they are exhausted, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian."'

He asks his own countrymen for bread. Succoth is an Israelite town on the east bank, and the request is modest and polite: loaves, for tired men, who are chasing the enemy of the whole nation.

'And the officials of Succoth said, "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?"'

The refusal is a sneer, and underneath the sneer is a calculation that is entirely rational.

Succoth sits east of the Jordan, exposed, on the Midianite side of the river. If Gideon succeeds, they have lost a few loaves. If he fails — and he has three hundred exhausted men and the kings are still at large — then Midian is back next harvest and will know exactly which towns fed the raiding party.

So they wait to see. Their sentence has a governing word in it: already. Come back when it is settled and we will know what to do.

That is the oldest form of practical unbelief there is. Not a denial that God can do it, but a refusal to be committed until the outcome is safe — and it is called prudence by everyone who practises it.

'So Gideon said, "Well then, when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will flail your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers." And from there he went up to Penuel... And he said to the men of Penuel, "When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower."'

And here the chapter turns, and it turns in Gideon.

Mark that his faith is intact: when the LORD has given. He has no doubt about the outcome now. What has entered is something else — a promise of torture, delivered to fellow Israelites, over bread.

The man who would not tear down an altar by daylight because he was afraid of the town is now threatening to flay two towns for insulting him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their army, about 15,000 men, all who were left of all the army of the people of the East, for there had fallen 120,000 men who drew the sword. And Gideon went up by the way of the tent dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah and attacked the army, for the army felt secure. And Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and he pursued them and captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and he threw all the army into a panic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their army, about 15,000 men, all who were left of all the army of the people of the East, for there had fallen 120,000 men who drew the sword.'

The arithmetic of the night in the valley is given here for the first time. A hundred and twenty thousand dead; fifteen thousand left.

Fifteen thousand is still fifty times the size of Gideon's force, and it is what remains after the disaster. The three hundred are pursuing an army that could still destroy them without difficulty if it turned round and looked.

'And Gideon went up by the way of the tent dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah and attacked the army, for the army felt secure.'

He takes the caravan route round to the east and comes at them from the desert side, which is the direction nobody watches, and the narrator gives the reason it worked in four words: the army felt secure.

They had put enough distance between themselves and the Jezreel valley to relax. Nobody chases a beaten army that far on foot; it is not done, and it is why it worked.

'And Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and he pursued them and captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and he threw all the army into a panic.'

Both kings are taken alive. The chapter has been building to that, and it will turn out in a few verses that Gideon had his own reasons for wanting them alive rather than dead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — What He Did on the Way Back
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gideon returns and keeps both promises. He catches a young man of Succoth who writes out the names of seventy-seven officials, and then works through the list with desert thorns (vv. 13-16). At Penuel he pulls down the tower and kills the men of the city (v. 17). Then he turns to the two captured kings and asks about the men they killed at Tabor, and the answer explains a great deal: they were my brothers, the sons of my mother (vv. 18-19). He orders his eldest son, still a boy, to execute them; the boy is too frightened to draw (v. 20), and Gideon does it himself and takes the gold crescents off the camels' necks (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 19 changes the shape of the whole pursuit. If you had saved them alive, I would not kill you. There has been a private account running underneath the national deliverance, and the man settling it is the judge.
verseByVerse.examples: Ordering a boy to kill two kings is a calculated humiliation — to die at a child's hand was the worst end a soldier could have. The child cannot do it. Whatever else verse 20 records, it is a father asking his son to become something, and the son refusing out of fear.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Gideon the son of Joash returned from the battle by the ascent of Heres. And he captured a young man of Succoth and questioned him. And he wrote down for him the officials and elders of Succoth, seventy-seven men. And he came to the men of Succoth and said, "Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, 'Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your men who are exhausted?'" And he took the elders of the city, and he took thorns of the wilderness and briers and with them taught the men of Succoth a lesson. And he broke down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And he captured a young man of Succoth and questioned him. And he wrote down for him the officials and elders of Succoth, seventy-seven men.'

He comes back, and the first thing he does is compile a list.

The detail is chilling in its ordinariness. He grabs a boy from the town, questions him, and the boy writes out seventy-seven names — every official and elder in Succoth. It is a literate young man doing clerical work under duress, and what he produces is an execution list.

'And he came to the men of Succoth and said, "Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, 'Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your men who are exhausted?'"'

He quotes their own sentence back at them with the kings standing there.

'And he took the elders of the city, and he took thorns of the wilderness and briers and with them taught the men of Succoth a lesson. And he broke down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.'

Two verses, and both promises are kept.

Desert thorns are not a figure of speech; this is torture, methodically applied to seventy-seven named men who had refused a meal. And at Penuel the tower comes down and the men of the city are killed — Israelites, killed by Israel's judge, for declining to feed his soldiers.

The book records it without comment, and the absence of comment is not approval. This is the same narrator who told us Gideon was afraid to pull down an altar by day, and who will shortly tell us the ephod became a snare. He is showing us a man, and the man is coming apart.

Set the two halves of Gideon side by side. In chapter 6 he says my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. In chapter 8 he tortures seventy-seven elders and destroys a town for wounding his dignity.

What changed between those two chapters was not his theology. It was that he won.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, "Where are the men whom you killed at Tabor?" They answered, "As you are, so were they. Every one of them resembled the son of a king." And he said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the LORD lives, if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you." So he said to Jether his firstborn, "Rise and kill them!" But the young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a young man. Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, "Rise yourself and fall upon us, for as the man is, so is his strength." And Gideon arose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and he took the crescent ornaments that were on the necks of their camels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, "Where are the men whom you killed at Tabor?" They answered, "As you are, so were they. Every one of them resembled the son of a king."'

A question comes out of nowhere, about an incident the book has never mentioned, and the answer is a piece of flattery from two men in chains: they looked like you. They looked like princes.

'And he said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the LORD lives, if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you."'

Here is the sentence that reorganises the whole pursuit.

Gideon's brothers — his full brothers, the sons of his own mother — had been killed by these two men at Tabor, and he has said nothing about it until now. And then the admission: if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you.

The execution of the Midianite kings is not, in this moment, an act of national deliverance. It is a blood feud, and he says so out loud. Somewhere under the trumpets and the torches and a sword for the LORD and for Gideon, there has been a private account running, and it is being settled now.

None of that makes the deliverance false. God did give Midian into his hand, and the barley loaf did flatten the tent. But the man God used had reasons of his own, and the book is honest enough to let us hear one of them.

'So he said to Jether his firstborn, "Rise and kill them!" But the young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a young man.'

Then he tells his eldest boy to do it.

This is a deliberate humiliation of the prisoners — to be executed by a child was the most degrading death available to a soldier — and it is being arranged by a father for his son to carry out.

The boy cannot. The text says why, plainly and without contempt: he was afraid, because he was still a young man.

There is a terrible echo in that line. The last person in this story who could not do something because he was afraid was Gideon himself, pulling down an altar at night. God met that fear with patience, a companion and a plan. Gideon meets his son's fear by handing the job to somebody else in front of everybody.

'Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, "Rise yourself and fall upon us, for as the man is, so is his strength." And Gideon arose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and he took the crescent ornaments that were on the necks of their camels.'

The kings ask him to do it himself, and he does. And then the last clause of the verse, which the narrator has put there on purpose: he took the gold off their camels.

Keep that detail. It is about to matter a great deal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — The Crown Refused and the Gold Requested
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel offers Gideon a dynasty: rule over us, you and your son and your grandson (v. 22). His answer is the best thing he ever says — I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you (v. 23). And then, in the next breath, a request: give me the earrings from your spoil (v. 24). They give willingly; the weight comes to seventeen hundred shekels of gold, besides the crescents, pendants and purple (vv. 25-26). He makes an ephod of it and sets it up in his own town, and all Israel whores after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 23 and verse 24 are consecutive sentences from the same mouth. He refuses the crown on impeccable theological grounds and asks for the treasury in the following breath, and there is no indication that he noticed any tension between them.
verseByVerse.examples: An ephod was a priest's garment. Gideon declines to be king and quietly sets himself up as a sanctuary in his own home town, and the word the narrator uses for the result is the word God used at Bochim: their gods shall be a snare to you (2:3). This one is made in Israel, out of the spoils of a victory God gave.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian." Gideon said to them, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian."'

Israel offers him a crown, and notice that they offer him three generations of it. This is not gratitude; it is a constitutional proposal. They want a dynasty, and they want it for the reason nations always want one: somebody delivered them and they would like the arrangement to be permanent.

It is also the exact error the whole book has been diagnosing. Every rest in Judges ends when the judge dies, and Israel's solution is not to hold on to God but to make the deliverer hereditary.

'Gideon said to them, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you."'

This is the finest sentence Gideon ever speaks.

He refuses all three generations, one at a time, and gives the reason without any softening: the LORD will rule over you. Israel has a king already, and the offer is not a compliment but a substitution.

It is theologically exact. Centuries later, when the nation finally demands a king so that they can be like the other nations, God tells Samuel what is really happening: they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them (1 Sam. 8:7). Gideon saw it clearly, in one sentence, standing in front of the men making the offer.

Whatever comes next, he said this, and he meant it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon said to them, "Let me make a request of you: every one of you give me the earrings from his spoil." (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.) And they answered, "We will willingly give them." And they spread a cloak, and every man threw in it the earrings of his spoil. And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was 1,700 shekels of gold, besides the crescent ornaments and the pendants and the purple garments worn by the kings of Midian, and besides the collars that were around the necks of their camels. And Gideon made an ephod of it and put it in his city, in Ophrah. And all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Gideon said to them, "Let me make a request of you: every one of you give me the earrings from his spoil."'

This is the next sentence out of the same mouth.

Read verses 23 and 24 together, because they are consecutive and nothing separates them. I will not rule over you... the LORD will rule over you. Let me make a request of you: give me the gold.

He declines the crown and asks for the treasury, and there is no sign in the text that he noticed any distance between the two.

'And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was 1,700 shekels of gold, besides the crescent ornaments and the pendants and the purple garments worn by the kings of Midian, and besides the collars that were around the necks of their camels.'

Seventeen hundred shekels is something over forty pounds of gold, and that is only the earrings. The list goes on: the crescents, the pendants, the purple — royal cloth, the most expensive dye in the ancient world — and the collars off the camels.

The man who would not be king now owns the wardrobe of two kings.

'And Gideon made an ephod of it and put it in his city, in Ophrah.'

Then he makes an ephod.

An ephod was a priest's garment. The high priest wore one, and attached to it was the breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim, by which Israel enquired of God. Whatever exactly Gideon made out of forty pounds of gold, it was a priestly object, and he set it up in his own home town.

So the shape of what he has done comes clear. He refused to be king and he made himself a shrine. The tabernacle was at Shiloh; the sanctioned way of enquiring of God was through the priesthood; and Ophrah now has a golden object made from the spoils of the deliverance, standing in the town of the man God used.

'And all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.'

The two verbs in that sentence are the two the book has been using all along.

Whored after is what Israel does with the Baals in 2:17. Snare is the word God used at Bochim about the gods of the nations he would no longer drive out: their gods shall be a snare to you (2:3).

Both words are now attached to a thing an Israelite judge made, out of the plunder of a victory God gave him, in the town where he had torn down an altar to Baal.

Gideon began by demolishing a false shrine at night because he was afraid, and ended by building one in daylight because he was asked for gold and did not refuse it. Nobody made him do it. He was never tempted by the crown. The snare came in through the one door he had left open.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Midian is subdued and the land has rest forty years (v. 28). Gideon goes home (v. 29), and the writer records what home was: seventy sons, because he had many wives (v. 30), and a concubine in Shechem who bore him a son he called Abimelech (v. 31). He dies in a good old age and is buried in his father's tomb (v. 32). As soon as he is dead Israel turns again and makes Baal-berith their god (v. 33), does not remember the LORD who delivered them (v. 34), and shows no loyalty to Gideon's family either (v. 35).
verseByVerse.theology: Seventy sons by many wives is not a private matter; it is a royal household. Gideon refused the title in verse 23 and then lived exactly like the thing he had refused to be called.
verseByVerse.examples: The name of the son in verse 31 is Abimelech, which means my father is king. Whatever was said out loud at the assembly, that is what was being said in the house — and the boy grows up to act on it in the next chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: So Midian was subdued before the people of Israel, and they raised their heads no more. And the land had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon. Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and lived in his own house. Now Gideon had seventy sons, his own offspring, for he had many wives. And his concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he called his name Abimelech. And Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age and was buried in the tomb of Joash his father, at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Midian was subdued before the people of Israel, and they raised their heads no more. And the land had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon.'

The formula closes the cycle properly. Midian is broken, permanently, and the land is quiet for forty years.

By the standard of this book that is a success, and it should be said before the rest. The raids stopped. A generation grew up who could plant a crop and eat it.

'Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and lived in his own house. Now Gideon had seventy sons, his own offspring, for he had many wives.'

Then the writer tells us what living in his own house looked like, and does it without a word of comment.

Seventy sons. Many wives. That is not a large family; it is a royal household. Keeping multiple wives at that scale required the income of a king, and the number of sons is precisely the currency of a dynasty — heirs, alliances, a name that cannot be extinguished.

He refused the crown in verse 23 and then lived exactly like the thing he had refused to be called. The title was declined and the life was adopted, which is a distinction that satisfies nobody but the man making it.

'And his concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he called his name Abimelech.'

Then the name.

Abimelech means my father is king.

Whatever Gideon said in public at the assembly, that is the sentence being carried round Shechem by a boy for the rest of his childhood. The son of a concubine in a town away from home, walking about with a name that announces a claim his father had formally refused.

He will spend the next chapter acting on it, and the first thing he does is kill the seventy sons of verse 30.

'And Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age and was buried in the tomb of Joash his father, at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.'

He dies old and full of years and is buried in his father's tomb — the same father whose altar he pulled down in the dark, and who defended him the next morning.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Gideon died, the people of Israel turned again and whored after the Baals and made Baal-berith their god. And the people of Israel did not remember the LORD their God, who had delivered them from the hand of all their enemies on every side, and they did not show steadfast love to the family of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) in return for all the good that he had done to Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'As soon as Gideon died, the people of Israel turned again and whored after the Baals and made Baal-berith their god.'

As soon as Gideon died. The trigger is a funeral, exactly as 2:19 said it always would be, and this time the narrator does not even leave a decent interval.

The god they choose has a name worth translating. Baal-berith means lord of the covenant, or Baal of the treaty. Israel is in a covenant already, with the God who brought them out of Egypt; they have gone and found a Baal who offers the same service.

'And the people of Israel did not remember the LORD their God, who had delivered them from the hand of all their enemies on every side.'

The verb is the ordinary one again, and by now it is the book's diagnosis: they did not remember. Not rejected, not argued with. Forgot — a nation that had watched three hundred men break jars in the dark.

'and they did not show steadfast love to the family of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) in return for all the good that he had done to Israel.'

The last verse of the chapter adds a second failure, and it is the human one.

The word is hesed — the loyal, covenant kindness that God shows his own people and expects them to show each other. They did not show it to Gideon's family.

The two failures belong together in one sentence for a reason. A people who stop remembering what God has done stop keeping faith with each other very shortly afterwards; the vertical and the horizontal go together, and the writer puts them in consecutive clauses.

This verse is the hinge into what follows. Seventy sons are living in Ophrah, a man named my father is king is living in Shechem, the town has just adopted a god called lord of the covenant, and nobody in Israel feels any obligation to the family of the man who saved them.

Everything needed for the next chapter is now in place, and every piece of it was assembled during forty years of rest.

8.theology:
What winning did to him. In chapter 6 Gideon says his clan is the weakest in Manasseh and he is the least in his father's house, and it is accurate. In chapter 8 he tortures seventy-seven elders and destroys an Israelite town for wounding his dignity. His theology has not changed — he still says when the LORD has given (v. 7). What changed is that he won, and the book records the second half of the man as carefully as the first.

The crown and the treasury. Verse 23 is theologically exact, and Samuel will say the same thing centuries later when Israel finally gets its king: they have rejected me from being king over them (1 Sam. 8:7). Verse 24 is the next sentence from the same mouth. Nobody forced the ephod on him and he was never tempted by the throne; the snare came through the one door he left open.

The vocabulary of the snare. Verse 27 uses two words the book has reserved for idolatry. Israel whored after the ephod, as they whored after the Baals in 2:17; and it became a snare, which is the exact word God used at Bochim about the gods of the nations (2:3). Both are now attached to an object made by an Israelite judge, out of the plunder of a victory God gave him, in the town where he had pulled down an altar to Baal.

The title refused, the life adopted. Seventy sons by many wives is a royal household, and the son born at Shechem is named my father is king. Whatever was said at the assembly, that is what was being said at home — and the last verse of the chapter notes that Israel showed no hesed to Gideon's family either. A people who stop remembering what God has done stop keeping faith with each other shortly afterwards, and the writer puts the two failures in consecutive clauses.
8.examples:
Then: A man who had refused to fight until he was told twice, and then pulled down an idol after dark because he was frightened, finished his career torturing the elders of an Israelite town over bread, executing two kings for the death of his brothers, refusing a crown in one sentence and asking for forty pounds of gold in the next.

Now: The chapter's question is not about Gideon's failures at the start but about what happened to him after the success. Note where the snare came from: not from the enemy, not from the crown he had the theology to refuse, but from the spoils of a genuine victory that everybody agreed was God's. And note the last verse. Forgetting God and failing your neighbour arrive in the same paragraph.

9.title: Abimelech the Bramble King
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to his mother's relatives and said to them and to the whole clan of his mother's family,<sup>2</sup>"Say in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, 'Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you?' Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh."<sup>3</sup>And his mother's relatives spoke all these words on his behalf in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, "He is our brother."<sup>4</sup>And they gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith with which Abimelech hired worthless and reckless fellows, who followed him.<sup>5</sup>And he went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.<sup>6</sup>And all the leaders of Shechem came together, and all Beth-millo, and they went and made Abimelech king, by the oak of the pillar at Shechem.<sup>7</sup>When it was told to Jotham, he went and stood on top of Mount Gerizim and cried aloud and said to them, "Listen to me, you leaders of Shechem, that God may listen to you.<sup>8</sup>The trees once went out to anoint a king over them, and they said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.'<sup>9</sup>But the olive tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my abundance, by which gods and men are honored, and go hold sway over the trees?'<sup>10</sup>And the trees said to the fig tree, 'You come and reign over us.'<sup>11</sup>But the fig tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my sweetness and my good fruit and go hold sway over the trees?'<sup>12</sup>And the trees said to the vine, 'You come and reign over us.'<sup>13</sup>But the vine said to them, 'Shall I leave my wine that cheers God and men and go hold sway over the trees?'<sup>14</sup>Then all the trees said to the bramble, 'You come and reign over us.'<sup>15</sup>And the bramble said to the trees, 'If in good faith you are anointing me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade, but if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon.'<sup>16</sup>"Now therefore, if you acted in good faith and integrity when you made Abimelech king, and if you have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house and have done to him as his deeds deserved—<sup>17</sup>for my father fought for you and risked his life and delivered you from the hand of Midian,<sup>18</sup>and you have risen up against my father's house this day and have killed his sons, seventy men on one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his female servant, king over the leaders of Shechem, because he is your relative—<sup>19</sup>if you then have acted in good faith and integrity with Jerubbaal and with his house this day, then rejoice in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you.<sup>20</sup>But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo; and let fire come out from the leaders of Shechem and from Beth-millo and devour Abimelech."<sup>21</sup>And Jotham ran away and fled and went to Beer and lived there, because of Abimelech his brother.<sup>22</sup>Abimelech ruled over Israel three years.<sup>23</sup>And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech,<sup>24</sup>that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid on Abimelech their brother, who killed them, and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.<sup>25</sup>And the leaders of Shechem put men in ambush against him on the mountaintops, and they robbed all who passed by them along that way. And it was told to Abimelech.<sup>26</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed moved into Shechem with his relatives, and the leaders of Shechem put confidence in him.<sup>27</sup>And they went out into the field and gathered the grapes from their vineyards and trod them and held a festival; and they went into the house of their god and ate and drank and reviled Abimelech.<sup>28</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who are we of Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his officer? Serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem; but why should we serve him?<sup>29</sup>Would that this people were under my hand! Then I would remove Abimelech. I would say to Abimelech, 'Increase your army, and come out.'"<sup>30</sup>When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled.<sup>31</sup>And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly, saying, "Behold, Gaal the son of Ebed and his relatives have come to Shechem, and they are stirring up the city against you.<sup>32</sup>Now therefore, go by night, you and the people who are with you, and set an ambush in the field.<sup>33</sup>Then in the morning, as soon as the sun is up, rise early and rush upon the city. And when he and the people who are with him come out against you, you may do to them as your hand finds to do."<sup>34</sup>So Abimelech and all the men who were with him rose up by night and set an ambush against Shechem in four companies.<sup>35</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed went out and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city, and Abimelech and the people who were with him rose from the ambush.<sup>36</sup>And when Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, "Look, people are coming down from the mountaintops!" And Zebul said to him, "You mistake the shadow of the mountains for men."<sup>37</sup>Gaal spoke again and said, "Look, people are coming down from the center of the land, and one company is coming from the direction of the Diviners' Oak."<sup>38</sup>Then Zebul said to him, "Where is your mouth now, you who said, 'Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?' Are not these the people whom you despised? Go out now and fight with them."<sup>39</sup>And Gaal went out at the head of the leaders of Shechem and fought with Abimelech.<sup>40</sup>And Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him. And many fell wounded, up to the entrance of the gate.<sup>41</sup>And Abimelech lived at Arumah, and Zebul drove out Gaal and his relatives, so that they could not dwell at Shechem.<sup>42</sup>On the following day, the people went out into the field, and Abimelech was told.<sup>43</sup>He took his people and divided them into three companies and set an ambush in the fields. And he looked and saw the people coming out of the city. So he rose against them and killed them.<sup>44</sup>Abimelech and the company that was with him rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the gate of the city, while the two companies rushed upon all who were in the field and killed them.<sup>45</sup>And Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed the people who were in it, and he razed the city and sowed it with salt.<sup>46</sup>When all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem heard of it, they entered the stronghold of the house of El-berith.<sup>47</sup>Abimelech was told that all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem were gathered together.<sup>48</sup>And Abimelech went up to Mount Zalmon, he and all the people who were with him. And Abimelech took an axe in his hand and cut down a bundle of brushwood and took it up and laid it on his shoulder. And he said to the men who were with him, "What you have seen me do, hurry and do as I have done."<sup>49</sup>So every one of the people cut down his bundle and following Abimelech put it against the stronghold, and they set the stronghold on fire over them, so that all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about 1,000 men and women.<sup>50</sup>Then Abimelech went to Thebez and encamped against Thebez and captured it.<sup>51</sup>But there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women and all the leaders of the city fled to it and shut themselves in, and they went up to the roof of the tower.<sup>52</sup>And Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it and drew near to the door of the tower to burn it with fire.<sup>53</sup>And a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.<sup>54</sup>Then he called quickly to the young man his armor-bearer and said to him, "Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" And his young man thrust him through, and he died.<sup>55</sup>And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, everyone departed to his home.<sup>56</sup>Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers.<sup>57</sup>And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads, and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.
9.overview:
Gideon refused a crown for himself, his son and his grandson. Within a generation one of his sons had taken it, and the first thing he did with it was kill the other sixty-nine on a single stone. The money came out of the temple of Baal-berith — the god Israel adopted in the week Gideon was buried — and it came to seventy pieces of silver, one for each brother.

They crown him at Shechem, by the oak, which is where Joshua set up a stone as a witness against Israel because it has heard all the words of the LORD (Josh. 24:26-27). One son escapes by hiding, climbs the mountain of blessing, and shouts down the oldest fable in the Bible: the trees go looking for a king, and the olive, the fig and the vine all decline, because each has work to do that is better than the position. The bramble accepts at once — and a bramble is a thorn scrub with no shade to offer and the most flammable thing on a dry hillside.

Then Jotham curses both parties in exactly reciprocal terms: fire out of Abimelech to devour Shechem, and fire out of Shechem to devour Abimelech (v. 20). Both halves happen before the chapter ends. A thousand people burn inside their own temple, and a woman on a roof at Thebez drops a millstone on the king's head.

God is not mentioned once between verses 25 and 55. He is named in verse 23, sending the spirit that breaks the alliance, and in verses 56-57, stating what the whole squalid business was — and those two verses hold everything in between.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abimelech goes to his mother's people in Shechem with a question designed to be answered one way: would you rather be ruled by seventy of Jerubbaal's sons or by one — and remember I am your bone and your flesh (vv. 1-2). Shechem's leaders agree, because he is our brother (v. 3), and finance him with seventy pieces of silver out of the temple of Baal-berith, which he spends on worthless and reckless men (v. 4). He goes to Ophrah and kills his seventy brothers on one stone; only Jotham, the youngest, escapes by hiding (v. 5). And Shechem crowns him by the oak (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Gideon refused a crown for himself, his son and his grandson (8:23). One son of his took it within a generation, and paid for the coup with money from the shrine of the god Israel adopted the week his father died (8:33).
verseByVerse.examples: Seventy pieces of silver, seventy brothers. It works out at one coin a head, and the coins came out of a temple.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to his mother's relatives and said to them and to the whole clan of his mother's family, "Say in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, 'Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you?' Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh." And his mother's relatives spoke all these words on his behalf in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, "He is our brother." And they gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith with which Abimelech hired worthless and reckless fellows, who followed him. And he went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself. And all the leaders of Shechem came together, and all Beth-millo, and they went and made Abimelech king, by the oak of the pillar at Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to his mother's relatives and said to them and to the whole clan of his mother's family, "Say in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, 'Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you?' Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh."'

The campaign opens with a question that has been written so that only one answer is possible, and it contains a lie in the premise. Nobody has offered Shechem seventy rulers. Gideon refused the crown for himself and his sons in as many words (8:23), and there is no suggestion anywhere that his seventy sons had any designs on anything.

The clinching argument is not policy but blood: I am your bone and your flesh. Vote for me because I am one of you.

'And his mother's relatives spoke all these words on his behalf... and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, "He is our brother."'

It works, for exactly the reason offered. He is our brother. Not he is competent, not he is godly, not he has any claim — he is ours.

'And they gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith with which Abimelech hired worthless and reckless fellows, who followed him.'

The money comes out of a temple, and the temple is Baal-berith — the god Israel adopted in the week Gideon was buried (8:33). The shrine that Israel set up in place of the LORD funds the murder of the deliverer's family.

Count the coins against the corpses: seventy pieces of silver, seventy brothers. One coin each. The going rate for a son of the man who saved the country was a single piece of temple silver, and it bought a gang of men the narrator describes as worthless and reckless — unemployed, unattached and available.

'And he went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.'

On one stone. The detail is there because it turns an atrocity into a ceremony. This is not a raid that got out of hand; it is an execution conducted at a single place, one man after another, in the courtyard of the house where the angel once sat under the tree.

One escapes, and the writer says how: he hid. Jotham survives by doing what his father did in chapter 6, which is to get out of sight of people who were looking for him.

'And all the leaders of Shechem came together, and all Beth-millo, and they went and made Abimelech king, by the oak of the pillar at Shechem.'

Then they crown him, and the place they choose is the worst possible one. Shechem is where Joshua gathered all Israel, read the whole law aloud, made them say three times that they would serve the LORD, and set up a great stone under an oak as a witness against us, for it has heard all the words of the LORD (Josh. 24:26-27).

They make a fratricide king at the foot of the stone that was put there to stop them dealing falsely with God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jotham climbs Mount Gerizim and shouts a fable down at the city (v. 7). The trees go looking for a king: the olive will not leave its oil, the fig will not leave its sweetness, the vine will not leave its wine — each of them asks why it should stop doing what it is for in order to hold sway over the trees (vv. 8-13). So they ask the bramble, which accepts at once and offers them its shade, with a threat attached: let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon (vv. 14-15). Then Jotham applies it (vv. 16-20) and runs for his life (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The joke in the fable is botanical. A bramble has no shade to offer — it is a thorn scrub a foot high — and it is the most flammable thing on a dry hillside. The one plant that produces nothing and burns easily is the one that wants the job.
verseByVerse.examples: Jotham's curse in verse 20 is exact and reciprocal: fire from Abimelech to devour Shechem, and fire from Shechem to devour Abimelech. Both halves come true in this chapter, and verse 57 names the curse when they do.

verseByVerse.quote: When it was told to Jotham, he went and stood on top of Mount Gerizim and cried aloud and said to them, "Listen to me, you leaders of Shechem, that God may listen to you. The trees once went out to anoint a king over them, and they said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.' But the olive tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my abundance, by which gods and men are honored, and go hold sway over the trees?' And the trees said to the fig tree, 'You come and reign over us.' But the fig tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my sweetness and my good fruit and go hold sway over the trees?' And the trees said to the vine, 'You come and reign over us.' But the vine said to them, 'Shall I leave my wine that cheers God and men and go hold sway over the trees?' Then all the trees said to the bramble, 'You come and reign over us.' And the bramble said to the trees, 'If in good faith you are anointing me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade, but if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When it was told to Jotham, he went and stood on top of Mount Gerizim and cried aloud and said to them, "Listen to me, you leaders of Shechem, that God may listen to you."'

The surviving son climbs a mountain and shouts.

Gerizim is the mountain of blessing — the one half the nation faced while the law was read in Joshua 8 — and it stands directly above Shechem with a natural acoustic that carries a voice down to the town. Jotham chooses the place where blessings were pronounced, to pronounce a curse.

'"The trees once went out to anoint a king over them, and they said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.' But the olive tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my abundance, by which gods and men are honored, and go hold sway over the trees?'"'

What follows is the oldest fable in the Bible, and it is very funny in a bleak way.

The trees want a king and go looking for one. They ask the olive first, which is the most valuable tree in the country — its oil lit the lamps of the tabernacle and anointed the kings. The olive declines, and its reason is the whole point of the fable: shall I leave my abundance... and go hold sway over the trees?

'"And the trees said to the fig tree, 'You come and reign over us.' But the fig tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my sweetness and my good fruit?'... And the trees said to the vine... 'Shall I leave my wine that cheers God and men?'"'

The fig says the same. So does the vine. Three times over, the trees that are actually producing something ask why they would stop doing it in order to wave about above everybody else.

Each refusal has the same shape. The productive have work to do, and the work is better than the position.

'"Then all the trees said to the bramble, 'You come and reign over us.' And the bramble said to the trees, 'If in good faith you are anointing me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade, but if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon.'"'

Then the bramble, which says yes immediately.

Two things about a bramble, and a Palestinian audience would have laughed at both. First, the offer of shade. A bramble is a thorn scrub that grows a foot or two off the ground; there is no shade under it, and anybody who tried to take refuge there would be cut to pieces. The one thing it promises is the one thing it cannot give.

Second, the threat. A dry bramble on a hillside is the most flammable thing in the country — it is what starts the fires that burn out whole slopes. The bramble cannot shelter anybody and it can burn everybody, and the cedars of Lebanon, the tallest and most magnificent trees there are, are precisely what it threatens.

The fable's argument is not that kingship is wrong. It is that the people most fit to lead will not usually want the job, and the person who wants it most is frequently the one with nothing to leave.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore, if you acted in good faith and integrity when you made Abimelech king, and if you have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house and have done to him as his deeds deserved— for my father fought for you and risked his life and delivered you from the hand of Midian, and you have risen up against my father's house this day and have killed his sons, seventy men on one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his female servant, king over the leaders of Shechem, because he is your relative— if you then have acted in good faith and integrity with Jerubbaal and with his house this day, then rejoice in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you. But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo; and let fire come out from the leaders of Shechem and from Beth-millo and devour Abimelech." And Jotham ran away and fled and went to Beer and lived there, because of Abimelech his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"Now therefore, if you acted in good faith and integrity when you made Abimelech king, and if you have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house and have done to him as his deeds deserved — for my father fought for you and risked his life and delivered you from the hand of Midian."'

Jotham drops the story and speaks plainly, and the case he makes is about debt.

His father fought for Shechem. He risked his life for them — the Hebrew is stronger, something like threw his life out in front of him — and delivered them from Midian. That is what they owed.

'"and you have risen up against my father's house this day and have killed his sons, seventy men on one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his female servant, king over the leaders of Shechem, because he is your relative."'

That is what they paid. He states the two facts side by side and lets the arithmetic stand, and he names the reason they gave: because he is your relative.

'"if you then have acted in good faith and integrity with Jerubbaal and with his house this day, then rejoice in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you."'

The conditional is heavy with sarcasm and it is also a real offer. If this was honourable, then enjoy each other. Live with what you have chosen.

'"But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo; and let fire come out from the leaders of Shechem and from Beth-millo and devour Abimelech."'

The curse is precise and it runs both ways.

Fire out of Abimelech to consume Shechem; fire out of Shechem to consume Abimelech. He does not ask for an army or a judgment from outside. He asks that the two parties destroy each other, which is what people who have made an alliance like this one generally do.

The bramble threatened fire in the fable, and here it is applied. Everything Jotham asks for in this verse happens before the chapter ends, and verse 57 will name him when it does.

'And Jotham ran away and fled and went to Beer and lived there, because of Abimelech his brother.'

Then he runs. He does not stay to see it, does not raise a faction, and never appears again. The last surviving son of the man who saved Israel spends the rest of his life in a town called Well, out of his brother's reach.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–29 — God Sent an Evil Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abimelech rules three years (v. 22), and then the narrator explains what happens next before it happens: God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, so that the violence done to the seventy sons might come back on the man who did it and on the men who financed him (vv. 23-24). Shechem starts robbing the roads (v. 25), a newcomer called Gaal moves in and wins their confidence (v. 26), and at the grape festival in the house of their god they curse Abimelech and Gaal makes a speech (vv. 27-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 24 is the chapter's engine, and it is stated in advance so that no reader can mistake the politics for the cause. Two parties are named and both are being repaid: the man who killed his brothers, and the men who strengthened his hands to do it.
verseByVerse.examples: The alliance falls apart on its own terms. Shechem backed Abimelech because he was their relative; Gaal's whole pitch in verse 28 is that Abimelech is not really one of them after all. The argument that made him king is the argument that unmakes him.

verseByVerse.quote: Abimelech ruled over Israel three years. And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech, that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid on Abimelech their brother, who killed them, and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers. And the leaders of Shechem put men in ambush against him on the mountaintops, and they robbed all who passed by them along that way. And it was told to Abimelech. And Gaal the son of Ebed moved into Shechem with his relatives, and the leaders of Shechem put confidence in him. And they went out into the field and gathered the grapes from their vineyards and trod them and held a festival; and they went into the house of their god and ate and drank and reviled Abimelech. And Gaal the son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who are we of Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his officer? Serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem; but why should we serve him? Would that this people were under my hand! Then I would remove Abimelech. I would say to Abimelech, 'Increase your army, and come out.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Abimelech ruled over Israel three years. And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech.'

Three years, and then the alliance begins to come apart — and the narrator will not let us call it politics.

God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem. Whatever precisely that means, and the phrase is deliberately unsettling, the writer's point is the agency. The suspicion that grows up between these two parties is not accidental, and it is not merely the natural fate of a conspiracy. It was sent.

'that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid on Abimelech their brother, who killed them, and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.'

Verse 24 is the engine of everything that follows, and it is placed here so that no reader can mistake the mechanism for the cause.

Two parties are named, and the second is the one that ordinarily escapes. Abimelech killed them. The men of Shechem strengthened his hands to kill them — they did not swing anything, they wrote a cheque out of a temple and let a hired gang do the work. The book holds both accountable in one sentence, and the financiers are not treated as bystanders.

'And the leaders of Shechem put men in ambush against him on the mountaintops, and they robbed all who passed by them along that way.'

The first symptom of the breakdown is banditry. Shechem's leaders start robbing travellers on the roads — which is exactly the condition Deborah's song described as the mark of oppression (5:6), and it is now being organised by Israelites against anybody who passes.

'And Gaal the son of Ebed moved into Shechem with his relatives, and the leaders of Shechem put confidence in him... And they went out into the field and gathered the grapes... and held a festival; and they went into the house of their god and ate and drank and reviled Abimelech.'

A newcomer arrives and the city takes to him at once, which is what a city does when it has already stopped trusting the man it crowned.

The scene is a harvest festival in the temple of their god, with the wine flowing and the talk turning against the king — and the god in question is the one whose treasury paid for his coronation.

'And Gaal the son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who are we of Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal?... Serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem; but why should we serve him?"'

Listen to the argument that finishes Abimelech, because it is the argument that made him.

Shechem crowned him on the grounds that he was their relative, their bone and their flesh. Gaal's whole case is that he is not — he is Jerubbaal's son, an outsider from Ophrah, and Shechem should be serving its own ancient line instead.

Nothing has changed about Abimelech. The city has simply applied its own principle in the other direction, which is what happens to every arrangement built on being one of us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zebul, Abimelech's officer in the city, sends word secretly and proposes a night ambush (vv. 30-33). Abimelech comes in four companies; Gaal, standing in the gate at dawn, sees men on the hills, and Zebul tells him he is looking at shadows until it is too late (vv. 34-38). Gaal fights, loses, and is driven out of the city (vv. 39-41). The next day Abimelech ambushes the townspeople in the fields, takes the city, kills the population, razes it and sows it with salt (vv. 42-45). The last of the leaders shut themselves into the stronghold of the temple of El-berith, and Abimelech cuts brushwood on Mount Zalmon, tells his men to copy him, and burns the place down with about a thousand men and women inside (vv. 46-49).
