verseByVerse.theology: The first half of Jotham's curse is now complete: fire has come out of Abimelech and devoured the leaders of Shechem. They die inside their own temple, in the house of the god whose treasury paid for the coup that made him king.
verseByVerse.examples: The instruction in verse 48 is a sentence Gideon's men once heard in a very different cause. What you have seen me do, hurry and do as I have done is almost word for word what Gideon told the three hundred at the edge of the Midianite camp (7:17). The son has his father's method and none of his father's commission.

verseByVerse.quote: When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly, saying, "Behold, Gaal the son of Ebed and his relatives have come to Shechem, and they are stirring up the city against you. Now therefore, go by night, you and the people who are with you, and set an ambush in the field. Then in the morning, as soon as the sun is up, rise early and rush upon the city. And when he and the people who are with him come out against you, you may do to them as your hand finds to do." So Abimelech and all the men who were with him rose up by night and set an ambush against Shechem in four companies. And Gaal the son of Ebed went out and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city, and Abimelech and the people who were with him rose from the ambush. And when Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, "Look, people are coming down from the mountaintops!" And Zebul said to him, "You mistake the shadow of the mountains for men." Gaal spoke again and said, "Look, people are coming down from the center of the land, and one company is coming from the direction of the Diviners' Oak." Then Zebul said to him, "Where is your mouth now, you who said, 'Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?' Are not these the people whom you despised? Go out now and fight with them." And Gaal went out at the head of the leaders of Shechem and fought with Abimelech. And Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him. And many fell wounded, up to the entrance of the gate. And Abimelech lived at Arumah, and Zebul drove out Gaal and his relatives, so that they could not dwell at Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly, saying, "Behold, Gaal the son of Ebed and his relatives have come to Shechem, and they are stirring up the city against you."'

Abimelech has a man inside. Zebul governs Shechem for him, keeps his position through the whole festival of insults, and sends a message out by night.

The plan he proposes is a night march and a dawn ambush — and it is the plan Gideon used, minus everything that made Gideon's work God's.

'And Gaal the son of Ebed went out and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city, and Abimelech and the people who were with him rose from the ambush. And when Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, "Look, people are coming down from the mountaintops!" And Zebul said to him, "You mistake the shadow of the mountains for men."'

Now a small scene of pure malice, and it is the best-written thing in the chapter.

Gaal is standing in the gate at dawn, half sober, and sees movement on the hills. He says so. And Zebul — who arranged the ambush, who knows exactly what is coming, and who is standing beside him — tells him he is seeing shadows.

He keeps him talking until the companies are too close to escape.

'Then Zebul said to him, "Where is your mouth now, you who said, 'Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?' Are not these the people whom you despised? Go out now and fight with them."'

Then he drops the pretence and quotes the man's own festival speech back at him. Where is your mouth now?

Gaal has to go out and fight, in front of the city, on ground he has not chosen, with the men he talked into it the night before. He is beaten to the gate, many fall, and Zebul throws him out of the city the same day.

That is the whole career of Gaal son of Ebed. He arrives, is trusted, makes a speech at a party, and is gone within two verses of the fighting starting.

verseByVerse.quote: On the following day, the people went out into the field, and Abimelech was told. He took his people and divided them into three companies and set an ambush in the fields. And he looked and saw the people coming out of the city. So he rose against them and killed them. Abimelech and the company that was with him rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the gate of the city, while the two companies rushed upon all who were in the field and killed them. And Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed the people who were in it, and he razed the city and sowed it with salt. When all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem heard of it, they entered the stronghold of the house of El-berith. Abimelech was told that all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem were gathered together. And Abimelech went up to Mount Zalmon, he and all the people who were with him. And Abimelech took an axe in his hand and cut down a bundle of brushwood and took it up and laid it on his shoulder. And he said to the men who were with him, "What you have seen me do, hurry and do as I have done." So every one of the people cut down his bundle and following Abimelech put it against the stronghold, and they set the stronghold on fire over them, so that all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about 1,000 men and women.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'On the following day, the people went out into the field, and Abimelech was told. He took his people and divided them into three companies and set an ambush in the fields.'

The next morning the townspeople go out to work, and Abimelech is waiting for them.

Note the tactics: three companies, an ambush, a rush at the gate. It is Gideon's plan from chapter 7 in every particular except the part where God does it. The son has inherited the method.

'Abimelech and the company that was with him rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the gate of the city, while the two companies rushed upon all who were in the field and killed them.'

He takes the gate first so that nobody can get back inside, and kills the people in the open — farmers, in the fields, in the morning.

'And Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed the people who were in it, and he razed the city and sowed it with salt.'

Then a day of street fighting, the population killed, and the town pulled down and sown with salt.

Sowing a site with salt is a formal act. It is not agriculture; the amounts involved could never sterilise a field. It is a curse performed in public, declaring that nothing will ever grow here again and no one will ever live here.

The man is destroying the city that made him king, in the ceremonial language reserved for places under a curse, three years after they crowned him at the oak.

'When all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem heard of it, they entered the stronghold of the house of El-berith.'

The last of them shut themselves into the temple stronghold. Where else would they go? It is the strongest building in the city and it belongs to their god — the same treasury that paid the seventy pieces of silver.

'And Abimelech went up to Mount Zalmon... and cut down a bundle of brushwood and took it up and laid it on his shoulder. And he said to the men who were with him, "What you have seen me do, hurry and do as I have done."'

Here is a sentence that ought to stop any reader who has just come through chapter 7.

What you have seen me do, hurry and do as I have done. That is almost exactly what Gideon said to the three hundred on the edge of the Midianite camp: look at me, and do likewise... when I blow the trumpet, then blow the trumpets also (7:17).

The same words, the same posture, one generation later. Gideon's men copied him and an army destroyed itself in the dark. Abimelech's men copy him and carry firewood up to a temple full of their own countrymen.

'So every one of the people cut down his bundle and following Abimelech put it against the stronghold, and they set the stronghold on fire over them, so that all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about 1,000 men and women.'

A thousand people, burned inside the house of their god.

The first half of Jotham's curse is now complete, and it happened exactly as he said it: let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem. The bramble has burned what asked it to reign.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abimelech moves on to Thebez and takes the town, but the people shut themselves in a strong tower and go up on the roof (vv. 50-51). He walks up to the door to burn it, and a woman drops an upper millstone on his head and crushes his skull (vv. 52-53). Dying, he calls his armour-bearer to run him through, lest they say of me, a woman killed him (v. 54). The men of Israel go home (v. 55). And the narrator states the meaning of the whole chapter: God returned the evil of Abimelech, and God made the evil of the men of Shechem return on their own heads, and upon them came the curse of Jotham (vv. 56-57).
verseByVerse.theology: He dies doing the thing that killed Shechem, at a door with fire in his hand, and the second half of Jotham's curse arrives from the last direction he was watching — from above, and from a woman he never saw.
verseByVerse.examples: His final act is a lie about his own death, and it fails. Israel remembered it exactly, and centuries later Joab assumes any soldier will know the story: who killed Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall? (2 Sam. 11:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abimelech went to Thebez and encamped against Thebez and captured it. But there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women and all the leaders of the city fled to it and shut themselves in, and they went up to the roof of the tower. And Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it and drew near to the door of the tower to burn it with fire. And a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull. Then he called quickly to the young man his armor-bearer and said to him, "Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" And his young man thrust him through, and he died. And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, everyone departed to his home. Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers. And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads, and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Abimelech went to Thebez and encamped against Thebez and captured it. But there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women and all the leaders of the city fled to it and shut themselves in, and they went up to the roof of the tower.'

He moves on to the next town, and it goes the same way — the city taken, the population shut into the tower. He has done this before, a week ago, and it worked.

'And Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it and drew near to the door of the tower to burn it with fire.'

He walks up to the door with fire in his hand, personally, because it is what he did at Shechem and there is no reason to think it will fail twice.

'And a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.'

An upper millstone is the top wheel of a hand mill — the stone a woman turned every morning to grind the day's flour. It weighs a few pounds and it is round, and from the roof of a tower it is a perfectly adequate weapon.

She is not named, and she is not a soldier. She is somebody on a roof with the household equipment, and she ends the career of the first man in Israel to call himself king.

'Then he called quickly to the young man his armor-bearer and said to him, "Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" And his young man thrust him through, and he died.'

His last recorded thought is about his reputation.

He has minutes to live with a crushed skull, and what occupies him is the sentence people will say afterwards. So he arranges an alternative version and has a boy stab him to secure it — which is a fair summary of the whole life. Everything he ever did was about what would be said about him.

It did not work. The story is told here, in full, with the millstone in it. And it was still being told three hundred years later: when Joab briefs a messenger on how to report a death at a wall, he expects the king to interrupt with who killed Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall? (2 Sam. 11:21).

Every soldier in Israel knew. The one thing he spent his dying breath preventing is the one detail that survived.

'And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, everyone departed to his home.'

The army goes home. There is no succession, no mourning, no burial recorded, and no rest for the land at the end of this cycle — because this was never a deliverance. Abimelech is the one man in this book who is never called a judge and never said to have saved anybody.

'Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers. And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads, and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.'

Then the narrator, who has told fifty-five verses of politics and ambushes without a word of comment, states the meaning in two sentences.

God returned it. Both halves, to both parties — to the man who killed his brothers, and to the men who paid for it out of a temple — and the writer names the mechanism as the curse of a young man who shouted from a mountainside and then went and lived quietly in a town called Well.

Nothing in this chapter looks like the hand of God while it is happening. It looks like a squalid provincial coup coming apart in the usual way: a rigged question, hired men, a conspiracy, a drunken speech, an ambush, a betrayal, a siege, a woman on a roof. That is exactly how it looked to everybody in it.

The blood of seventy brothers had been crying out from one stone in Ophrah for three years, and it was answered by a millstone and a bramble and a piece of bad advice at a city gate. God is not mentioned once between verses 25 and 55. He is named in verse 23 and again in verse 56, and those two verses hold everything in between.

9.theology:
The financiers are not bystanders. Verse 24 names two parties and repays both: Abimelech, who killed them, and the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers. They swung nothing. They wrote a cheque out of a temple and let hired men do the work, and the book puts them in the same sentence as the murderer.

The bramble. The fable's argument is not that kingship is wrong. It is that the trees worth following will not leave their fruit to hold sway over the trees, and the one plant that produces nothing is the one that accepts instantly — offering a shade it does not have and threatening a fire it certainly can start. Every generation recognises the candidate with nothing to leave.

The argument that makes you can unmake you. Shechem crowned Abimelech because he is our brother, and Gaal destroyed him with the claim that he was not really one of them after all (v. 28). Nothing about Abimelech had changed. Any loyalty built on being one of us can be dismantled with the same tool.

Providence that looks like nothing. Between verse 25 and verse 55 this reads as an ordinary provincial coup coming apart: a rigged question, hired men, a drunken speech, an ambush, a betrayal at a gate, a siege, a woman on a roof. That is exactly how it looked to everybody in it. The narrator brackets the whole thing with two sentences about God — he sent the spirit (v. 23) and he returned the evil (vv. 56-57) — and names the agent as the curse of a young man who shouted from a hillside and then went away and lived quietly.
9.examples:
Then: A man bought a crown with temple money at a rate of one silver piece per brother, ruled three years, burned a thousand of his own supporters inside their sanctuary, and died at a tower door because somebody's mother dropped the top half of her kitchen mill on his head. His last request was that nobody should be told how it happened.

Now: Two things carry straight across. The first is verse 24 and the men who strengthened his hands — the people who fund, vote for, excuse or quietly enable what they would never do themselves, and who are named in the same sentence as the man who did it. The second is the fable: the person campaigning hardest for the position is very often the one with no fruit to leave behind, and the olive, the fig and the vine are usually busy.

10.title: Tola, Jair, and Renewed Apostasy
10.text: <sup>1</sup>After Abimelech there arose to save Israel Tola the son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, and he lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.<sup>2</sup>And he judged Israel twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried at Shamir.<sup>3</sup>After him arose Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years.<sup>4</sup>And he had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty cities, called Havvoth-jair to this day, which are in the land of Gilead.<sup>5</sup>And Jair died and was buried in Kamon.<sup>6</sup>The people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines. And they forsook the LORD and did not serve him.<sup>7</sup>So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of the Philistines and into the hand of the Ammonites,<sup>8</sup>and they crushed and oppressed the people of Israel that year. For eighteen years they oppressed all the people of Israel who were beyond the Jordan in the land of the Amorites, which is in Gilead.<sup>9</sup>And the Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight also against Judah and against Benjamin and against the house of Ephraim, so that Israel was severely distressed.<sup>10</sup>And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, saying, "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God and have served the Baals."<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to the people of Israel, "Did I not save you from the Egyptians and from the Amorites, from the Ammonites and from the Philistines?<sup>12</sup>The Sidonians also, and the Amalekites and the Maonites oppressed you, and you cried out to me, and I saved you out of their hand.<sup>13</sup>Yet you have forsaken me and served other gods; therefore I will save you no more.<sup>14</sup>Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress."<sup>15</sup>And the people of Israel said to the LORD, "We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day."<sup>16</sup>So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and he became impatient over the misery of Israel.<sup>17</sup>Then the Ammonites were called to arms, and they encamped in Gilead. And the people of Israel came together, and they encamped at Mizpah.<sup>18</sup>And the people, the leaders of Gilead, said one to another, "Who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."
10.overview:
Two men and almost no narrative: Tola judges twenty-three years, Jair twenty-two, and between them forty-five years pass in five verses with nothing whatever going wrong. Coming straight after a chapter in which a thousand people burned inside a temple, that is not a dull passage. It is the best stretch the book has recorded since Deborah, and there is nothing to tell because nothing was wrong.

Then the formula returns with the longest list in the book. Israel serves the Baals, the Ashtaroth, and the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon and the Philistines — seven sets, every neighbour on every border — and the summary is flat: they forsook the LORD and did not serve him. Two oppressors come at once, east and west, and they will run on to the end of the book.

Israel then prays the best prayer it has prayed so far, a real confession rather than a complaint — and God refuses. He recites seven rescues against their seven gods, some of the names appearing on both lists, and says I will save you no more. Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen. Nowhere else in the book is a cry for help met with a refusal, and it is not a threat but a referral.

They do not argue. They accept the sentence, ask anyway, and then do what no generation in this book has done: they put away the foreign gods and served the LORD, with nothing promised them. And the chapter ends with the elders of Gilead advertising for somebody, anybody, to lead them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After Abimelech, two men and almost no narrative. Tola of Issachar arose to save Israel, lived at Shamir, judged twenty-three years, died and was buried (vv. 1-2). Jair the Gileadite judged twenty-two years, had thirty sons who rode thirty donkeys and held thirty towns still called by his name, and died and was buried (vv. 3-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Forty-five years pass in five verses and nothing goes wrong in any of them. After the carnage at Shechem and Thebez, a stretch of the book in which the only events are two men doing their job and being buried is a mercy, and it is the nearest thing to good news since chapter 5.
verseByVerse.examples: Jair's thirty sons on thirty donkeys is a display of rank — a donkey was what a man of standing rode — and it is Gideon's seventy sons in miniature. The judges have begun to look like dynasties, and Ibzan and Abdon will do the same thing again (12:9, 14).

verseByVerse.quote: After Abimelech there arose to save Israel Tola the son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, and he lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim. And he judged Israel twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried at Shamir. After him arose Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years. And he had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty cities, called Havvoth-jair to this day, which are in the land of Gilead. And Jair died and was buried in Kamon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After Abimelech there arose to save Israel Tola the son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, and he lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim. And he judged Israel twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried at Shamir.'

After the fire and the millstone, two verses about a man who did nothing worth reporting.

Tola is given a father, a grandfather, a tribe, an address, a length of service and a grave. There is no oppression named, no battle, no crisis, no failure. He arose to save Israel — from what, we are not told — and then he judged for twenty-three years and was buried where he lived.

'After him arose Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years. And he had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty cities, called Havvoth-jair to this day... And Jair died and was buried in Kamon.'

Jair gets one detail, and it is about status. Thirty sons, thirty donkeys, thirty towns.

A donkey was what a man of rank rode in that country, and thirty sons each with his own mount and his own town is a display — a family that has arranged the map to suit itself. It is Gideon's seventy sons in miniature, and the same thing will be said of Ibzan with his thirty sons and thirty daughters and of Abdon with his forty sons on seventy donkeys (12:9, 14).

The office is quietly becoming a family business, and nobody says a word against it.

Before the criticism, though, notice what these five verses actually contain: forty-five years in which nothing goes wrong.

No apostasy is recorded. No raiders come. Nobody is oppressed, and nobody has to be rescued. Two men do their work for a working lifetime each and are buried in their own towns, and the writer has almost nothing to say about either of them.

Coming immediately after a chapter in which a thousand people burned inside a temple, that is not a dull passage. It is the best stretch of years the book has recorded since Deborah, and the reason there is nothing to tell is that nothing was wrong.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then the formula returns, and the list attached to it is the longest in the book: Israel served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon and the Philistines — seven in all — and they forsook the LORD and did not serve him (v. 6). So God sells them into two hands at once, the Philistines and the Ammonites (v. 7), who crush and oppress them for eighteen years east of the Jordan (v. 8), and the Ammonites cross over to attack Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim as well, until Israel is severely distressed (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Every previous apostasy named the Baals. This one names the gods of every neighbour Israel has: north, west, east and south. They have not drifted into one local cult; they have collected the complete set.
verseByVerse.examples: This is also the first oppression that comes from two directions at once. Ammon holds Gilead in the east and the Philistines press from the west, and the two threats will run on into the next six chapters — Jephthah against Ammon, Samson against the Philistines.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines. And they forsook the LORD and did not serve him. So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of the Philistines and into the hand of the Ammonites, and they crushed and oppressed the people of Israel that year. For eighteen years they oppressed all the people of Israel who were beyond the Jordan in the land of the Amorites, which is in Gilead. And the Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight also against Judah and against Benjamin and against the house of Ephraim, so that Israel was severely distressed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines. And they forsook the LORD and did not serve him.'

Count the entries in that list.

The Baals and the Ashtaroth, which is the usual charge in this book. Then the gods of Syria to the north, Sidon on the coast, Moab and Ammon across the Jordan, and the Philistines to the south-west. Seven in all, and between them they are every neighbour Israel has, in every direction.

This is not a nation drifting into one local cult because the rain matters. It is a nation that has collected the full set — taken up the religion of every people on every border, and kept them all.

The summary at the end of the verse is the flattest sentence in the book: they forsook the LORD and did not serve him. No qualification, no partial credit. Not that they served him badly or intermittently. They did not serve him.

'So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of the Philistines and into the hand of the Ammonites, and they crushed and oppressed the people of Israel that year. For eighteen years they oppressed all the people of Israel who were beyond the Jordan.'

Seven gods, and two oppressors at once.

Every previous cycle had a single enemy: Cushan, Eglon, Jabin, Midian. Now Israel is being worked from two sides simultaneously — Ammon across the Jordan in the east and the Philistines on the western plain — and the two of them between them will occupy the rest of this book. Jephthah will fight Ammon in the next chapter. Samson will fight the Philistines for the four chapters after that, and lose.

'And the Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight also against Judah and against Benjamin and against the house of Ephraim, so that Israel was severely distressed.'

Then it spreads. Gilead had been taking it for eighteen years on the east bank, and now the Ammonites cross the river and go for the heartland — Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim.

That is a fair picture of what tolerated evil eventually does. The trouble that could be lived with while it stayed on the far side of the water does not stay there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — I Will Save You No More
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They cry out, and for the first time the cry contains a confession rather than a complaint: we have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God and have served the Baals (v. 10). And God refuses. He recites seven deliverances — Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, Philistines, Sidonians, Amalekites, Maonites — and the pattern of every one of them: you cried out to me, and I saved you (vv. 11-12). Then: yet you have forsaken me and served other gods; therefore I will save you no more (v. 13). And a sentence with no comfort in it at all: go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Seven gods in verse 6; seven rescues in verses 11-12. The arithmetic is not accidental. God sets the list of what they chose beside the list of what he did, and the reply follows from the comparison.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 14 is the most frightening sentence in the book, and it is not a threat. It is a referral. Take your request to the department you have been paying, and see what they can do for you.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, saying, "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God and have served the Baals." And the LORD said to the people of Israel, "Did I not save you from the Egyptians and from the Amorites, from the Ammonites and from the Philistines? The Sidonians also, and the Amalekites and the Maonites oppressed you, and you cried out to me, and I saved you out of their hand. Yet you have forsaken me and served other gods; therefore I will save you no more. Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, saying, "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God and have served the Baals."'

This is the best prayer Israel has prayed in the book so far.

Every earlier cycle records only that they cried out. This time the cry has content, and the content is a confession: we have sinned against you. They name the offence, they name the party offended, and they specify what they did. Nobody is asking for the raiders to stop without mentioning why they came.

By any ordinary reckoning this is exactly what God has been waiting for.

'And the LORD said to the people of Israel, "Did I not save you from the Egyptians and from the Amorites, from the Ammonites and from the Philistines? The Sidonians also, and the Amalekites and the Maonites oppressed you, and you cried out to me, and I saved you out of their hand."'

God's answer begins with a list, and the list is the point.

Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, Philistines, Sidonians, Amalekites, Maonites. Seven oppressors, seven rescues — against the seven sets of gods in verse 6.

The arithmetic is not accidental, and the shape of the argument is unanswerable. Here is the list of everyone you have worshipped. Here is the list of everyone I have saved you from. They are the same length, and some of the names appear on both.

Read that last point again, because it is the sharpest thing in the passage. Israel is serving the gods of the Ammonites and the gods of the Philistines — and God's list of past rescues includes the Ammonites and the Philistines. They have adopted the religion of people God delivered them from.

The recurring clause in his summary is the one they have just used again: you cried out to me, and I saved you. He is quoting their own history of crying out.

'"Yet you have forsaken me and served other gods; therefore I will save you no more."'

Then the refusal.

Nowhere else in this book is a cry for help answered with a refusal. There is no precedent for it and no softening after it, and it is spoken in answer to the most honest confession Israel has managed in ten chapters.

'"Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress."'

The last verse is the most frightening sentence in Judges, and its force is that it is not a threat.

He is referring them elsewhere. You have been paying seven other departments for years; take the request to them. Let them save you in the time of your distress — the very thing they are advertised as doing.

The judgment is Bochim's, made explicit. There God said he would no longer drive out the nations Israel had declined to remove. Here he says he will no longer answer prayers a people have not really addressed to him. In both cases the sentence is that they may keep what they chose, and the horror of it is that God does not have to do anything at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–16 — They Put Away the Gods
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel does not argue. We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day (v. 15). And then a clause that appears nowhere else in the book: so they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD (v. 16). The verse ends with God unable to bear it any longer.
verseByVerse.theology: Every previous cycle records a cry. This one records a clear-out. They accept the sentence, ask anyway, and then go home and get rid of the idols before anything has been promised them.
verseByVerse.examples: The last clause of verse 16 is hard to translate and worth the effort: literally, his soul was shortened over the misery of Israel. It is the idiom used of a man at the end of his endurance, and it is used again of Samson when nagging shortened his soul to death (16:16). Here God's patience runs out — and it runs out in the direction of mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel said to the LORD, "We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day." So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and he became impatient over the misery of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the people of Israel said to the LORD, "We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day."'

Israel does not argue with the verdict.

That is the remarkable thing about this verse. God has just said he will not save them and told them to try their other gods, and Israel does not protest, or bargain, or point out how long they have served him. They agree with the sentence — do to us whatever seems good to you — and then ask anyway.

Only please deliver us this day. It is a prayer with no claim in it whatever. They have conceded that they deserve nothing and asked for everything, and there is nothing else in their hands.

'So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD.'

Then a clause that has not appeared once in ten chapters.

They went home and got rid of them. All seven sets — the Baals, the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria and Sidon and Moab and Ammon and the Philistines — taken out of the houses and disposed of, and the LORD served instead.

Every earlier repentance in this book is a noise. This one has furniture moving in it.

The order matters, and it is the whole point. Nothing has been promised. God has said he will not save them; they have accepted it and asked anyway; and now, with no assurance of any kind, they clear out the shrines. That is not repentance bought by a guarantee. It is repentance performed in the dark.

'and he became impatient over the misery of Israel.'

The last clause of the verse is difficult in Hebrew and repays the trouble. Literally, his soul was shortened over the misery of Israel.

The phrase is the idiom for a man at the end of his tether — and the book uses it once more, about Samson, when Delilah's daily nagging shortened his soul to death (16:16). It describes an endurance that has run out.

So the sentence says that God could not stand it any longer. Not that he changed his mind about their guilt, and not that they had earned anything in the two verses since he refused them. He looked at the misery of a people who deserved every bit of it, and his patience gave way — in the direction of mercy.

Everything the book has said about him since 2:18 is in that clause. He was moved by their groaning then. Here, having formally declined to save them, he cannot watch.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The armies gather: Ammon in Gilead, Israel at Mizpah (v. 17). And the last verse of the chapter is a job advertisement. The leaders of Gilead say to one another: who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Nobody volunteers. A whole leadership stands in a camp asking each other the question, and the office is offered as an inducement because no one wants the job at any lower price.
verseByVerse.examples: They will find their man in the next chapter, and he is somebody they had already thrown out of town for being the wrong kind of son. The advertisement in verse 18 is what makes the negotiation of chapter 11 possible.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Ammonites were called to arms, and they encamped in Gilead. And the people of Israel came together, and they encamped at Mizpah. And the people, the leaders of Gilead, said one to another, "Who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the Ammonites were called to arms, and they encamped in Gilead. And the people of Israel came together, and they encamped at Mizpah.'

Two armies face each other and the chapter has one problem left to solve.

'And the people, the leaders of Gilead, said one to another, "Who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."'

Israel has no leader.

Read the scene as it stands. The elders of Gilead are standing in a camp, in front of an enemy, asking each other a question — and the question is not what is the plan but who is the man. Nobody steps forward. They are reduced to advertising the post, and the salary offered is the highest office in the region: whoever will begin the fight becomes head over all Gilead.

That is what it has come to. In chapter 4 God had already commissioned Barak and he had to be sent for. In chapter 6 God had to go and find a man threshing in a pit. Here there is no commission recorded at all, and a committee is offering a promotion to anybody who will volunteer.

Weigh also what they are prepared to pay. Gideon was offered the crown after he won; this man is offered the headship before he starts, by men who have run out of alternatives.

They will get an answer to their advertisement in the next chapter, and it will be a man they had already thrown out of town — the son of a prostitute, driven off by his own brothers so that he would not inherit, living in the badlands with a gang of empty men.

The leaders of Gilead are about to discover that the only person willing to take the job is somebody they had personally disqualified.

10.theology:
Seven and seven. The list of gods in verse 6 and the list of rescues in verses 11-12 are the same length, and the argument runs on the comparison. Sharper still: Israel is serving the gods of the Ammonites and the Philistines, and God's list of past deliverances includes the Ammonites and the Philistines. They have adopted the religion of the people he saved them from.

The refusal. Therefore I will save you no more... go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen (vv. 13-14) is the one refusal in the book, and it answers the most honest confession Israel has yet made. It is not a threat; it is a referral to the department they have been paying. It is Bochim made explicit — the judgment that consists in being allowed to keep what you insisted on having, and it requires God to do nothing at all.

Repentance performed in the dark. Every earlier cycle records a cry; this one records a clear-out (v. 16). And the order is everything: God has already said no, they have accepted the verdict, nothing has been promised — and they go home and get rid of the gods anyway. That is not repentance bought with a guarantee.

His soul was shortened. The last clause of verse 16 is the idiom for a man at the end of his endurance, used again of Samson when nagging shortened his soul to death (16:16). God did not change his mind about their guilt and they had earned nothing in the two verses since the refusal. He looked at the misery of a people who deserved all of it, and his patience gave way in the direction of mercy — which is what 2:18 said about him and what the cross would say again.
10.examples:
Then: A nation that had collected the gods of all seven of its neighbours finally said so out loud, was told to go and ask them for help, agreed that it deserved the answer, asked anyway, and then went home and threw the idols out before anyone had promised it a thing.

Now: Verse 16 is the model and verse 15 is the hard part. They made no claim — do to us whatever seems good to you — and cleared the house without any assurance that it would make a difference. Most repentance waits for terms. And verse 14 is the warning underneath it all: the worst thing God can say to a person is not no. It is go and ask the thing you have actually been serving, and see what it can do for you.

11.title: Jephthah
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute. Gilead was the father of Jephthah.<sup>2</sup>And Gilead's wife also bore him sons. And when his wife's sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, "You shall not have an inheritance in our father's house, for you are the son of another woman."<sup>3</sup>Then Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob, and worthless fellows collected around Jephthah and went out with him.<sup>4</sup>After a time the Ammonites made war against Israel.<sup>5</sup>And when the Ammonites made war against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob.<sup>6</sup>And they said to Jephthah, "Come and be our leader, that we may fight against the Ammonites."<sup>7</sup>But Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why have you come to me now when you are in distress?"<sup>8</sup>And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "That is why we have turned to you now, that you may go with us and fight against the Ammonites and be our head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."<sup>9</sup>Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "If you bring me home again to fight against the Ammonites, and the LORD gives them over to me, I will be your head."<sup>10</sup>And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "The LORD will be witness between us, if we do not do as you say."<sup>11</sup>So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and leader over them. And Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.<sup>12</sup>Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites and said, "What do you have against me, that you have come to me to fight against my land?"<sup>13</sup>And the king of the Ammonites answered the messengers of Jephthah, "Because Israel on coming up from Egypt took away my land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan; now therefore restore it peaceably."<sup>14</sup>Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites<sup>15</sup>and said to him, "Thus says Jephthah: Israel did not take away the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites,<sup>16</sup>but when they came up from Egypt, Israel went through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh.<sup>17</sup>Israel then sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, 'Please let us pass through your land,' but the king of Edom would not listen. And they sent also to the king of Moab, but he would not consent. So Israel remained at Kadesh.<sup>18</sup>"Then they journeyed through the wilderness and went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab and arrived on the east side of the land of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon. But they did not enter the territory of Moab, for the Arnon was the boundary of Moab.<sup>19</sup>Israel then sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, king of Heshbon, and Israel said to him, 'Please let us pass through your land to our country,'<sup>20</sup>but Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory, so Sihon gathered all his people together and encamped at Jahaz and fought with Israel.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, and they defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites, who inhabited that country.<sup>22</sup>And they took possession of all the territory of the Amorites from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan.<sup>23</sup>So then the LORD, the God of Israel, dispossessed the Amorites from before his people Israel; and are you to take possession of them?<sup>24</sup>Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you to possess? And all that the LORD our God has dispossessed before us, we will possess.<sup>25</sup>Now are you any better than Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever contend against Israel, or did he ever go to war with them?<sup>26</sup>While Israel lived in Heshbon and its villages, and in Aroer and its villages, and in all the cities that are on the banks of the Arnon, 300 years, why did you not deliver them within that time?<sup>27</sup>I therefore have not sinned against you, and you do me wrong by making war on me. The LORD, the Judge, decide this day between the people of Israel and the people of Ammon."<sup>28</sup>But the king of the Ammonites did not listen to the words of Jephthah that he sent to him.<sup>29</sup>Then the Spirit of the LORD was upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh and passed on to Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he passed on to the Ammonites.<sup>30</sup>And Jephthah made a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will give the Ammonites into my hand,<sup>31</sup>then whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering."<sup>32</sup>So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the LORD gave them into his hand.<sup>33</sup>And he struck them from Aroer to the neighborhood of Minnith, twenty cities, and as far as Abel-keramim, with a great blow. So the Ammonites were subdued before the people of Israel.<sup>34</sup>Then Jephthah came to his home at Mizpah. And behold, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and with dances. She was his only child; besides her he had neither son nor daughter.<sup>35</sup>And as soon as he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, "Alas, my daughter! You have brought me very low, and you have become the cause of great trouble to me. For I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow."<sup>36</sup>And she said to him, "My father, you have opened your mouth to the LORD; do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth, now that the LORD has avenged you on your enemies, on the Ammonites."<sup>37</sup>So she said to her father, "Let this thing be done for me: leave me alone two months, that I may go up and down on the mountains and weep for my virginity, I and my companions."<sup>38</sup>So he said, "Go." Then he sent her away for two months, and she departed, she and her companions, and wept for her virginity on the mountains.<sup>39</sup>And at the end of two months, she returned to her father, who did with her according to his vow that he had made. She had never known a man, and it became a custom in Israel<sup>40</sup>that the daughters of Israel went year by year to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in the year.
11.overview:
Gilead's elders, having advertised at the end of chapter 10 for anyone who would fight Ammon, come to Tob and hire the man their own community had legally thrown out — the son of a prostitute, disinherited by his half-brothers, living off raiding with a band of empty men. He negotiates hard, takes the headship in advance, and repeats every clause of the deal before the LORD at Mizpah.

Then he does something no other judge does. Before fighting, he writes to the king of Ammon and argues the case: sixteen verses of history establishing that the disputed land was taken from Sihon the Amorite in a war Sihon started, that Israel had asked three times for peaceful passage, that Balak of Moab never contested it and Ammon has not pressed the claim in three hundred years. He ends by handing the verdict to God: the LORD, the Judge, decide this day. Ammon does not listen.

Then the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him — and in the very next verse, with the Spirit already on him and the outcome already settled, he vows to burn as an offering whatever comes out of the doors of his house to meet him if God gives him the victory. God gives him the victory, which was never for sale. And his only child comes out of the door with tambourines.
11.theology:
Verse 29 before verse 30. The Spirit came first. Everything the vow asked for had already been given, unasked and unpriced, one verse earlier — and the victory in v. 32 answers the Spirit in v. 29, not the bargain in v. 30. This is a man who had never gone anywhere without terms agreed in advance, bringing that habit into the presence of God. A person can receive something wholly by grace and then spend a life paying for it, calling it gratitude, and do great damage in his own house.

Prayer learned in Tob. Trading a life for a battle is what the neighbours did — the king of Moab does exactly this on his wall (2 Kings 3:27) — and of such offerings God says he never commanded them and they never came into his mind (Jer. 7:31). Jephthah knows the national history well enough to lecture a king from it. He does not know how his own God is approached.

Leviticus 27:1-8. A person vowed to the LORD could be redeemed for a fixed valuation — thirty shekels for a woman, ten for a girl. There was a lawful way out, written down, in the same law he had been quarrying for three hundred years of border history. I cannot take back my vow was sincere and it was wrong. This is what ignorance of Scripture costs when the ignorant man is devout.

Did he kill her? The old reading that he dedicated her to lifelong virginity rests on a possible or in v. 31 and the triple stress on her virginity. It is not foolish, but it is the weaker case: olah never means anything but a whole burnt sacrifice, v. 35 is unintelligible if the outcome is religious service, Israel had no order of celibate women, and the daughters go out to lament her. Either way the vow was faithless, unnecessary and pagan in shape when he made it.

Moriah and Mizpah. Two fathers, two only children, two burnt offerings. On Moriah God commanded it, stopped it, and provided the ram himself (Gen. 22:12-14). At Mizpah God commanded nothing, stopped nothing and provided nothing — because nobody had asked him for any of it, and man's own religion has never yet produced a ram. So God brought his own Son up a hill and did not stop it, because that time there was no substitute to provide: he was the substitute.

Hebrews 11:32. Jephthah is named for faith alongside Gideon, Barak and Samson — the roll of this book's failures. Hebrews commends what these men did by faith (Heb. 11:33-34), not everything they did. He went out against Ammon believing the LORD would judge the case, and God honoured that. The chapter is not thereby approved.
11.examples:
Then: A man his family had written off argued Israel's case better than any leader in the book, referred the verdict to God, went out with the Spirit of the LORD upon him — and then offered to buy the victory he had already been given, and paid with his only child.

Now: Two tests come out of this chapter. First, examine the promises you have made to God in a crisis. If a vow was made to secure something, ask whether God had not already promised it — and whether the arrangement you call devotion is really a payment plan for grace. Second, note what destroyed Jephthah's house: not unbelief, but sincerity operating on a law he had never read. He is the warning to every earnest person who takes God seriously and does not take his Bible seriously. Thirty shekels and a chapter of Leviticus stood between his daughter and the altar, and he did not know it was there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Son of a Prostitute
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jephthah is introduced with a commendation and a disqualification in one sentence: a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute (v. 1). His father's legitimate sons drove him out with a legal formula — you shall not have an inheritance in our father's house (v. 2) — and he settled in Tob, where worthless fellows collected around him and went out with him (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The phrase for the men who joined him is the same class of word used of the gang Abimelech hired with the silver of Baal-berith (9:4). Empty men, with nothing to lose. On paper the new leader of Gilead has Abimelech's résumé.
verseByVerse.examples: Note where the disgrace actually sits. Jephthah did not choose his mother, and the brothers who threw him out had done nothing to earn the inheritance they were protecting. The book is about to make a great deal turn on a man his own family had written off.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute. Gilead was the father of Jephthah. And Gilead's wife also bore him sons. And when his wife's sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, "You shall not have an inheritance in our father's house, for you are the son of another woman." Then Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob, and worthless fellows collected around Jephthah and went out with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute. Gilead was the father of Jephthah.'

Two facts in one sentence, and the second one had already decided his life.

He is a mighty warrior — the same phrase the angel used of Gideon in the winepress, and in Jephthah's case demonstrably true. And he is the son of a prostitute, which in that society settled where he could live, what he could inherit and who would speak to him.

'And Gilead's wife also bore him sons. And when his wife's sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, "You shall not have an inheritance in our father's house, for you are the son of another woman."'

They waited until they were old enough to enforce it.

What they say to him is a legal formula, not an insult. They are not calling him names; they are issuing a ruling on the estate, and the grounds are his mother's occupation. He is being evicted from his father's house for something that happened before he was born.

Consider who is doing the evicting. These are the legitimate sons of Gilead, the respectable half of the family, protecting an inheritance they had done nothing to earn against a brother who had done nothing to lose it.

'Then Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob, and worthless fellows collected around Jephthah and went out with him.'

He goes over the border and becomes what men in his position became.

Tob is outside Israel, up towards Syria, and what forms around him there is a band of worthless fellows — empty men, the word means, men with nothing. It is the same class of word used of the crew Abimelech hired with the seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal (9:4).

Read that comparison carefully before the chapter goes any further. On paper, the man Gilead is about to make its head has Abimelech's exact profile: an irregular son, thrown out by his brothers, living off raiding with a company of empty men behind him.

The difference between them will not be their backgrounds. It will be that in verse 29 the Spirit of the LORD comes on this one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–11 — Hiring the Man They Threw Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: War comes, and the elders of Gilead go to Tob (vv. 4-5). Jephthah's reply is not gracious and it is not wrong: did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why have you come to me now when you are in distress? (v. 7). Their answer concedes everything — that is why we have turned to you now (v. 8) — and they raise the offer from commander to permanent head. He closes the deal, they swear by the LORD as witness, and he repeats every word of it before the LORD at Mizpah (vv. 9-11).
verseByVerse.theology: This is a negotiation, not a call. Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon: God raised them up or spoke to them. Here a committee that has run out of options hires a man on terms, and the terms are settled before the fighting starts.
verseByVerse.examples: Yet notice how carefully he brings the contract into God's presence at Mizpah (v. 11). Jephthah takes the LORD seriously throughout this chapter. That is precisely what makes what he does later so terrible.

verseByVerse.quote: After a time the Ammonites made war against Israel. And when the Ammonites made war against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob. And they said to Jephthah, "Come and be our leader, that we may fight against the Ammonites." But Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why have you come to me now when you are in distress?" And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "That is why we have turned to you now, that you may go with us and fight against the Ammonites and be our head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After a time the Ammonites made war against Israel. And when the Ammonites made war against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob.'

Here is the answer to the advertisement at the end of chapter 10.

The leaders of Gilead stood in a camp asking each other who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? (10:18). They have now worked their way through the list of respectable candidates, and the man they have come out to find is the one their own community had legally expelled.

'But Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why have you come to me now when you are in distress?"'

He does not make it easy for them, and he is not wrong.

Two questions, and both of them land. Did you not hate me — the elders were part of that, or at least signed off on it; a formal disinheritance is a public act, not a family quarrel. And why have you come to me now when you are in distress — which is to say, we both know you would not be standing in Tob if Ammon were quiet.

There is bitterness in it. There is also complete accuracy. He has correctly identified that he is being valued for his usefulness by people who never valued him for anything else.

'And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "That is why we have turned to you now, that you may go with us and fight against the Ammonites and be our head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."'

They concede the whole charge.

It is an unusual reply, and worth pausing over. They do not deny driving him out, do not explain, do not apologise. They say, in effect: yes, and that is exactly why we are here. Distress is the reason. We want you because we are desperate.

They have also raised the offer. Verse 6 asked him to be their leader, a battlefield commander for one campaign. Verse 8 offers him head over all the inhabitants of Gilead, which is the permanent civil office they had advertised. The price has gone up in two verses because they can see he might say no.

verseByVerse.quote: Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "If you bring me home again to fight against the Ammonites, and the LORD gives them over to me, I will be your head." And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "The LORD will be witness between us, if we do not do as you say." So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and leader over them. And Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "If you bring me home again to fight against the Ammonites, and the LORD gives them over to me, I will be your head."'

He accepts, and he gets it in writing.

Weigh the middle clause, because it is the best thing in the sentence: and the LORD gives them over to me. Jephthah is not promising to win. He is saying that if there is a victory it will be God's doing, and only then will he take the office. The outcast raider has better theology in his contract than the elders have in their crisis.

Set against that, he is still bargaining. He will not go without the headship, in advance, on terms. Nothing here is disinterested.

'And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "The LORD will be witness between us, if we do not do as you say."'

They swear. And since Jephthah has no standing to enforce anything against the men who disinherited him once already, the oath is all he has.

'So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and leader over them. And Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.'

Then he takes the contract to church.

That last clause matters for everything that follows. He repeats the whole agreement in God's presence at the sanctuary — every clause of it, out loud, before the LORD. This is a man who believes that words spoken to God are binding, and who wants God to have heard this one.

Hold that thought for twenty verses. When he stands in his own doorway and says I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow, it will not be a sudden attack of scruple. It is the same conviction, running all the way through the chapter, and it is a right conviction. What he does not know is what God's own law says about vows, and it will cost him everything he has.

Set the whole appointment beside the appointments earlier in the book, though. Othniel: the Spirit of the LORD was upon him. Ehud: the LORD raised up a deliverer. Deborah: she was already judging. Gideon: the angel of the LORD came and sat under the oak. Here, no one is sent. A committee negotiates terms with an available man, and the arrangement is ratified at Mizpah after it has been agreed.

God will honour it anyway (v. 29). But nobody in the chapter asked him first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–28 — A History Lesson to a King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before he fights, Jephthah writes. Ammon claims Israel stole its land coming up from Egypt (v. 13), and Jephthah answers with sixteen verses of history: Israel asked Edom and Moab for passage and was refused, went round both, and did not cross Moab's border at the Arnon (vv. 16-18). The land in dispute was taken from Sihon the Amorite, who attacked first and lost (vv. 19-22). He adds two arguments from precedent: Balak of Moab never went to war over it (v. 25), and Ammon has left the claim unpressed for three hundred years (v. 26). Then he refers the case upward: the LORD, the Judge, decide this day (v. 27). Ammon does not listen (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: It is the longest speech by any judge in the book, and its instinct is right: settle the history, establish the claim, and put the verdict in God's hands rather than assert it.
verseByVerse.examples: The details are shakier than the argument. He runs Moab and Ammon together throughout, and at v. 24 he names Chemosh your god — Chemosh was Moab's god; Ammon's was Milcom. A man who can lecture a king from the national archive and still confuse which god he is talking to is exactly the man who is about to make this vow.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites and said, "What do you have against me, that you have come to me to fight against my land?" And the king of the Ammonites answered the messengers of Jephthah, "Because Israel on coming up from Egypt took away my land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan; now therefore restore it peaceably." Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites and said to him, "Thus says Jephthah: Israel did not take away the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites and said, "What do you have against me, that you have come to me to fight against my land?"'

The mercenary's first act as head of Gilead is to open negotiations.

Everything in his background predicts otherwise. He is a raider by trade, with a band of empty men, hired specifically to fight. And he sends a letter, and the letter asks a question: what is your actual grievance?

Deuteronomy 20:10 requires exactly this — offer terms of peace before you besiege a city. Whether Jephthah knows the statute or is simply doing the sensible thing, he does what the law asks and what no one else in this half of the book bothers with.

'And the king of the Ammonites answered the messengers of Jephthah, "Because Israel on coming up from Egypt took away my land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan; now therefore restore it peaceably."'

The answer is a territorial claim with a date on it, and it deserves to be heard properly.

Ammon is not saying that Israel is offensive or that the borders are inconvenient. He is saying: that land was ours, you took it on the way up from Egypt, give it back. It is the kind of claim that gets made in every century, and the man making it evidently believes it.

'Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites and said to him, "Thus says Jephthah: Israel did not take away the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites..."'

The reply, when it comes, is not a threat. It is an argument.

There are sixteen verses of it, beginning with a flat denial of the premise and then producing the evidence. Thus says Jephthah is the formula a prophet uses, and there is a certain swagger in a border chieftain adopting it; but what follows is a serious piece of work, and it is the longest speech any judge makes in this book.

verseByVerse.quote: but when they came up from Egypt, Israel went through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh. Israel then sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, 'Please let us pass through your land,' but the king of Edom would not listen. And they sent also to the king of Moab, but he would not consent. So Israel remained at Kadesh. "Then they journeyed through the wilderness and went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab and arrived on the east side of the land of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon. But they did not enter the territory of Moab, for the Arnon was the boundary of Moab. Israel then sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, king of Heshbon, and Israel said to him, 'Please let us pass through your land to our country,' but Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory, so Sihon gathered all his people together and encamped at Jahaz and fought with Israel. And the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, and they defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites, who inhabited that country. And they took possession of all the territory of the Amorites from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"...but when they came up from Egypt, Israel went through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh. Israel then sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, 'Please let us pass through your land,' but the king of Edom would not listen. And they sent also to the king of Moab, but he would not consent. So Israel remained at Kadesh."'

The defence opens by establishing what Israel asked for and did not get.

Twice Israel requested passage, from Edom and from Moab. Twice it was refused. And twice Israel accepted the refusal and stayed put — which is the point of the detail. A nation that took land by force when it was told no would not have sat at Kadesh.

'"Then they journeyed through the wilderness and went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab and arrived on the east side of the land of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon. But they did not enter the territory of Moab, for the Arnon was the boundary of Moab."'

They went the long way round rather than cross a border they had no right to cross.

Jephthah names the boundary precisely: the Arnon. Everything south of that river is Moab's, and Israel camped on the far side of it and stayed there. He is arguing from a survey.

'"Israel then sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, king of Heshbon, and Israel said to him, 'Please let us pass through your land to our country,' but Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory, so Sihon gathered all his people together and encamped at Jahaz and fought with Israel."'

A third request, and this time the refusal came with an army attached.

Everything turns on that. Israel asked Sihon for passage on the same terms it had asked Edom and Moab, and Sihon did not merely say no. He mobilised and marched out to Jahaz to attack.

'"And the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, and they defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites, who inhabited that country, and they took possession of all the territory of the Amorites from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan."'

There is the answer to Ammon's claim, in one word: Amorites.

Compare the two descriptions. Ammon claimed the land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan (v. 13). Jephthah has just said Israel took, from the Amorites, the territory from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan (v. 22). The same boundaries, to the mile — and a different previous owner.

The disputed land was not Ammonite when Israel arrived. It was Sihon's, and Sihon had taken it from Moab a generation earlier (Num. 21:26). Israel took it from the man who attacked them, in a war they did not start, having asked first. Ammon is claiming compensation for a loss somebody else suffered.

verseByVerse.quote: So then the LORD, the God of Israel, dispossessed the Amorites from before his people Israel; and are you to take possession of them? Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you to possess? And all that the LORD our God has dispossessed before us, we will possess.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"So then the LORD, the God of Israel, dispossessed the Amorites from before his people Israel; and are you to take possession of them?"'

Having proved the case in court, he moves it to a higher one.

The argument so far has been legal and historical: whose land was it, who attacked whom, where does the boundary run. Now Jephthah says the thing that actually settles it. The Amorites were not evicted by Israelite arms. The LORD, the God of Israel, dispossessed them. And what God has granted, a king of Ammon is not in a position to reassign.

'"Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you to possess? And all that the LORD our God has dispossessed before us, we will possess."'

Then comes a verse that has troubled readers for a long time, because it sounds as though Jephthah thinks Chemosh is real.

Take the difficulty at full strength first. He appears to be saying: your god gives you land, our God gives us land, and each nation keeps what its own deity provides. That is henotheism — not the denial that other gods exist, but the claim that each people has its own — and it is not what Israel was taught. Deuteronomy 4:39 says the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath, there is no other.

Two things can be said, and the first is that this is diplomacy. Jephthah is writing to a foreign king in that king's own terms, arguing from a premise his correspondent already holds: by your own principles, you keep what Chemosh gives; by that same principle, leave alone what the LORD has given. It is the form of argument, not necessarily the writer's creed.

The second is more uncomfortable and probably also true. Jephthah's theology is roughly right and imprecise in its details, and this chapter will show us that again. He has just spent seven verses on the map with impressive accuracy, and he has confused which nation he is addressing: Chemosh was the god of Moab. Ammon's god was Milcom. He runs the two peoples together here and at verses 15, 17-18 and 25 as well.

He knows the history well enough to lecture a king about it, and he does not have the details straight. Remember that when he opens his mouth in verse 30.

verseByVerse.quote: Now are you any better than Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever contend against Israel, or did he ever go to war with them? While Israel lived in Heshbon and its villages, and in Aroer and its villages, and in all the cities that are on the banks of the Arnon, 300 years, why did you not deliver them within that time? I therefore have not sinned against you, and you do me wrong by making war on me. The LORD, the Judge, decide this day between the people of Israel and the people of Ammon." But the king of the Ammonites did not listen to the words of Jephthah that he sent to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'"Now are you any better than Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever contend against Israel, or did he ever go to war with them?"'

A last argument from precedent, and it is a good one.

Balak had every reason to fight for that land and never did. He was frightened enough of Israel to hire a prophet to curse them from a hilltop (Num. 22), which tells you what he thought of his chances in the field. But he never disputed the title, and he never went to war over it. If the rightful owner did not press the claim, why is Ammon pressing it now?

'"While Israel lived in Heshbon and its villages, and in Aroer and its villages, and in all the cities that are on the banks of the Arnon, 300 years, why did you not deliver them within that time?"'

Three hundred years of settled possession, and not one attempt to recover it.

Any lawyer would reach for this argument: if it was yours, you have had three centuries to say so. Jephthah even names the towns — Heshbon, Aroer, the villages along the Arnon — so the king can check the roll himself.

The figure is also the one solid chronological marker in the book, and it puts the exodus roughly three hundred years before Jephthah.

'"I therefore have not sinned against you, and you do me wrong by making war on me. The LORD, the Judge, decide this day between the people of Israel and the people of Ammon."'

He ends by refusing to be the judge of his own case.

He has made his argument; he does not then declare himself the winner. He hands the file upward: the LORD, the Judge, decide this day. In a book called Judges, where every strong man has so far settled his own quarrels with his own hands, a leader who submits a territorial dispute to God for a verdict is doing something the others never thought of.

'But the king of the Ammonites did not listen to the words of Jephthah that he sent to him.'

One flat verse for the reply.

Sixteen verses of careful history, three arguments from precedent, and a formal referral to God — and it changed nothing at all. Weigh that before we go on to the fighting. Jephthah did everything right here, and it did not work, and the war happened anyway. A good case, well made, does not always end a quarrel; sometimes it simply establishes who was in the right when the quarrel turned violent.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–33 — The Spirit, and Then the Vow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then the Spirit of the LORD was upon Jephthah (v. 29). He passes through Gilead and Manasseh raising the muster. And then, with the Spirit already on him, he makes a vow: if God gives Ammon into his hand, whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me... shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering (vv. 30-31). God gives Ammon into his hand and twenty cities fall (vv. 32-33).
verseByVerse.theology: The order of verses 29 and 30 is the whole tragedy. The Spirit came first. Everything the vow asks for had already been given, unasked and unpurchased, one verse earlier.
verseByVerse.examples: And the shape of the bargain is not Israelite. Offering a life in exchange for a victory is what the neighbours did — the king of Moab does exactly this on his city wall (2 Kings 3:27). Jephthah has spent a chapter proving he knows whose land it is, and prays like a man who has learned to pray from Ammon.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Spirit of the LORD was upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh and passed on to Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he passed on to the Ammonites. And Jephthah made a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will give the Ammonites into my hand, then whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the Spirit of the LORD was upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh and passed on to Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he passed on to the Ammonites.'

Read that verse and then read the next one, and do not let the chapter division or the paragraph break soften what stands between them.

The Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah. This is the formula the book uses for Othniel, Gideon and Samson — God taking hold of a man and equipping him for the work. Whatever the elders negotiated at Mizpah, God has now put his own hand on the appointment. Jephthah is raising the muster with divine authority on him and moving towards the enemy.

He has everything he needs. The commission is settled. The outcome is not in doubt.

'And Jephthah made a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will give the Ammonites into my hand, then whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering."'

Then, with the Spirit of God already upon him, he tries to buy what he has just been given.

That is the tragedy of this chapter in two verses, and everything after it follows from the order they come in. Verse 29 is grace: unasked, unpriced, already granted. Verse 30 is a purchase offer for the same goods. If you will give the Ammonites into my hand — he is negotiating for a thing he is already carrying.
