He has done this before, of course. He would not go with the elders until the headship was agreed in advance; he would not fight without terms. A man who has survived by getting everything in writing has now brought that habit into the presence of God, and God does not do business on those terms.

Consider what he actually offers. Whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me. The Hebrew is not whatever in the sense of any stray animal; the phrase is personal, and houses in that country were not full of livestock waiting at the door. What comes out of the doors of a man's house to meet him when he comes home in triumph, with tambourines, is his household.

People have tried hard to make this a promise about a goat. The text does not read that way.

Trace where this kind of prayer comes from. Trading a life for a victory is precisely what the surrounding nations did — the king of Moab does it on his own city wall when the battle turns against him, and offers his eldest son as a burnt offering (2 Kings 3:27). Of Israel's God, Jeremiah says he never commanded such a thing, and that it never came into his mind (Jer. 7:31).

Jephthah has just spent sixteen verses proving to a foreign king that he knows whose land this is and who gave it. He has learned the history. He has not learned how his own God is to be approached, and he prays like a man who picked up his religion in Tob.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the LORD gave them into his hand. And he struck them from Aroer to the neighborhood of Minnith, twenty cities, and as far as Abel-keramim, with a great blow. So the Ammonites were subdued before the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the LORD gave them into his hand. And he struck them from Aroer to the neighborhood of Minnith, twenty cities, and as far as Abel-keramim, with a great blow. So the Ammonites were subdued before the people of Israel.'

God kept his side of a bargain he had never made.

Say it plainly, because that is what these two verses record. The LORD gave Ammon into Jephthah's hand — comprehensively; twenty cities, a great blow, the oppression broken. The eighteen years of chapter 10 are over.

It was never conditional on the vow. Verse 29 had already settled the outcome before the vow was spoken. The victory in verse 32 is the answer to the Spirit in verse 29, not the payment due on verse 30.

But Jephthah does not know that, and it is the source of everything that happens next. He is riding home from the greatest day of his life convinced that he owes for it.

Carry this away, because it is not confined to the Iron Age. A man can receive something entirely by grace and spend the rest of his life paying for it. He will call that gratitude, and it will look like devotion, and it will do damage in his house — because underneath it is the settled belief that God gave on terms, and the terms are now due.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He comes home and his daughter comes out to meet him with tambourines and dancing — she was his only child (v. 34). His first words blame her: you have brought me very low, and you have become the cause of great trouble to me (v. 35). Her reply is the noblest speech in the chapter: do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth (v. 36). She asks for two months on the mountains, returns, and he did with her according to his vow (vv. 37-39). The daughters of Israel go out to lament her four days a year (v. 40).
verseByVerse.theology: Leviticus 27:1-8 sets a redemption price for a person vowed to the LORD — thirty shekels for a woman, ten for a girl. There was a lawful way out, in the law he had just spent sixteen verses quarrying for history, and he did not know it was there.
verseByVerse.examples: Two fathers, two only children, two burnt offerings asked for. On Moriah God commanded it and then stopped it and provided the ram himself (Gen. 22:12-13). Here nobody commanded it, nobody stopped it, and no substitute was provided — because no one had asked God for any of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jephthah came to his home at Mizpah. And behold, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and with dances. She was his only child; besides her he had neither son nor daughter. And as soon as he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, "Alas, my daughter! You have brought me very low, and you have become the cause of great trouble to me. For I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Jephthah came to his home at Mizpah. And behold, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and with dances.'

The behold is the narrator making us stand in the road with him.

What comes out of the doors of the house is exactly what should come out of the doors of a house on such a day: a girl with a tambourine, doing what Miriam did at the sea and what the women would do for Saul and David. Israel's victories were met with dancing daughters. This is the customary, joyful, entirely proper thing.

She has no idea. She is the first out of the door because she is the gladdest person in Gilead.

'She was his only child; besides her he had neither son nor daughter.'

The narrator stops the story to tell us this, and the sentence says it twice.

Jephthah was thrown out of his father's house with the words you shall not have an inheritance. He has fought his way to the headship of all Gilead, and this girl is everything he has to leave it to. The line ends here either way.

'And as soon as he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, "Alas, my daughter! You have brought me very low, and you have become the cause of great trouble to me. For I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow."'

The grief is real and the sentence is monstrous.

Look at the pronouns. You have brought me very low. You have become the cause of great trouble to me. She has done nothing but come home to meet her father, and in the first words out of his mouth she is the agent, he is the victim, and the trouble is his own.

Not once in the verse does he say what have I done.

Then the reason: I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow. And here is the terrible part, because he is half right. He is right that vows to God are not disposable. Ecclesiastes says it flatly — better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Eccl. 5:5). Jephthah's reverence is real. That is why it kills.

What he is wrong about is I cannot. The law he is appealing to had made provision for exactly this case, and he does not know it is there.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said to him, "My father, you have opened your mouth to the LORD; do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth, now that the LORD has avenged you on your enemies, on the Ammonites." So she said to her father, "Let this thing be done for me: leave me alone two months, that I may go up and down on the mountains and weep for my virginity, I and my companions." So he said, "Go." Then he sent her away for two months, and she departed, she and her companions, and wept for her virginity on the mountains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And she said to him, "My father, you have opened your mouth to the LORD; do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth, now that the LORD has avenged you on your enemies, on the Ammonites."'

The person with the least to gain from it speaks better than anyone else in the chapter.

She does not argue, does not run, does not point out that she is not the one who opened his mouth. She takes her father's premise more seriously than he does — a word given to God must be kept — and she puts God's victory over Ammon in the sentence as the reason. The LORD has done his part, she says. Do yours.

Nobody has taught her badly. That is the awful thing. She has evidently been raised to believe that God is to be taken at his word and honoured at cost, and she is about to be destroyed by a man who half believes the same thing.

'So she said to her father, "Let this thing be done for me: leave me alone two months, that I may go up and down on the mountains and weep for my virginity, I and my companions." So he said, "Go." Then he sent her away for two months, and she departed, she and her companions, and wept for her virginity on the mountains.'

She asks for two months, and she does not ask for a reprieve.

Name exactly what she is grieving. Not her life, in the first instance, but her virginity — that she will never marry, never bear a child, never carry her father's name into another generation. In that world a woman's future was her children, and the loss is total: the family ends, and she ends with it.

She takes her friends with her. The last two months of her life are spent on the hills with the other girls of Gilead, weeping, and then she walks back down.

He says one word to her in these verses. Go.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of two months, she returned to her father, who did with her according to his vow that he had made. She had never known a man, and it became a custom in Israel that the daughters of Israel went year by year to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in the year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And at the end of two months, she returned to her father, who did with her according to his vow that he had made. She had never known a man.'

The narrator will not describe it.

Ten words for the thing itself — who did with her according to his vow that he had made — and then a sentence about her, not him: she had never known a man. The writer who gave us the tent peg through Sisera's temple and the fat closing over Ehud's blade turns his face away here.

Now the question every reader asks, and it deserves a straight answer: did Jephthah kill her?

There is a long-standing view that he did not — that he dedicated her to lifelong service at the sanctuary instead, and that what she and Israel mourned was her perpetual virginity. Two things are urged for it. The Hebrew connective in verse 31 can sometimes be read as or: whatever comes out shall be the LORD's, or I will offer it up. And the passage is strikingly insistent about her virginity — three times in four verses — which would be an odd thing to stress if the point were her death.

It is not a foolish reading, and it has been held by serious men. But it is the less likely one, and honesty requires saying so.

Against it: burnt offering is not a flexible term. An olah is an animal killed and wholly consumed on an altar; the word never means dedicated service anywhere in the Old Testament. Verse 35 makes no sense if the outcome is a religious vocation — a man does not tear his clothes and cry that he has been brought very low because his daughter is going to serve at the tabernacle. There was no order of celibate women in Israel for her to join. And the daughters of Israel do not visit her four days a year; they go out to lament her.

The plain reading is that he burned her, and the plain reading is almost certainly right.

What does not depend on the answer is the thing that matters most, so hold on to it either way: the vow was faithless when he made it, unnecessary when he made it, and pagan in shape when he made it. God had already given him the victory one verse earlier. Nothing was owed. The whole catastrophe grew out of a man trying to pay for grace.

There was a way out, too. Leviticus 27:1-8 legislates for precisely this — a person vowed to the LORD may be redeemed by paying a fixed valuation to the sanctuary; thirty shekels for a woman between twenty and sixty, ten for a girl. Thirty shekels of silver, and she comes home. It is not a loophole; it is the law making room for exactly the situation Jephthah is standing in. He could quote three hundred years of national history to a foreign king, and he did not know what his own God's book said about vows.

That is what ignorance of Scripture costs when a sincere man is the one who is ignorant.

'and it became a custom in Israel that the daughters of Israel went year by year to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in the year.'

The book gives her no name.

Her father has a name, a genealogy, a tribe, a hometown, an office and sixteen verses of speech. She has four days a year and a description: the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite. The girls of Israel kept her memory when the record did not.

One more thing, because someone will have thought of it and it is right to answer it here: Jephthah is named in Hebrews 11 among those commended for faith (Heb. 11:32). So how does this chapter stand in that list?

Consider the company he keeps there — Gideon, Barak, Samson. Hebrews is not certifying those lives; it is naming men who, at particular moments, believed God and acted on it, and the verses that follow describe what they did: conquered kingdoms... were made strong out of weakness... put foreign armies to flight (Heb. 11:33-34). Jephthah went out against Ammon believing that the LORD, the Judge, would decide the case, and God honoured that. Hebrews commends a man for the faith he had. It has never said that everything the man did was faith.

Now stand this chapter beside the one other place in Scripture where a father takes his only child up a mountain for a burnt offering.

On Moriah, God commanded it — and then stopped it with a shout, and provided a ram caught in the thicket, and the mountain was named the LORD will provide (Gen. 22:12-14). At Mizpah, God commanded nothing, no voice came from heaven, and no substitute was found — because nobody had asked God for any of this. It was a man's own idea from beginning to end, and man's own religion has never yet produced a ram.

So God, in the end, brought his own only Son up a hill and did not stop it. There was no substitute available that day either, and for the opposite reason: he was the substitute. Jephthah's daughter died for nothing, because of a word her father should never have spoken and could have redeemed for thirty pieces of silver. The Son of God died for everything, because of a word the Father had spoken before the world began — and the thirty pieces of silver that changed hands that week were the price of betraying him, not of buying him back.

No unnamed girl need ever again walk down off a mountain to pay for a victory. It has been paid for.

12.title: Jephthah's Conflict and the Minor Judges
12.text: <sup>1</sup>The men of Ephraim were called to arms, and they crossed to Zaphon and said to Jephthah, "Why did you cross over to fight against the Ammonites and did not call us to go with you? We will burn your house over you with fire."<sup>2</sup>And Jephthah said to them, "I and my people had a great dispute with the Ammonites, and when I called you, you did not save me from their hand.<sup>3</sup>And when I saw that you would not save me, I took my life in my hand and crossed over against the Ammonites, and the LORD gave them into my hand. Why then have you come up to me this day to fight against me?"<sup>4</sup>Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought with Ephraim. And the men of Gilead struck Ephraim, because they said, "You are fugitives of Ephraim, you Gileadites, in the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh."<sup>5</sup>And the Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan against the Ephraimites. And when any of the fugitives of Ephraim said, "Let me go over," the men of Gilead said to him, "Are you an Ephraimite?" When he said, "No,"<sup>6</sup>they said to him, "Then say Shibboleth," and he said, "Sibboleth," for he could not pronounce it right. Then they seized him and slaughtered him at the fords of the Jordan. At that time 42,000 of the Ephraimites fell.<sup>7</sup>Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his city in Gilead.<sup>8</sup>After him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.<sup>9</sup>He had thirty sons, and thirty daughters he gave in marriage outside his clan, and thirty daughters he brought in from outside for his sons. And he judged Israel seven years.<sup>10</sup>Then Ibzan died and was buried at Bethlehem.<sup>11</sup>After him Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel, and he judged Israel ten years.<sup>12</sup>Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.<sup>13</sup>After him Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel.<sup>14</sup>He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys, and he judged Israel eight years.<sup>15</sup>Then Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
12.overview:
Ephraim crosses the Jordan to confront Jephthah with the same complaint they made to Gideon — why did you not call us — and this time with a threat of arson attached. Jephthah's reply is factually correct and theologically right: I did call you, you did not come, and the LORD gave them into my hand. Gideon had answered the same charge with a compliment and the anger subsided. Jephthah stands on the record, and forty-two thousand Israelites die.

The Gileadites take the fords of the Jordan — the tactic Ehud used against Moab and Ephraim itself used against Midian — and set a one-word examination at the crossing. Not a password, which could be guessed or betrayed, but a dialect trap: say Shibboleth. A man from the western hills could not make the sound, and was killed for an accent he had never chosen and could not hear.

Then Jephthah dies after six years, with the formula that closed every earlier account conspicuously missing — the land does not rest. Three more judges follow in eight verses: Ibzan with sixty arranged marriages, Elon with nothing recorded at all, Abdon with forty sons and thirty grandsons on seventy donkeys. No oppressor is named in any of the three. And the last line of the chapter buries a judge of Israel in Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
12.theology:
Right, and wrong. Every sentence Jephthah speaks in vv. 2-3 is true, and the outcome is the worst slaughter in the book. Gideon met the identical complaint by handing over credit he had earned (8:2-3), and nobody died — Proverbs 15:1 acted out in narrative. Being right is not the same as being wise, and a man who insists on his accuracy in a family quarrel can win the argument and bury the consequences.

Shibboleth. The test at the ford examines nothing the man believes and nothing he has done. It examines how he says a word he has been saying all his life. The church has kept the practice, which is why the term survives: the phrase you must use, the version you must carry, the line you must take on a secondary question that marks you as one of us. It sorts people efficiently, and it leaves on the far bank a great many who love the Lord Jesus and only say so with a different accent. At his crossing there is no such test — everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved, and Paul's argument for it is precisely that there is no distinction (Rom. 10:12-13).

The missing rest. The land had rest closed the accounts of Othniel, Ehud, Deborah and Gideon. It is not said of Jephthah and is never said again in the book. He broke Ammon and spent the peace on a civil war, and a deliverer who kills forty-two thousand of the delivered has given nobody rest.

Amalek on the map. Abdon is buried in Ephraim, the heartland, in the hill country of the Amalekites — named for the people who attacked Israel first at Rephidim and whose memory God swore to blot out (Ex. 17:8, 14; Deut. 25:17-19). Three hundred years on it is a district with an address, and nobody in the chapter thinks it needs explaining. That is how a compromise finishes: not with a decision, but with a place name no one notices any more.
12.examples:
Then: A tribe too proud to fight the war showed up in force to argue about the credit, was answered with the plain facts, and lost forty-two thousand men at a river crossing to a test that examined nothing but their accent.

Now: Two things to take away. First, in the next disagreement where you are demonstrably in the right, ask what it would cost to give away credit you had actually earned — because Gideon did that and the quarrel ended, and Jephthah proved his case and buried the dead. Second, name your own shibboleths. Every congregation has a word, a translation, a position on a secondary matter that quietly decides who is one of us. Test it honestly: is this the gospel, or is it an accent? The Lord asks nobody at his ford to prove himself by pronunciation.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim musters, crosses the Jordan, and threatens the man who has just won the war: why did you cross over to fight against the Ammonites and did not call us to go with you? We will burn your house over you with fire (v. 1). Jephthah's reply is a correction of fact — I did call you, and you did not come — followed by the only claim that matters: the LORD gave them into my hand (vv. 2-3).
verseByVerse.theology: They made this same complaint to Gideon after Midian fell (8:1). Gideon answered with a compliment and the anger subsided. Jephthah answers with the record, and every word of it is true, and it ends in a massacre.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice what Ephraim was not doing during the eighteen years Ammon crushed Gilead. They cross the Jordan quickly enough now that there is credit to be argued over.

verseByVerse.quote: The men of Ephraim were called to arms, and they crossed to Zaphon and said to Jephthah, "Why did you cross over to fight against the Ammonites and did not call us to go with you? We will burn your house over you with fire." And Jephthah said to them, "I and my people had a great dispute with the Ammonites, and when I called you, you did not save me from their hand. And when I saw that you would not save me, I took my life in my hand and crossed over against the Ammonites, and the LORD gave them into my hand. Why then have you come up to me this day to fight against me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The men of Ephraim were called to arms, and they crossed to Zaphon and said to Jephthah, "Why did you cross over to fight against the Ammonites and did not call us to go with you? We will burn your house over you with fire."'

Ephraim has said this before, almost word for word.

After Gideon broke Midian, they came to him with the same grievance: why did you not call us (8:1). It is a complaint about credit dressed as a complaint about procedure, and it comes from the largest and proudest tribe in the north, which does not like a victory it did not share.

But look at the difference in the threat. To Gideon they only accused him fiercely. To Jephthah they promise arson with the family inside.

Weigh also where they were for the previous eighteen years. Ammon had been crushing Gilead since 10:8, and Ephraim did not cross the river once. They cross it now, in force, with an army, because somebody else won.

'And Jephthah said to them, "I and my people had a great dispute with the Ammonites, and when I called you, you did not save me from their hand. And when I saw that you would not save me, I took my life in my hand and crossed over against the Ammonites, and the LORD gave them into my hand. Why then have you come up to me this day to fight against me?"'

His answer is entirely accurate, and it is the wrong answer.

Take the accuracy first. Ephraim says he did not call; Jephthah says he did, and they did not come. One of them is lying, and nothing in chapter 11 suggests it is Jephthah — that chapter showed a man who researched his facts before he opened his mouth. I took my life in my hand is the phrase of a man who went out without support and knew it.

The centre of the reply is right where it should be: the LORD gave them into my hand. He is not claiming the victory. He is claiming that the argument about who deserves credit is beside the point, because neither party won it.

So why is it the wrong answer? Because Gideon had the same complaint from the same tribe and handled it differently.

Gideon said: what have I done in comparison with you? Is not the gleaning of Ephraim's grapes better than the whole vintage of Abiezer? (8:2). It was flattery, and it was not strictly true, and their anger against him subsided when he said it. A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger (Prov. 15:1). Gideon gave away credit he had earned, and nobody died.

Jephthah stands on the record. He is right about the facts and right about the theology, and in the next three verses forty-two thousand Israelites are killed.

There is a hard lesson sitting in the gap between chapter 8 and chapter 12, and it will not go away by being uncomfortable. Being right is not the same as being wise, and the man who insists on his accuracy in a quarrel may win the argument and bury the consequences.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gilead is taunted as a colony of Ephraimite runaways (v. 4), so Jephthah fights, and the Gileadites seize the fords of the Jordan behind the retreating Ephraimites. Every man who asks to cross is made to say one word. Shibboleth — and a man of Ephraim cannot get the first consonant out, and says Sibboleth, and is killed on the riverbank. Forty-two thousand fell (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The test is not what a man believes or what he has done. It is how he pronounces a word he has been saying all his life without ever hearing anything wrong with it.
verseByVerse.examples: Forty-two thousand is the largest Israelite death toll the book has recorded, and it was inflicted entirely by Israelites. Jephthah wrote sixteen careful verses to a pagan king trying to avoid a war. He sent no letter at all to his own countrymen.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought with Ephraim. And the men of Gilead struck Ephraim, because they said, "You are fugitives of Ephraim, you Gileadites, in the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh." And the Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan against the Ephraimites. And when any of the fugitives of Ephraim said, "Let me go over," the men of Gilead said to him, "Are you an Ephraimite?" When he said, "No," they said to him, "Then say Shibboleth," and he said, "Sibboleth," for he could not pronounce it right. Then they seized him and slaughtered him at the fords of the Jordan. At that time 42,000 of the Ephraimites fell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought with Ephraim. And the men of Gilead struck Ephraim, because they said, "You are fugitives of Ephraim, you Gileadites, in the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh."'

The insult that starts the killing is about status.

Ephraim's taunt is that the Gileadites are nobodies — runaways and leftovers of Ephraim and Manasseh, living out east on land nobody wanted, with no proper standing among the tribes. It is an old sneer directed at people on the far side of the river.

Of all the men in Israel to say that to, they say it to Jephthah. A man who was thrown out of his father's house as the wrong sort of son, told he would have no inheritance, and who has spent his whole life being the outsider that respectable people call in when they are desperate.

'And the Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan against the Ephraimites. And when any of the fugitives of Ephraim said, "Let me go over," the men of Gilead said to him, "Are you an Ephraimite?" When he said, "No," they said to him, "Then say Shibboleth," and he said, "Sibboleth," for he could not pronounce it right.'

Seizing the fords of the Jordan is a manoeuvre this book has praised twice.

Ehud took the fords against Moab and not a man escaped (3:28). Gideon sent to Ephraim to take the waters against Midian, and they did it and killed Oreb and Zeeb (7:24). It is the standard way of finishing a beaten enemy in this country: hold the crossings and let the retreat come to you.

Here it is Israelites holding the river against Israelites, and the tribe manning the checkpoint learned the tactic from the tribe now trying to get through it.

Then the word. Shibboleth means an ear of grain, or a flowing stream, and it is not a password — there is nothing to guess and no secret to betray. It is a dialect trap. The Ephraimite pronunciation of that first consonant was different, and a man from the western hills simply could not make the sound, however hard he tried, however loudly he swore he was not an Ephraimite.

He was condemned by an accent he had never chosen and could not hear.

'Then they seized him and slaughtered him at the fords of the Jordan. At that time 42,000 of the Ephraimites fell.'

Forty-two thousand.

Set that figure beside the rest of the book. It is the largest number of Israelites recorded dead in Judges, and not one of them was killed by Ammon, Moab, Midian, Canaan or Philistia. They were killed by other Israelites, one at a time, at a river crossing, after a hearing that lasted one word.

The man who ran that checkpoint had written sixteen verses of patient history to a foreign king in an effort to prevent a war. To his own countrymen he sent nothing at all.

The church has kept the practice, which is why the word is still in the language. A shibboleth is a test of belonging that has nothing to do with the truth being tested — the phrase you must use, the version you must carry, the position on a secondary question that marks you as one of us. It sorts people efficiently. It also puts on one side of the river a great many who love the Lord Jesus and merely say it with a different accent.

The Judge himself sets no such test at his crossing. Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved — and Paul's whole point in writing it is that there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, no dialect that disqualifies (Rom. 10:12-13). He knows his own, and he has never once asked a man to prove it by his pronunciation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — Six Years, No Rest, and Seventy Donkeys
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jephthah judged six years and died — the shortest tenure of any major judge, and the first whose account does not end and the land had rest (v. 7). Three more judges follow in eight verses. Ibzan of Bethlehem had thirty sons and thirty daughters and arranged sixty marriages, thirty out of the clan and thirty in (vv. 8-9). Elon the Zebulunite judged ten years, and nothing else is said about him (vv. 11-12). Abdon had forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode on seventy donkeys, and was buried at Pirathon in Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: No oppressor is named in any of the three notices, and no deliverance is recorded. What is recorded is families — sons, marriages, mounts. The office has quietly become an estate to be managed and passed on.
verseByVerse.examples: And the last line of the chapter drops a detail without comment. Deep inside Ephraim, in the promised land, there is a stretch of hill country named after Amalek. Nobody in these verses seems to think that needs explaining.

verseByVerse.quote: Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his city in Gilead. After him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel. He had thirty sons, and thirty daughters he gave in marriage outside his clan, and thirty daughters he brought in from outside for his sons. And he judged Israel seven years. Then Ibzan died and was buried at Bethlehem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his city in Gilead.'

Six years, and no rest.

Both halves of that sentence matter. Six years is the shortest tenure of any major judge in the book — Othniel had forty, Ehud eighty, Deborah forty, Gideon forty. And the formula that closed all four of those accounts is missing here. The land had rest. It is not said of Jephthah, and it will not be said again.

He broke Ammon, and the land did not rest, and the reason is in the verses just above: the peace was spent on a civil war. A deliverer who kills forty-two thousand of the people he delivered has not given anybody rest.

He is buried in his own city in Gilead, in the country he was driven out of, as its head. He got everything he negotiated for and lost the only person he had.

'After him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel. He had thirty sons, and thirty daughters he gave in marriage outside his clan, and thirty daughters he brought in from outside for his sons. And he judged Israel seven years. Then Ibzan died and was buried at Bethlehem.'

Sixty marriages, arranged in both directions.

That is the whole record of the man, and it reads as exactly what it is: a description of a political operation. Thirty daughters sent out to other clans and thirty daughters brought in for his sons is a network of sixty families tied to his house by marriage. It is how dynasties were built.

No oppressor is named in his notice. No enemy, no battle, no deliverance, no cry to God. He judged seven years and consolidated.

Here is what the office has become. Othniel, Ehud, Deborah and Gideon were raised up against an enemy. Ibzan is raised up against nobody, and spends his term arranging weddings.

verseByVerse.quote: After him Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel, and he judged Israel ten years. Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun. After him Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel. He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys, and he judged Israel eight years. Then Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After him Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel, and he judged Israel ten years. Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.'

Ten years, and the writer has nothing whatever to report.

Not one act, not one word, not one enemy. His name, his tribe, his term, his grave. The verse tells us where he was buried and nothing about what he did there while he was alive.

'After him Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel. He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys, and he judged Israel eight years.'

Seventy donkeys.

The count has been rising all through this section. Jair had thirty sons on thirty donkeys (10:4). Ibzan had thirty sons and sixty marriage alliances. Abdon has forty sons and thirty grandsons, and seventy mounts for them — and a donkey was a mark of rank in that country, so this is a family that rides out in a body, seventy strong, and everybody in the district knows who they are.

Seventy is also the number of Gideon's sons, and the number of brothers Abimelech killed on one stone. The book does not press the point. It simply keeps counting.

'Then Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.'

Read the last four words of the chapter slowly, because the writer drops them and walks away.

Pirathon is in Ephraim. Ephraim is the heartland — Joshua's own tribe, the centre of the promised inheritance, as far from the frontier as it is possible to get. And a district in those hills is called after the Amalekites.

Amalek was the people who attacked Israel first, at Rephidim, before Sinai, before the law, picking off the stragglers at the back (Ex. 17:8; Deut. 25:17-18). God swore that day to blot out their memory from under heaven. Three hundred years later there is countryside in the middle of Israel that carries their name on the map, and a judge of Israel is buried in it, and nobody in the chapter thinks it worth a comment.

That is how a compromise ends. Not with a decision, but with a place name that nobody notices any more. The thing you failed to remove stops being an enemy and becomes an address.

So the chapter closes: twenty-five years, three judges, no oppression named, no deliverance recorded, one hundred sons and grandsons, seventy donkeys, sixty marriages, and a stretch of Amalekite hill country in the middle of the promised land.

Israel has leaders, and no one is leading it anywhere.

13.title: Samson's Birth
13.text: <sup>1</sup>And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, so the LORD gave them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years.<sup>2</sup>There was a certain man of Zorah, of the tribe of the Danites, whose name was Manoah. And his wife was barren and had no children.<sup>3</sup>And the angel of the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, "Behold, you are barren and have not borne children, but you shall conceive and bear a son.<sup>4</sup>Therefore be careful and drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean,<sup>5</sup>for behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. No razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines."<sup>6</sup>Then the woman came and told her husband, "A man of God came to me, and his appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, very awesome. I did not ask him where he was from, and he did not tell me his name,<sup>7</sup>but he said to me, 'Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. So then drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.'"<sup>8</sup>Then Manoah prayed to the LORD and said, "O Lord, please let the man of God whom you sent come again to us and teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born."<sup>9</sup>And God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman as she sat in the field. But Manoah her husband was not with her.<sup>10</sup>So the woman ran quickly and told her husband, "Behold, the man who came to me the other day has appeared to me."<sup>11</sup>And Manoah arose and went after his wife and came to the man and said to him, "Are you the man who spoke to this woman?" And he said, "I am."<sup>12</sup>And Manoah said, "Now when your words come true, what is to be the child's manner of life, and what is his mission?"<sup>13</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "Of all that I said to the woman let her be careful.<sup>14</sup>She may not eat of anything that comes from the vine, neither let her drink wine or strong drink, or eat any unclean thing. All that I commanded her let her observe."<sup>15</sup>Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "Please let us detain you and prepare a young goat for you."<sup>16</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "If you detain me, I will not eat of your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, then offer it to the LORD." (For Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the LORD.)<sup>17</sup>And Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "What is your name, so that, when your words come true, we may honor you?"<sup>18</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to him, "Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?"<sup>19</sup>So Manoah took the young goat with the grain offering, and offered it on the rock to the LORD, to the one who works wonders, and Manoah and his wife were watching.<sup>20</sup>And when the flame went up toward heaven from the altar, the angel of the LORD went up in the flame of the altar. Now Manoah and his wife were watching, and they fell on their faces to the ground.<sup>21</sup>The angel of the LORD appeared no more to Manoah and to his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the LORD.<sup>22</sup>And Manoah said to his wife, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God."<sup>23</sup>But his wife said to him, "If the LORD had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands, or shown us all these things, or now announced to us such things as these."<sup>24</sup>And the woman bore a son and called his name Samson. And the young man grew, and the LORD blessed him.<sup>25</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
13.overview:
The cycle turns for the sixth time, and one clause is missing. Israel does evil and is given into Philistine hands for forty years — the longest oppression in the book — and nobody cries out. Every earlier oppression produced a cry (3:9, 3:15, 4:3, 6:6, 10:10). Judah explains the silence two chapters later: do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? (15:11). They have settled down under it. God sends a deliverer to a people who never asked for one.

The angel of the LORD comes to a barren woman in a border village of the failing tribe of Dan. Her son is to be a Nazirite from the womb — no vine, no razor, no corpse — and she must keep the food restrictions herself while she carries him. And the commission has a ceiling written into it from the start: he shall begin to save Israel. David finishes that war two centuries later.

Manoah prays the best prayer any man prays in this book — teach us what we are to do with the child — and God answers by sending the angel back to his wife again, in a field, with Manoah not there. Manoah asks what the boy's mission will be and is told nothing at all about it: keep the vow, and wait. He offers the visitor a meal and is told to offer a sacrifice instead; asks his name and is told it is wonderful; and watches him ascend to heaven in the flame of his own burnt offering. Then Manoah says they will die, and his unnamed wife reasons better than any man in the book.
13.theology:
Grace to people who did not send for it. Forty years and not one recorded prayer, and God raises up a deliverer anyway. The initiative through all four Samson chapters is entirely God's, towards a nation too comfortable in its captivity to want rescuing — which is what grace has always looked like: while we were still weak, at the right time, Christ died for the ungodly (Rom. 5:6).

The three vows. Numbers 6:1-8 gives the Nazirite three restrictions: nothing from the vine, no razor, no contact with the dead. Samson's is not chosen, not temporary, and begins before conception. He will break all three — the drinking feast (14:10), the lion's carcass (14:8-9), and last of all the razor (16:19). By the time the hair goes, the other two are long gone.

Begin, not finish. No other judge is given a limited brief. This one is announced as a start before he is conceived, and the wall he cracks is pulled down by David (2 Sam. 5:17-25; 8:1). It is a hard word for anyone who wants a completed work to show, and a true one.

Wonderful. The visitor appears as a man, speaks as God, refuses a meal but accepts a burnt offering made to the LORD, will not give a name that can be handled, and ascends in the altar flame. The word is pele', the root Isaiah uses for the child born to us (Isa. 9:6). And the picture in v. 20 is one the Old Testament cannot resolve: the one who receives the offering is carried up inside it (cf. Heb. 9:26). Manoah wanted a name to honour; the name was given twelve hundred years later to another couple in another small town (Matt. 1:21).

The woman's argument (v. 23). Manoah's doctrine is right — man shall not see me and live (Ex. 33:20) — and his conclusion is wrong. His wife tests the fear against the evidence and produces three items: God accepted the offering, God revealed himself, God announced a future. Each runs from what God has already done to what he must therefore intend, which is exactly Romans 8:32. If the offering has been accepted, whatever else is coming it is not your condemnation.
13.examples:
Then: A childless couple in a frontier village were told they would have a son who would only begin the work, were refused any account of his mission, and were given instead a set of instructions for the next nine months. Then the messenger went up in the fire of their own sacrifice, and the husband concluded they were about to die and the wife proved they were not.

Now: Manoah asked the question everyone asks — what is this for, where is it going — and got today's obedience in detail with the future left in God's hands. That is not a refusal to answer; it is the answer. And when the fear comes that God has shown you kindness in order to destroy you afterwards, use his wife's method rather than his: list what God has already done. He accepted the offering. He has shown you these things. He has told you what is coming. Nobody pays a price like Calvary and then changes his mind.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 1 — The Cycle With No Cry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, so the LORD gave them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years (v. 1). And then the sentence stops.
verseByVerse.theology: Five times already this book has run the cycle, and five times the next clause is that Israel cried out to the LORD (3:9, 3:15, 4:3, 6:6, 10:10). This time nobody cries. Forty years — the longest oppression in the book — and not one recorded prayer.
verseByVerse.examples: Judah will say why in two chapters' time: do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? (15:11). They are not groaning under it. They have settled down under it, and God is about to send a deliverer to a people who have not asked for one.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, so the LORD gave them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, so the LORD gave them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years.'

Now read the next verse and notice what is not in it.

Five times this book has run its cycle, and five times the same clause has followed the oppression. Israel cried out to the LORD (3:9). Israel cried out to the LORD (3:15). The people of Israel cried out to the LORD (4:3). The people of Israel cried out for help to the LORD (6:6). And in chapter 10, the fullest confession of the lot (10:10).

Here, nothing. Forty years in Philistine hands, and no recorded prayer from anybody.

Forty years is the longest oppression in the book. Cushan had eight, Eglon eighteen, Jabin twenty, Midian seven, Ammon eighteen. This one runs twice as long as any of them and produces not a single groan the writer thought worth recording.

Two chapters on, Judah will explain it. When Samson is hiding in a rock and three thousand men of Judah come out — not to fight the Philistines but to hand him over — their opening words are: do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? (15:11). That is not the language of a people in agony. It is the language of a people who have looked at the arrangement, decided it is survivable, and are annoyed with the man who is disturbing it.

That is what makes this cycle worse than the ones before it, and why God's response to it is so strange. Israel is not oppressed enough to pray. And God sends a deliverer anyway.

That is the note to keep hold of through all four Samson chapters. Nobody asked for him. The initiative from first to last is God's, to a nation too comfortable in its captivity to want rescuing. Which is what grace has always looked like: while we were still weak, at the right time, Christ died for the ungodly (Rom. 5:6). Not for people who sent for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–7 — To a Woman Who Is Never Named
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The angel of the LORD appears to the barren wife of Manoah of Zorah and tells her she will bear a son (vv. 2-3). The boy is to be a Nazirite from the womb — no razor on his head — and she herself must keep the vow while she carries him: no wine, no strong drink, nothing unclean (vv. 4-5). And there is a limit written into the commission from the start: he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines (v. 5). She reports it all to her husband, including how frightening the visitor was and that she never learned his name (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The angel comes to her, not to him, and the book never tells us what she was called. Manoah is named five times in this chapter. His wife is the woman throughout, and she is the one who sees, listens, reports accurately and works out what it means.
verseByVerse.examples: Barrenness opening onto an announced son is a road Scripture has been down before — Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, and later Hannah and Elizabeth. Every time, the point is the same: the deliverer is a gift, not a product, and the family that receives him could not have produced him.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a certain man of Zorah, of the tribe of the Danites, whose name was Manoah. And his wife was barren and had no children. And the angel of the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, "Behold, you are barren and have not borne children, but you shall conceive and bear a son. Therefore be careful and drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. No razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'There was a certain man of Zorah, of the tribe of the Danites, whose name was Manoah. And his wife was barren and had no children.'

Two ordinary people in a border village, and one closed womb.

Zorah sits on the western edge of the hill country, right on the frontier where Israel's land runs down into the Philistine plain. Dan is the tribe that failed to take its allotted territory (1:34) and will shortly abandon it altogether (ch. 18). This is a family living on the losing edge of a losing tribe.

The wife is barren, which Scripture has taught us to read as the beginning of something. Sarah was barren, and Isaac came. Rebekah was barren, and Jacob came. Rachel, and Joseph. Hannah, and Samuel. Elizabeth, and John. Each time God shuts a womb and then opens it, the child that comes out belongs to God in a way no ordinary child does, and the parents know perfectly well they did not produce him.

'And the angel of the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, "Behold, you are barren and have not borne children, but you shall conceive and bear a son."'

He goes to her.

Not to her husband, who is named in verse 2 and will be named repeatedly. To the woman, who is never named at all. Through this entire chapter she is the woman, his wife, the woman — and she is the one heaven talks to, twice.

He also names the problem before he solves it. Behold, you are barren and have not borne children. He does not soften it or step around it. He says out loud the thing she has lived with for years, and then contradicts it in the same breath.

'"Therefore be careful and drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. No razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines."'

The vow arrives before the child does, and it is laid on the mother first.

A Nazirite vow is set out in Numbers 6, and it has three parts. Nothing from the vine — no wine, no strong drink, no grapes, not even the skins or the seeds. No razor on the head, the hair left uncut as the visible sign. And no contact with a dead body, not even a parent's (Num. 6:3-7). It was normally something a person chose, for a set period, and then ended with a sacrifice.

Nothing about Samson's is normal. He does not choose it, it is not temporary, and it starts before he is conceived: a Nazirite to God from the womb. His mother takes the food restrictions on herself for the pregnancy so that the boy is under the vow from his first cell.

Fix the three parts in your mind, because this is the last time in the story that all three are intact. Samson will hold a seven-day drinking feast at his wedding — the Hebrew word for the party is built on the verb to drink (14:10). He will scoop honey out of a lion's carcass and eat it and give it to his parents (14:8-9). And the razor will come at last in Delilah's lap (16:19). He breaks all three, and he breaks the third one last, and by then the first two had already gone.

Then the commission, and it has a ceiling built into it. He shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines.

Begin. Not finish. God tells this couple, before the child is conceived, that their son's life work will be incomplete. No other judge is given a limited brief; the others are simply raised up to save. Samson is announced as a start.

The Philistine war he begins is not won until David, two hundred years later, breaks them at Baal-perazim and again in the valley of Rephaim and subdues them (2 Sam. 5:17-25; 8:1). Samson is the first crack in a wall somebody else pulls down.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the woman came and told her husband, "A man of God came to me, and his appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, very awesome. I did not ask him where he was from, and he did not tell me his name, but he said to me, 'Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. So then drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the woman came and told her husband, "A man of God came to me, and his appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, very awesome. I did not ask him where he was from, and he did not tell me his name."'

She is exact about what she does not know.

Look at how carefully she reports. She calls him a man of God, which is the term for a prophet — the safe, sober description of what she can be sure of. Then she says his appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, and she does not push the comparison further than that. And she volunteers the two gaps in her information: she did not ask where he came from, and he did not say who he was.

She has met something overwhelming and is not exaggerating about it. Very awesome is her one word for the impression, and it is a word for holy fear, not for admiration.

'"but he said to me, 'Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. So then drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.'"'

She adds four words: to the day of his death.

The angel had said from the womb, and she says from the womb to the day of his death. It may be that she was told more than verse 5 records. It may be that she has understood correctly what a lifelong vow means and said so. Either way it is not carelessness — she has thought about the length of this thing and grasped that there is no end date and no releasing sacrifice at the finish.

She also leaves something out. The angel had said the boy would begin to save Israel from the Philistines, and she does not repeat it.

The text does not tell us why, and it would be easy to make too much of it. But look at what she has kept and what she has dropped. She has held on to every word about the vow — the part that is her responsibility, starting today — and said nothing about the national mission, which is God's business and years away.

That is not a bad instinct in a person who has just been handed something enormous. She has been given a promise and a duty, and she goes home talking about the duty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Teach Us What We Are to Do
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Manoah prays — let the man of God whom you sent come again to us and teach us what we are to do with the child (v. 8) — and God listens. But the angel comes back to the woman again, sitting in a field, with Manoah not there (v. 9). She runs for him; he arrives and asks what the child's manner of life and mission are to be (vv. 10-12). And the angel answers a different question: of all that I said to the woman let her be careful (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: It is the first prayer in Judges that asks for instruction rather than rescue, and it is answered — God listened to the voice of Manoah. He simply does not get the answer he asked for.
verseByVerse.examples: Twice now heaven has arranged the meeting so that the wife is the one present. And the instruction that comes back is not about the boy's career but about the mother's diet. What is to be done with the child is: keep the vow, and wait.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Manoah prayed to the LORD and said, "O Lord, please let the man of God whom you sent come again to us and teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born." And God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman as she sat in the field. But Manoah her husband was not with her. So the woman ran quickly and told her husband, "Behold, the man who came to me the other day has appeared to me." And Manoah arose and went after his wife and came to the man and said to him, "Are you the man who spoke to this woman?" And he said, "I am."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Manoah prayed to the LORD and said, "O Lord, please let the man of God whom you sent come again to us and teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born."'

This is the best prayer prayed by a man in the book of Judges.

Consider what he does not ask for. He does not ask for a sign to test the message, as Gideon did twice with the fleece. He does not bargain, as Jephthah did. He does not ask for the Philistines to be dealt with, which is the only thing anyone in this book ever asks for.

He asks to be taught. Teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born — a man who has been told he is going to be a father to somebody set apart for God, and whose first reaction is that he does not know how to do this and needs instructing.

Note also that he believes the message completely. He does not ask whether it is true; he asks for the curriculum. And he prays for both of them: teach us.

'And God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman as she sat in the field. But Manoah her husband was not with her.'

God listened. And then arranged the meeting exactly as before.

Read that verse twice, because it is nearly comic and entirely deliberate. Manoah prays that the man of God would come again to us. God grants the request — the messenger comes back — and he comes back to the woman, sitting alone in a field, with her husband somewhere else.

Heaven has now twice chosen to speak to the wife and twice arranged for the husband not to be there. God answers Manoah's prayer, and answers it in a way that says quietly whose word is to be trusted in that house.

'So the woman ran quickly and told her husband, "Behold, the man who came to me the other day has appeared to me." And Manoah arose and went after his wife and came to the man and said to him, "Are you the man who spoke to this woman?" And he said, "I am."'

She runs. He follows her.

The picture is of a woman moving fast because she knows what this is, and a man going after his wife to be shown. She leads him to the place. And his first words are a verification question: are you the man who spoke to this woman?

There is nothing wrong with the question. But note that she never asked one. She has believed the message since verse 3, and has spent this whole scene as the person who knows.

verseByVerse.quote: And Manoah said, "Now when your words come true, what is to be the child's manner of life, and what is his mission?" And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "Of all that I said to the woman let her be careful. She may not eat of anything that comes from the vine, neither let her drink wine or strong drink, or eat any unclean thing. All that I commanded her let her observe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Manoah said, "Now when your words come true, what is to be the child's manner of life, and what is his mission?"'

Two questions, and the second one is the one every parent secretly wants answered.

What is to be the child's manner of life — how is he to be raised, what is the rule for him. Fair enough; that is what Manoah prayed for. But then: what is his mission? What is he going to do? What is this boy for?

'And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "Of all that I said to the woman let her be careful. She may not eat of anything that comes from the vine, neither let her drink wine or strong drink, or eat any unclean thing. All that I commanded her let her observe."'

He answers the first question and ignores the second entirely.

Not one word about the mission. Nothing about the Philistines, nothing about what the boy will grow up to do, no outline of a career. The angel simply repeats the instructions already given — and repeats them, twice over, as instructions given to her. Of all that I said to the woman. All that I commanded her.

He even expands the detail slightly: not merely no wine, but anything that comes from the vine, which is the full Numbers 6 restriction. He is making sure she has it exactly.

So the answer to what is he for? is: keep the vow, and wait.

Take that seriously, because it is how God usually deals with people who want the plan. Manoah wanted the shape of his son's life laid out in advance, and what he was given was today's obedience, in detail, with the future left in God's hands. It is not a refusal to answer. It is the answer: your job is the vow, not the mission.

There is an irony coming that neither of them can see. The one thing they were told to guard is the one thing that will finally matter. Samson's whole story turns on the vow — not on strategy, not on armies, but on whether the hair is cut. The parents were told to watch the very thing the son eventually threw away.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Manoah offers hospitality; the angel redirects it to worship — if you prepare a burnt offering, then offer it to the LORD (vv. 15-16). Manoah asks his name, and gets an answer that is a question: why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful? (vv. 17-18). Then the offering is made on the rock, and as the flame goes up, the angel of the LORD goes up in it, and the two of them fall on their faces (vv. 19-21).
verseByVerse.theology: The word rendered wonderful is the root Isaiah will use for the child who is born to us: Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God (Isa. 9:6). Here is a person who appears as a man, accepts a sacrifice offered to the LORD, will not give a name that can be handled, and is carried to heaven in the fire of the altar.
verseByVerse.examples: Manoah asked for a name so that he could honor the visitor when the words came true (v. 17). He was given a fire instead. The name would be given later, and to a different couple, in another town: you shall call his name Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "Please let us detain you and prepare a young goat for you." And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "If you detain me, I will not eat of your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, then offer it to the LORD." (For Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the LORD.) And Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "What is your name, so that, when your words come true, we may honor you?" And the angel of the LORD said to him, "Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "Please let us detain you and prepare a young goat for you."'

Feeding a visitor is what a decent man does in that country.

Abraham did exactly this at Mamre — ran to the herd, took a calf, and stood by while three strangers ate under the tree (Gen. 18:7-8). Manoah is offering ordinary hospitality to someone he still takes to be a prophet.

'And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "If you detain me, I will not eat of your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, then offer it to the LORD." (For Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the LORD.)'

The offer is redirected, firmly, from a meal to an altar.

I will not eat your food, he says. If you want to bring that goat, bring it as a burnt offering, and bring it to the LORD. He will not receive as a guest what should be given as worship — and the narrator steps in with a parenthesis to make sure we notice the point Manoah is missing: he did not know who he was talking to.

So the visitor has just told a man to sacrifice to the LORD, standing in front of him, and will in a moment go up in that sacrifice's flame.

'And Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "What is your name, so that, when your words come true, we may honor you?"'

The motive is good and the request is impossible.

He wants to know who to thank. When the baby is born and the promise is proved, he intends to honour the man who brought the news, and for that he needs a name.

'And the angel of the LORD said to him, "Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?"'

Jacob asked the same question at the Jabbok and got the same non-answer (Gen. 32:29). Moses asked it at the bush and was given I am who I am, which is a name that cannot be used as a handle (Ex. 3:14).

The word here is pele' — wonderful, and not in the weak modern sense. Pele' is the word for what only God does, the category of the miraculous. Verse 19 will call the LORD the one who works wonders, from the same root, in the very next breath.

It is also the word Isaiah reaches for when he needs a name for the child who is to be born: and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace (Isa. 9:6).

So gather what is standing on this hillside. A person who appears in the form of a man. Who speaks as God and is called the angel of the LORD. Who refuses food but accepts a burnt offering made to the LORD. Whose name is beyond asking for, and is wonderful. And who, in three verses, will ascend to heaven in fire.

Manoah wanted a name so that he might honour him when the words came true. He was not given one. It would be another twelve hundred years before the name was given — and it was given to another couple, in another small town, by another angel: you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21).

Not begin to save. Save.

verseByVerse.quote: So Manoah took the young goat with the grain offering, and offered it on the rock to the LORD, to the one who works wonders, and Manoah and his wife were watching. And when the flame went up toward heaven from the altar, the angel of the LORD went up in the flame of the altar. Now Manoah and his wife were watching, and they fell on their faces to the ground. The angel of the LORD appeared no more to Manoah and to his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Manoah took the young goat with the grain offering, and offered it on the rock to the LORD, to the one who works wonders, and Manoah and his wife were watching.'

He does as he was told, on a rock, in a field, with no priest and no tabernacle.

The narrator adds a description of God that has just been supplied by the conversation: he offered it to the LORD, to the one who works wonders. The visitor said his name was wonderful; Manoah offers to the God who does wonders. The writer is joining those two things together before Manoah has worked it out for himself.

'And when the flame went up toward heaven from the altar, the angel of the LORD went up in the flame of the altar. Now Manoah and his wife were watching, and they fell on their faces to the ground.'

He goes up in the fire.

Stand in that field for a moment. The goat is on the rock, the flame climbs, and the man who has been standing there talking to them steps into the column of fire and rises with it. They are, the text says twice, watching. And then their faces are in the dirt.

Consider what the picture actually shows. The one who receives the offering is carried up inside the offering. He is not standing beside the altar taking delivery; he is in the flame, going up with the smoke, as though the sacrifice and the one it is made to were going home together.

There is a mystery here that the Old Testament keeps circling and cannot resolve, and it is resolved at Calvary. The one to whom the offering is made turned out to be the offering. He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself (Heb. 9:26).

'The angel of the LORD appeared no more to Manoah and to his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the LORD.'

He worked it out at the last possible moment, and one moment too late to ask anything.

The narrator has been telling us since verse 3. Manoah has been in the presence of the angel of the LORD through two conversations, has asked his name and been refused, has been told to offer a sacrifice, and has understood none of it until the fire took him away. Then Manoah knew.

Say that as description rather than criticism. God is often recognised in the rear-view mirror. The two on the Emmaus road knew who had been walking with them at the exact moment he vanished from their sight (Luke 24:31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–25 — She Reasons Better Than He Fears
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Manoah draws the obvious conclusion: we shall surely die, for we have seen God (v. 22). His wife draws a better one. If the LORD had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted the offering, or shown us these things, or told us this (v. 23). Then the son is born and named Samson, the LORD blesses him, and the Spirit of the LORD begins to stir him at Mahaneh-dan (vv. 24-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Her argument runs from what God has already done to what God must therefore intend, and it is exactly the logic of Romans 8:32. He did not spare his own Son; how will he not also with him freely give us all things? The accepted sacrifice is the proof that he does not intend your death.
verseByVerse.examples: The verb in v. 25 means to thrust or impel — the Spirit begins to make the young man restless. And the place named is where he will be buried, twenty years and four chapters later, between Zorah and Eshtaol (16:31).

verseByVerse.quote: And Manoah said to his wife, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God." But his wife said to him, "If the LORD had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands, or shown us all these things, or now announced to us such things as these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Manoah said to his wife, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God."'

His theology is correct and his conclusion is wrong.

He is not being superstitious. He is quoting the settled understanding of Israel, and it is right: man shall not see me and live (Ex. 33:20). Gideon said the same thing when he realised who had been sitting under his oak (6:22). A sinful man cannot look at a holy God and walk away. Manoah has the doctrine exactly.

What he does with it is another matter. He has reasoned from a true principle straight to despair, and he tells his wife they are both about to die.

'But his wife said to him, "If the LORD had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands, or shown us all these things, or now announced to us such things as these."'

Then the woman with no name reasons better than anyone else in the book of Judges.

Follow the argument, because it is tight. She does not deny his premise. She does not say God is too kind to kill anyone, or that they had not really seen what they saw. She takes his fear and tests it against the evidence, and produces three pieces.

First: he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands. God took the sacrifice. He did not refuse it, he consumed it, and he went up in its flame. A God who intends to destroy you does not first accept your offering.

Second: or shown us all these things. He revealed himself — twice to her, once in the fire to both of them. Revelation is not how executions begin.

Third: or now announced to us such things as these. He has promised them a son who will begin to deliver Israel. You do not tell a dead couple about the future of their child.

Every one of her three arguments runs the same direction: from what God has already done, to what God must therefore intend. She reasons forward from grace received to grace to come.

That is precisely the logic the New Testament will use for Christian assurance, and Paul puts it in a single sentence: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Rom. 8:32).

The argument is identical, and the sacrifice is infinitely greater. If God has already accepted an offering on your behalf — and he has, and it was his Son — then whatever else is coming, it is not your condemnation. That question was settled at the altar. You may not know what he is doing with your life; you may be as much in the dark about the mission as Manoah was. But you can know this: he did not accept that offering in order to destroy you afterwards. Nobody pays a price like that and then changes his mind.

Manoah looked at the fire and saw his death in it. His wife looked at the same fire and saw that their offering had been received. She was right.

verseByVerse.quote: And the woman bore a son and called his name Samson. And the young man grew, and the LORD blessed him. And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the woman bore a son and called his name Samson. And the young man grew, and the LORD blessed him.'

She names him, and the name means little sun.

It is an odd, bright, hopeful name for a boy born on the Philistine frontier — and there is something poignant in it, because the village of Beth-shemesh, the house of the sun, was just down the valley. A mother who had waited years for a child called him sunshine.

The LORD blessed him. Whatever comes later, that is the sentence over his childhood.

'And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.'

The verb is a strong one. It means to thrust or impel — to push at something until it moves.

So the picture at the end of this chapter is of a young man being made restless by the Spirit of God. Not yet sent anywhere, not yet doing anything, but stirred: something in him will not settle, and it is God who is doing the unsettling. The great strength has not yet appeared. The first thing the Spirit produces in him is discontent.

Then the place: Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol. Hold on to those two village names.

Four chapters from now, when the temple has come down at Gaza and his brothers have carried the body up out of Philistine country, the last verse of his story reads: and they buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father (16:31).

He is buried where the Spirit first stirred him. Everything in between — the riddle, the foxes, the jawbone, the harlot, the lap, the mill, the shaven head — happens between those two villages and comes back to them.

The last thing said about him here is that the LORD blessed him and the Spirit began to move him. Whatever we make of what he does with the next twenty years, that is where he starts: an answered prayer, a kept promise, and the Spirit of God stirring a boy in a field on the edge of enemy territory.

14.title: Samson's Marriage
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Samson went down to Timnah, and at Timnah he saw one of the daughters of the Philistines.<sup>2</sup>Then he came up and told his father and mother, "I saw one of the daughters of the Philistines at Timnah. Now get her for me as my wife."<sup>3</sup>But his father and mother said to him, "Is there not a woman among the daughters of your relatives, or among all our people, that you must go to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" But Samson said to his father, "Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes."<sup>4</sup>His father and mother did not know that it was from the LORD, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.<sup>5</sup>Then Samson went down with his father and mother to Timnah, and they came to the vineyards of Timnah. And behold, a young lion came toward him roaring.<sup>6</sup>Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and although he had nothing in his hand, he tore the lion in pieces as one tears a young goat. But he did not tell his father or his mother what he had done.<sup>7</sup>Then he went down and talked with the woman, and she was right in Samson's eyes.<sup>8</sup>After some days he returned to take her. And he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion, and behold, there was a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey.<sup>9</sup>He scraped it out into his hands and went on, eating as he went. And he came to his father and mother and gave some to them, and they ate. But he did not tell them that he had scraped the honey from the carcass of the lion.<sup>10</sup>His father went down to the woman, and Samson prepared a feast there, for so the young men used to do.<sup>11</sup>As soon as the people saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.<sup>12</sup>And Samson said to them, "Let me now put a riddle to you. If you can tell me what it is, within the seven days of the feast, and find it out, then I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes,<sup>13</sup>but if you cannot tell me what it is, then you shall give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes." And they said to him, "Put your riddle, that we may hear it."<sup>14</sup>And he said to them, "Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet." And in three days they could not solve the riddle.<sup>15</sup>On the fourth day they said to Samson's wife, "Entice your husband to tell us what the riddle is, lest we burn you and your father's house with fire. Have you invited us here to impoverish us?"<sup>16</sup>And Samson's wife wept over him and said, "You only hate me; you do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, and you have not told me what it is." And he said to her, "Behold, I have not told my father nor my mother, and shall I tell you?"<sup>17</sup>She wept before him the seven days that their feast lasted, and on the seventh day he told her, because she pressed him hard. Then she told the riddle to her people.<sup>18</sup>And the men of the city said to him on the seventh day before the sun went down, "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" And he said to them, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle."<sup>19</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men of the town and took their spoil and gave the garments to those who had told the riddle. In hot anger he went back to his father's house.<sup>20</sup>And Samson's wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man.
14.overview:
Samson goes down to Timnah, sees a Philistine girl, and comes home with an instruction rather than a request. His parents object on exactly the right grounds (Deut. 7:3-4) and he does not answer the argument; he repeats the order and gives his reason — she is right in my eyes. That phrase is the book's own verdict on the whole period (17:6; 21:25), and here the deliverer says it about himself.

On the road he kills a lion bare-handed when the Spirit rushes on him, and tells nobody. Returning, he turns aside to the carcass, scrapes honey out of it with his hands, eats, feeds his parents, and does not tell them either.
