A Nazirite may not go near a dead body even for his own mother (Num. 6:6-7), and the concealment is the proof that he knew. Two of the three vows are gone before the wedding starts — the corpse and, at a seven-day drinking feast, the vine. Only the razor is left.

He then wagers sixty garments on a riddle nobody could solve, because its answer is a private memory. His bride's townsmen threaten to burn her alive, she weeps at him for seven days, he gives way, and they win. He calls her a heifer in public, walks twenty miles to Ashkelon, kills thirty men who had nothing to do with any of it, pays the debt with their clothes and goes home to his parents in a temper. His wife is given to the best man.
14.theology:
Right in my eyes. Yashar b'einay (v. 3) is the phrase the book uses for the anarchy of the whole period. Samson offers it to godly parents quoting Scripture, and it wins. He is not merely living in that age; he is its portrait.

Verse 4, held at both ends. It was from the LORD, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines — and not one word of the parents' objection is thereby withdrawn. God did not give the appetite, approve the marriage or suspend the commandment. He governed a sin he did not author, exactly as at Genesis 50:20 and Acts 2:23, where lawless hands and a definite plan are named in one sentence with no attempt to relieve the tension.

The strength was never in the hair. The Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and the narrator notes he had nothing in his hand (v. 6). The uncut hair is the sign of the vow, not the battery.

Gifts are not certificates. The same Spirit-rushing that killed the lion sends him to Ashkelon to kill thirty strangers over a bet (v. 19), and both halves stand in one verse. The first blow of the deliverance promised in 13:5 is struck by a man in a private rage. Never build a doctrine of your own soundness on what God has done through you — I never knew you is addressed to people with a list of mighty works (Matt. 7:22-23).

He was shown the method and did not learn it. The tears, the accusation that he does not love her, the daily pressing until he gives way, the secret carried straight to his enemies — all of it happens at his own wedding (vv. 15-17), and all of it happens again, in almost the same words, in Delilah's house (16:15-16). Thirty men died teaching him this lesson and it did not take.
14.examples:
Then: A man raised up to deliver Israel married into the enemy because she looked good to him, broke his vow at a carcass and hid it, cheated thirty villagers with an unanswerable riddle, and murdered thirty strangers in another city to cover the loss — and God used the whole squalid business to begin breaking the Philistine grip on a nation that had never asked him to.

Now: Two tests, and the first is v. 9. What you keep quiet is what you already know is wrong; nobody conceals a clear conscience, and the surest sign that a thing needs dealing with is that you would rather not say where the honey came from. The second is v. 19. If God has used you — a word that landed, a work that prospered — do not read it as a verdict on your walk with him. He struck the first blow for Israel through a man settling a gambling debt.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samson goes down to Timnah, sees a Philistine woman, and comes home with an instruction for his parents: get her for me as my wife (vv. 1-2). They object on the right grounds — is there no woman among your own people? — and he does not argue. He repeats the demand and gives his reason: she is right in my eyes (v. 3). Then a note from the narrator that his parents could not have known: it was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion against the Philistines (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Right in my eyes is this book's verdict on the whole period, and here it comes out of the deliverer's own mouth (cf. 17:6; 21:25). Samson is not merely living in the age of everyone doing what was right in his own eyes. He is its portrait.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 does not excuse a word of it. Scripture holds both ends without embarrassment: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen. 50:20), and men crucified Christ by lawless hands according to God's definite plan (Acts 2:23). God governs the sin he never authors, and the sinner is answerable for every bit of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Samson went down to Timnah, and at Timnah he saw one of the daughters of the Philistines. Then he came up and told his father and mother, "I saw one of the daughters of the Philistines at Timnah. Now get her for me as my wife." But his father and mother said to him, "Is there not a woman among the daughters of your relatives, or among all our people, that you must go to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" But Samson said to his father, "Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes." His father and mother did not know that it was from the LORD, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Samson went down to Timnah, and at Timnah he saw one of the daughters of the Philistines.'

Two verbs, and the whole man is in them: he went down, and he saw.

Timnah is down. Zorah sits up in the hills; Timnah lies four miles away in the valley, on the Philistine side of the line. The writer uses the word three times in this chapter — he went down, he went down with his father and mother, he went down and talked with the woman — and the geography is accurate every time. It is also doing other work.

Then he saw. The Spirit had begun to stir him at Mahaneh-dan (13:25); the first recorded result is that he walked into enemy territory and looked at a girl.

'Then he came up and told his father and mother, "I saw one of the daughters of the Philistines at Timnah. Now get her for me as my wife."'

He does not ask. He reports and instructs.

There is no please, no case made, no acknowledgement that this is a difficulty. The sentence is get her for me, addressed to the two people who had waited years for him and kept a vow through a pregnancy on his behalf.

'But his father and mother said to him, "Is there not a woman among the daughters of your relatives, or among all our people, that you must go to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?"'

They are entirely right, and they say so gently.

The law was explicit about marrying into the nations of the land: you shall not intermarry with them... for they would turn away your sons from following me (Deut. 7:3-4). And the reason given is not racial but spiritual — the danger is to the worship. His parents put it as a question, offer an alternative, and appeal to the covenant sign: these people are uncircumcised. They are not being snobs. They are being Israelites.

'But Samson said to his father, "Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes."'

The argument goes unanswered. He repeats the order and supplies a reason, and the reason is the most important sentence in the chapter.

She is right in my eyes. In Hebrew, yashar b'einay — and this is the phrase the book will use twice more, in the last five chapters, as its whole diagnosis of the period: everyone did what was right in his own eyes (17:6; 21:25).

Read it again with that in view. The book's summary judgment on the age is spoken here by the man God raised up to deliver it. Samson is not simply living through a time when everybody pleased himself. He is that time, walking about in one body.

Be honest about what the phrase covers. He is not making a case for missionary marriage, or claiming a leading, or arguing that the girl fears the LORD. He looked at her, and she suited him. That is the entire justification offered, and it is offered to godly parents quoting Scripture, and it wins.

'His father and mother did not know that it was from the LORD, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.'

Now the verse that gives readers the most trouble, dropped in by the narrator as an aside.

It was from the LORD. Behind Samson's appetite, unknown to his parents and unknown to Samson, God was working: he was seeking an occasion against the Philistines, and this marriage was going to provide it.

Be careful with what that does and does not say. It does not say God gave Samson the lust, or approved the marriage, or suspended the commandment in Deuteronomy 7. Every criticism his parents made stands, and God's use of the episode removes not one ounce of Samson's guilt in it.

What it says is that God is not blocked by human sin, and does not wait for it to finish before he acts. Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant good, and the same event was both (Gen. 50:20). Men took Jesus and crucified him by the hands of lawless men, and it happened according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, in one sentence, with no attempt to relieve the tension (Acts 2:23).

Hold both ends. God governs the sin he never authors. The sinner answers for all of it. And the last clause of the verse explains why God was seeking an occasion at all: at that time the Philistines ruled over Israel — and nobody in Israel had asked him to do anything about it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — The Lion and the Honey
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A young lion comes roaring at him in the vineyards of Timnah, the Spirit of the LORD rushes on him, and he tears it apart bare-handed — but he did not tell his father or his mother what he had done (vv. 5-6). Returning later for the wedding, he turns aside to look at the carcass, finds bees and honey in it, scrapes it into his hands, eats as he walks, and gives some to his parents — without telling them where it came from (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: A Nazirite may not go near a dead body, not even his father's or his mother's (Num. 6:6-7). He turns aside on purpose, handles the carcass, eats out of it, and makes his parents unclean without their knowledge. The concealment is the proof that he knew.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice where the lion met him: the vineyards of Timnah. A man forbidden anything from the vine, walking through the vineyards on his way to marry outside the covenant. The narrator does not comment. He does not need to.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samson went down with his father and mother to Timnah, and they came to the vineyards of Timnah. And behold, a young lion came toward him roaring. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and although he had nothing in his hand, he tore the lion in pieces as one tears a young goat. But he did not tell his father or his mother what he had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Samson went down with his father and mother to Timnah, and they came to the vineyards of Timnah. And behold, a young lion came toward him roaring.'

Note the address before the lion arrives: the vineyards of Timnah.

Samson is a Nazirite. The first restriction in Numbers 6 is not merely no wine, but nothing from the vine at all — no grapes, fresh or dried, not the skins, not the seeds (Num. 6:3-4). And here he is, walking through the vineyards on the road to his Philistine wedding.

The writer does not say a word about it. He just tells us where the man was standing.

'Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and although he had nothing in his hand, he tore the lion in pieces as one tears a young goat.'

Here is the first display of the strength, and its source needs stating precisely.

The strength is not in his muscles and not in his hair. The Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him — the verb is violent, a sudden seizing — and the narrator adds that he had nothing in his hand so that no one can suppose a weapon did it. What happens next is that a man tears a lion the way an ordinary man might tear a kid goat for the pot.

The hair, when we come to chapter 16, is not a battery. It is a sign. The power was always the Spirit's, and the uncut hair was the visible token of the vow that marked him as God's.

'But he did not tell his father or his mother what he had done.'

There is the first of this chapter's three secrets.

He tells nobody. Not the parents walking down the road with him, who would have understood better than anyone alive what had just happened to their son. The greatest thing God has ever done through him, and he keeps it to himself.

Watch this habit, because it runs right through him. He does not tell them about the lion (v. 6). He does not tell them about the honey (v. 9). He boasts to his wife that he has not told his father or mother the riddle (v. 16). Samson is a man who holds things back — and in the end the one secret he cannot keep is the only one that mattered.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went down and talked with the woman, and she was right in Samson's eyes. After some days he returned to take her. And he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion, and behold, there was a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey. He scraped it out into his hands and went on, eating as he went. And he came to his father and mother and gave some to them, and they ate. But he did not tell them that he had scraped the honey from the carcass of the lion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then he went down and talked with the woman, and she was right in Samson's eyes.'

The narrator repeats the phrase, and this time he says it himself.

In verse 3 it was Samson's excuse. Here it is the writer's flat description of the state of affairs: she was right in his eyes, and that is all there is to say about the courtship. He went down, he talked with her, and she suited him.

'After some days he returned to take her. And he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion, and behold, there was a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey.'

He turned aside. It was a deliberate detour.

Nobody made him do this. He was on the road to his wedding, and he went out of his way to look at a dead animal — and a Nazirite is forbidden to go near a dead body at all. The restriction is severe and explicit: he may not make himself unclean even for his father, his mother, his brother or his sister, when they die (Num. 6:6-7). Samson is not caught out by a corpse on the path. He walks over to it.

'He scraped it out into his hands and went on, eating as he went.'

Then he reaches into the carcass with his bare hands and eats.

Read it slowly, because familiarity has worn the shock off. He is scooping honey out of the body of a rotting lion, in his palms, walking along and licking his fingers. Under the law he is unclean from the moment he touches it. Under his own vow he is a Nazirite handling the dead, and there is a whole procedure in Numbers 6:9-12 for what a Nazirite must do when this happens — shave the head, bring offerings, start the count again.

He does none of it. He eats and keeps walking.

'And he came to his father and mother and gave some to them, and they ate. But he did not tell them that he had scraped the honey from the carcass of the lion.'

Then he makes them unclean too, without telling them.

That is the second secret, and it is worse than the first. Withholding the story of the lion was pride, or reticence. This is deception with a consequence: two people who had ordered their whole lives around this vow are handed food out of a carcass by their son and eat it, and are defiled, and do not know.

The concealment is the thing that convicts him. A man who did not know he had done wrong would have said where the honey came from — it is a marvellous story. He says nothing, because he knows exactly what he has done.

Take that as the test, because it works on all of us. What you have to keep quiet is what you already know is wrong. Nobody hides a clear conscience.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–18 — A Riddle Nobody Could Answer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samson holds a seven-day feast — the word is built on the verb to drink — and thirty companions are produced to keep him company (vv. 10-11). He wagers sixty garments on a riddle: out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet (vv. 12-14). It cannot be solved, because the answer is a private memory. So the thirty threaten to burn his bride and her father's house, she weeps at him for seven days, and on the last he tells her (vv. 15-17). Their answer comes back in the form of a taunt, and so does his (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: It is not a riddle; it is a trap. No one at that table could have known about the lion, and Samson knew they could not. He has staked sixty garments on a wager his opponents cannot win, in front of thirty men who cannot afford to lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then read verses 15-17 and keep them. The tears, the accusation that he does not love her, the pressing every day until he gives way — that is the exact method Delilah will use, in almost the same words, two chapters later (16:15-16). He survives it here. He does not survive it there.

verseByVerse.quote: His father went down to the woman, and Samson prepared a feast there, for so the young men used to do. As soon as the people saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him. And Samson said to them, "Let me now put a riddle to you. If you can tell me what it is, within the seven days of the feast, and find it out, then I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes, but if you cannot tell me what it is, then you shall give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes." And they said to him, "Put your riddle, that we may hear it." And he said to them, "Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet." And in three days they could not solve the riddle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'His father went down to the woman, and Samson prepared a feast there, for so the young men used to do.'

The Hebrew word for the feast is mishteh, and it is built on the verb to drink.

This is a seven-day drinking party, thrown by a Nazirite, in Philistine Timnah, according to the local custom for young men. The text does not say that Samson drank, and it is fair to say so. It says he made the drinking-feast and presided over it for a week.

Line up where he now stands with the vow. The corpse: broken outright, twice over. The vine: he has walked through the vineyards and is hosting the drinking. The razor: still intact. Two of the three are gone before Delilah is born, and nobody has noticed, including him.

'As soon as the people saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.'

Thirty men appear, and they are not groomsmen.

The phrasing is careful: as soon as they saw him, they brought thirty companions. This is a Philistine town looking at a very large Israelite and deciding he needs an escort. They are a guard, arranged on the spot, and the week will prove it.

'And Samson said to them, "Let me now put a riddle to you. If you can tell me what it is, within the seven days of the feast, and find it out, then I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes, but if you cannot tell me what it is, then you shall give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes."'

Sixty garments, one for each man on the losing side, and the stake is far beyond what ordinary men could raise.

Linen garments and changes of clothes were serious property in that world — the sort of thing given as a reward or taken as spoil. He is proposing a wager thirty villagers cannot cover, at his own wedding, with his bride's people.

'And he said to them, "Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet." And in three days they could not solve the riddle.'

It is a good line and a dishonest game.

A riddle is meant to be solvable. It hides an answer in an image, and a clever hearer can work it out. This one cannot be worked out by anybody, because the answer is not an image at all — it is a private memory of a dead lion in a field that only Samson has ever seen inside. He has staked sixty garments on a question with no route to the answer, against thirty men who cannot pay.

He is not playing. He is fleecing them, and he knows the odds because he wrote them.

Something else is in the riddle that he cannot see and we can. He has made a joke out of the fact that sweetness came out of a killer, and life came out of a carcass. It is the one moment in his life when he says something larger than himself — the true and terrible pattern by which God brings food out of death — and he uses it to win clothes off villagers.

verseByVerse.quote: On the fourth day they said to Samson's wife, "Entice your husband to tell us what the riddle is, lest we burn you and your father's house with fire. Have you invited us here to impoverish us?" And Samson's wife wept over him and said, "You only hate me; you do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, and you have not told me what it is." And he said to her, "Behold, I have not told my father nor my mother, and shall I tell you?" She wept before him the seven days that their feast lasted, and on the seventh day he told her, because she pressed him hard. Then she told the riddle to her people. And the men of the city said to him on the seventh day before the sun went down, "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" And he said to them, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'On the fourth day they said to Samson's wife, "Entice your husband to tell us what the riddle is, lest we burn you and your father's house with fire. Have you invited us here to impoverish us?"'

The wedding turns into a hostage situation on day four.

Weigh what the threat reveals. They cannot pay. Have you invited us here to impoverish us is the complaint of men who know exactly what sixty garments would cost them, and who have concluded that the bride's family set them up. So they threaten to burn her alive, with her father's household, unless she gets the answer.

She is a girl caught between a husband she has known for days and a town that has just promised to kill her. Whatever she does next, remember where she is standing.

'And Samson's wife wept over him and said, "You only hate me; you do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, and you have not told me what it is." And he said to her, "Behold, I have not told my father nor my mother, and shall I tell you?"'

Her weapon is tears and an accusation about love, and his defence is a boast about secrecy.

Look at his reply. He does not say the riddle is not hers to have; he says he has not even told his parents, so why should she rank above them? It is the third secret of the chapter, produced as a trophy. He is proud of what he withholds.

'She wept before him the seven days that their feast lasted, and on the seventh day he told her, because she pressed him hard. Then she told the riddle to her people.'

Seven days of crying, and on the seventh he gives way.

Now fix this scene in your mind, because it will happen again. A Philistine woman in Samson's company weeps and says he does not love her; she presses him every day; he holds out and holds out, and then tells her the one thing he should not have told her; and she takes it straight to his enemies.

Two chapters from here, Delilah says: how can you say, "I love you," when your heart is not with me? — and the narrator writes, when she pressed him hard with her words day after day, and urged him, his soul was vexed to death (16:15-16). Identical method. Nearly identical words. The same man.

Nothing at Timnah deceives him that he could not have foreseen. He is shown the whole method in week one, at his own wedding, at a cost of thirty lives, and twenty years later he walks into it again.

'And the men of the city said to him on the seventh day before the sun went down, "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?"'

They put the answer as two questions, which is a taunt.

They could have simply said honey and a lion. Instead they hand it back in his own rhythm, in front of the wedding party, a few minutes before the deadline expires.

'And he said to them, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle."'

His answer is coarse, and it blames her.

It is an ugly thing to call a woman, said in public, at the feast that was supposed to be her wedding — and it is not even the right target. Nobody ploughed with anybody. Thirty men threatened to burn her alive and she believed them, and the only reason she had anything to tell was that Samson gave it to her.

He has lost a wager he designed to be unloseable, and his instinct is that somebody else has cheated.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and he walks more than twenty miles to Ashkelon, kills thirty men who had nothing to do with any of it, strips their clothes, and pays his gambling debt with them (v. 19). Then he goes home to his father's house in hot anger, and his wife is handed to the best man (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the deliverance beginning, and it looks like a tantrum. God said this man would begin to save Israel from the Philistines (13:5), and here is the first blow struck — by a furious young man settling a private score in a town that had never heard of him.
verseByVerse.examples: The Spirit came on him for it, and that settles nothing about him. Power to do a thing has never been God's certificate on the heart of the man doing it — which is exactly why the Lord says that on the last day some will list the mighty works done in his name and hear I never knew you (Matt. 7:22-23).

verseByVerse.quote: And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men of the town and took their spoil and gave the garments to those who had told the riddle. In hot anger he went back to his father's house. And Samson's wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men of the town and took their spoil and gave the garments to those who had told the riddle.'

Read that verse without softening either half of it.

The Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him — the same phrase as the lion, the same divine enabling. And what he does with it is walk over twenty miles to a city on the coast, kill thirty men who were not at his wedding, had never heard his riddle and owed him nothing, strip the clothes off their bodies, and carry them back to settle a bet.

Both things are in the sentence, and the sentence does not blush.

So take the theological point carefully, because it matters for more than Samson. The Spirit's coming upon a man is not God's endorsement of the man. It is God equipping him for a purpose that belongs to God. Ashkelon is the first blow of the deliverance announced in 13:5 — the Philistine oppression has begun to be answered — and it is struck by a furious young man in the middle of a private grudge, and the two facts sit in one verse.

Do not build a doctrine of your own soundness on what God has done through you. The Lord himself put it as plainly as it can be put: many will say on that day, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name? And he will declare to them, I never knew you (Matt. 7:22-23). Gifts prove God's power. They prove nothing else.

'In hot anger he went back to his father's house.'

He goes home to his parents. He does not take his wife.

There is a kind of comedy in it, and it is bleak. The man who told his father and mother get her for me, who overrode their objection with she is right in my eyes, is back in their house within a fortnight in a temper, without the bride, having killed thirty strangers to pay for a joke.

'And Samson's wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man.'

The last verse hands her to the best man.

She has been threatened with fire, used as a lever, publicly called a heifer, abandoned at her own wedding feast, and married off to one of the thirty. She is not named. She will be dead within a chapter, burned along with her father by the same townsmen who threatened it here (15:6), and the reason will be something else Samson did.

Everyone in this chapter is doing what is right in his own eyes, and it is the woman nobody names who pays for it. That is what the phrase costs when it is finally totalled up, and it is why the book keeps repeating it.

15.title: Samson's Vengeance
15.text: <sup>1</sup>After some days, at the time of wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife with a young goat. And he said, "I will go in to my wife in the chamber." But her father would not allow him to go in.<sup>2</sup>And her father said, "I really thought that you utterly hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her instead."<sup>3</sup>And Samson said to them, "This time I shall be innocent in regard to the Philistines, when I do them harm."<sup>4</sup>So Samson went and caught 300 foxes and took torches. And he turned them tail to tail and put a torch between each pair of tails.<sup>5</sup>And when he had set fire to the torches, he let the foxes go into the standing grain of the Philistines and set fire to the stacked grain and the standing grain, as well as the olive orchards.<sup>6</sup>Then the Philistines said, "Who has done this?" And they said, "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he has taken his wife and given her to his companion." And the Philistines came up and burned her and her father with fire.<sup>7</sup>And Samson said to them, "If this is what you do, I swear I will be avenged on you, and after that I will quit."<sup>8</sup>And he struck them hip and thigh with a great blow, and he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.<sup>9</sup>Then the Philistines came up and encamped in Judah and made a raid on Lehi.<sup>10</sup>And the men of Judah said, "Why have you come up against us?" They said, "We have come up to bind Samson, to do to him as he did to us."<sup>11</sup>Then 3,000 men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam, and said to Samson, "Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? What then is this that you have done to us?" And he said to them, "As they did to me, so have I done to them."<sup>12</sup>And they said to him, "We have come down to bind you, that we may give you into the hands of the Philistines." And Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves."<sup>13</sup>They said to him, "No; we will only bind you and give you into their hands. We will surely not kill you." So they bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.<sup>14</sup>When he came to Lehi, the Philistines came shouting to meet him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that has caught fire, and his bonds melted off his hands.<sup>15</sup>And he found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, and put out his hand and took it, and with it he struck 1,000 men.<sup>16</sup>And Samson said, "With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps, with the jawbone of a donkey have I struck down a thousand men."<sup>17</sup>As soon as he had finished speaking, he threw away the jawbone out of his hand. And that place was called Ramath-lehi.<sup>18</sup>And he was very thirsty, and he called upon the LORD and said, "You have granted this great salvation by the hand of your servant, and shall I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?"<sup>19</sup>And God split open the hollow place that is at Lehi, and water came out from it. And when he drank, his spirit returned, and he revived. Therefore the name of it was called En-hakkore; it is at Lehi to this day.<sup>20</sup>And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.
15.overview:
Samson comes back to Timnah with a goat, expecting to resume a marriage he had walked out on, and finds his wife given to the best man. He declares himself innocent in advance — a man appointing himself judge of his own revenge — catches three hundred foxes over what must have been weeks, and burns the Philistine harvest at harvest time: the stacked grain, the standing grain, and the olive orchards that take a generation to replace.

The Philistines respond by burning the woman and her father alive. That is exactly what the thirty threatened at the wedding, and it is the reason she had betrayed the riddle in the first place. She was burned anyway, and what finally brought it on her was Samson's revenge for losing her.

Then Judah. Three thousand men of the tribe God named to go up first (1:1-2) march out — not against the raiders camped in their own territory, but to arrest their own deliverer and hand him to the occupier bound. Their opening words, do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us?, explain the missing cry at 13:1. They are not in agony; they are irritated.

The Spirit rushes on him at Lehi, the new ropes burn off like flax, and a thousand men fall to a fresh donkey's jawbone. He sings a two-line pun with no God in it. Four verses later he is beaten by thirst, prays for the first time in his life, calls the victory God's salvation and himself God's servant — and God splits open the ground and gives him water.
15.theology:
Marking your own paper. This time I shall be innocent... when I do them harm (v. 3) is a verdict pronounced before the act by the man who intends to commit it. The danger is not confined to strong men with grudges: the reasoning by which a wronged person establishes that his response is now justified is always available and always convincing, because he is grading it himself. Scripture takes the pen away — never avenge yourselves, not because revenge is always unjust, but because you are not the judge (Rom. 12:19).

The chain that killed her. An unwinnable riddle; a threat of fire; a betrayal made to escape the fire; a public insult; an abandonment; a burnt harvest; and the fire, on her, in the end. Every link is somebody doing what was right in his own eyes, and the person who dies is the one with the fewest choices in the story. She is never named.

Judah's quiet sin. Samson's failures are loud and you can see each one coming. Judah's is sensible, collective and unremarkable: three thousand reasonable men who had made their peace with the thing God sent a deliverer to destroy, and whose only complaint was that he was disturbing it. Their handing-over of their own rescuer to the occupying power to keep the peace has a later echo: we have no king but Caesar (John 19:15).

Power without holiness. Two of the three Nazirite strands are in ribbons by v. 15 — the vineyards, the drinking feast, the honey out of the carcass, and now a fresh jawbone taken up without a thought — and the strength keeps coming. It was always the Spirit and never the man. That is mercy, and it is also a trap: a man who goes on succeeding while disobeying concludes that the disobedience does not matter. Chapter 16 is what happens when he finds out.

En-hakkore. The spring of him who called — not of the deserving. On the day he called he had broken his vow on a corpse, killed a thousand men in a private feud, and sung a victory song with no God in it, and God split a rock for him without a word of rebuke. Israel had drunk from a split rock before, and the Rock was Christ (Ex. 17:6; 1 Cor. 10:4). At Lehi a strong man cried that he was dying of thirst and God split the ground to save his servant. At Golgotha another man said I thirst, and there was no spring, only sour wine — and then a spear, and at once there came out blood and water (John 19:28-34). God split his own Son open to save his enemies, and the water came out of him.
15.examples:
Then: A deliverer burned a nation's harvest to settle a private score and got a woman killed by it; his own tribe mustered three thousand men to arrest him rather than fight the occupier; he killed a thousand of the enemy with a corpse's jawbone and sang about himself; and then he got thirsty, prayed for the first time in his life, and God gave him water without one word of reproach.

Now: Watch for the two sins in this chapter, because they are opposite and you will be tempted by one of them. Samson's is the private verdict: deciding alone that what you are about to do is justified because of what was done to you. Judah's is the settled arrangement: making your peace with the thing God means to destroy, and coming to resent whoever disturbs it. Then take En-hakkore with you. When you come to pray after a day you are not proud of, the spring is not named for the deserving. It is named for the man who called.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samson turns up at Timnah with a goat, expecting to be let into his wife's room, and finds she has been given away — her father had concluded, not unreasonably, that a man who stormed off in hot anger and never came back had finished with her (vv. 1-2). The offer of the younger sister is refused. And Samson announces his position: this time I shall be innocent in regard to the Philistines, when I do them harm (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: He declares his own verdict before the act. That sentence is the tell: a man building a legal case for a revenge he has already decided on, and appointing himself the judge of it.
verseByVerse.examples: The grievance is real — his wife has been given to another man. It became possible because he walked out of his own wedding feast in a temper and went home to his parents (14:19-20).

verseByVerse.quote: After some days, at the time of wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife with a young goat. And he said, "I will go in to my wife in the chamber." But her father would not allow him to go in. And her father said, "I really thought that you utterly hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her instead." And Samson said to them, "This time I shall be innocent in regard to the Philistines, when I do them harm."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After some days, at the time of wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife with a young goat. And he said, "I will go in to my wife in the chamber." But her father would not allow him to go in.'

He arrives with a present and an assumption.

The goat is the ordinary gift a man brought, and the assumption is that the marriage is simply resumed. Nothing has been said, no apology offered, no message sent since he walked out of the wedding feast in a rage and went home to his parents. Some days have passed, his temper has cooled, and he turns up at the door expecting the door to open.

'And her father said, "I really thought that you utterly hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her instead."'

The father's reasoning is not unreasonable, and he is frightened.

Put yourself in his house. His daughter's bridegroom lost a wager at his own wedding, called her a heifer in front of the whole town, disappeared, and was next heard of killing thirty men in Ashkelon. I really thought that you utterly hated her. Anybody would have thought so.

So he did what a father in that position did: he gave her to the best man rather than leave her abandoned. And now, faced with the man himself at the door, he offers the younger daughter as a substitute, which tells you how badly he wants this settled without violence.

'And Samson said to them, "This time I shall be innocent in regard to the Philistines, when I do them harm."'

He pronounces himself not guilty before he has done anything.

That is the sentence to weigh, because it shows how the man's conscience works. He is not reacting in blind fury. He is reasoning, in advance, with a formula: this time I shall be innocent — implying he knows the Ashkelon business was another matter — and therefore what follows is permitted.

He has drawn up the charge, heard the case, delivered the verdict and licensed the sentence, and every one of those offices is his own. Nobody else in the chapter has been consulted, least of all God.

Recognise the habit, because it is not confined to strong men with a grudge. The most dangerous thing a person can do with a wrong done to him is to establish, quietly and alone, that his response is now justified. The reasoning is always available and always convincing, and the reason it convinces is that it is being marked by the person who wrote it.

Scripture takes the pen out of his hand: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord" (Rom. 12:19). The prohibition is not that revenge is unjust. It is that you are not the judge.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–8 — Foxes, Fire, and a Woman Burned
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three hundred foxes, tied in pairs, a torch between every pair of tails, loosed into the standing grain at harvest — and the stacked grain goes, and the standing grain, and the olive orchards (vv. 4-5). The Philistines ask who did it, are told why, and go and burn the woman and her father to death (v. 6). Samson swears one more round of vengeance and says he will stop after it, strikes them hip and thigh, and goes down to hide in the cleft of the rock of Etam (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Read verse 6 against 14:15. The thirty threatened to burn her and her father's house unless she got the riddle out of him. She betrayed him to avoid the fire, and the fire came anyway — because of what he did to avenge the loss of her.
verseByVerse.examples: Grain at harvest is a year's food; olive trees are a generation's work. This is not a raid on soldiers. And Samson's promise in v. 7 — after that I will quit — is the promise every man makes at this stage of a feud, and he never keeps it.

verseByVerse.quote: So Samson went and caught 300 foxes and took torches. And he turned them tail to tail and put a torch between each pair of tails. And when he had set fire to the torches, he let the foxes go into the standing grain of the Philistines and set fire to the stacked grain and the standing grain, as well as the olive orchards. Then the Philistines said, "Who has done this?" And they said, "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he has taken his wife and given her to his companion." And the Philistines came up and burned her and her father with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Samson went and caught 300 foxes and took torches. And he turned them tail to tail and put a torch between each pair of tails.'

Three hundred, caught alive, one at a time.

The detail nobody notices is how long this took. This is not a flash of rage; it is weeks of patient trapping. He caught them, kept them, tied them in pairs by their tails with a torch between, and did it a hundred and fifty times over. The whole scheme was carried out cold.

'And when he had set fire to the torches, he let the foxes go into the standing grain of the Philistines and set fire to the stacked grain and the standing grain, as well as the olive orchards.'

Verse 1 told us the season: wheat harvest.

Three things burn, and the order is the order of ruin. The stacked grain — what is already cut and gathered, this year's food, in the barn. The standing grain — what is still in the field, the rest of the same year. And the olive orchards — which are not a year at all. An olive tree takes a decade to come into bearing and a lifetime to mature. Burning the orchards takes food out of the mouths of children not yet born.

These are farmers. Not the lords of the five cities, not the soldiers who came to his wedding — the growers of Timnah, whose harvest is now smoke.

'Then the Philistines said, "Who has done this?" And they said, "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he has taken his wife and given her to his companion." And the Philistines came up and burned her and her father with fire.'

Now turn back one chapter and read 14:15 again.

Entice your husband to tell us what the riddle is, lest we burn you and your father's house with fire.

That was the threat. It is why she wept at him for seven days; it is why she betrayed the riddle to her people; it is the reason for everything she did that Samson took as treachery. She was a girl trying not to be burned alive.

She is burned alive. By the same men. In the same manner they had promised. And the thing that finally brought it on her was not her betrayal — it was Samson's revenge for losing her.

Follow the chain, because the writer means us to. He designs an unwinnable riddle; they threaten her with fire; she gives them the answer; he calls her a heifer and abandons her; her father marries her to somebody else; he burns their harvest for it; and they burn her for that. Every link is a man doing what was right in his own eyes, and the one who dies is the girl who had the fewest choices of anybody in the story.

She has no name in this book. She is Samson's wife, and then the daughter of the Timnite, and then ash.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samson said to them, "If this is what you do, I swear I will be avenged on you, and after that I will quit." And he struck them hip and thigh with a great blow, and he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Samson said to them, "If this is what you do, I swear I will be avenged on you, and after that I will quit."'

Every man in a feud says this, and none of them mean it.

After that I will quit. One more round, and then it stops. It is the oldest sentence in the history of grudges, and it has never once been true, because a feud does not end when one side is satisfied — the other side is now owed as well, and the reckoning has no natural stopping place.

Note also that his sworn purpose has quietly changed. In verse 3 the harm was to be his compensation. Now it is his answer to their answer. He is no longer setting a price; he is taking a turn.

'And he struck them hip and thigh with a great blow, and he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.'

The phrase is an idiom, probably from wrestling, and it means comprehensively — he took them apart.

Then he goes and lives in a cleft in a rock. The judge of Israel, at the height of his strength, is now in hiding in a crevice in the hills, and the next thing that happens is that his own countrymen come to fetch him out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — Judah Comes Out Three Thousand Strong
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines raid Lehi, and Judah asks them why they have come. To bind Samson, they say, and do to him as he did to us (vv. 9-10). So three thousand men of Judah go down to the rock with a question of their own: do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? What then is this that you have done to us? (v. 11). They bind him with two new ropes, on his one condition — that they will not kill him themselves — and hand him over (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Here is the explanation of the missing cry at 13:1. Forty years of Philistine rule and no recorded prayer, because Israel is not in agony. Judah has read the arrangement, found it survivable, and is annoyed with the man disturbing it.
verseByVerse.examples: And this is Judah — the tribe God named to go up first (1:1-2), the tribe of the coming king. Three thousand men muster, and march in the wrong direction, to arrest their own deliverer on behalf of the occupier.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Philistines came up and encamped in Judah and made a raid on Lehi. And the men of Judah said, "Why have you come up against us?" They said, "We have come up to bind Samson, to do to him as he did to us." Then 3,000 men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam, and said to Samson, "Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? What then is this that you have done to us?" And he said to them, "As they did to me, so have I done to them." And they said to him, "We have come down to bind you, that we may give you into the hands of the Philistines." And Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves." They said to him, "No; we will only bind you and give you into their hands. We will surely not kill you." So they bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the Philistines came up and encamped in Judah and made a raid on Lehi. And the men of Judah said, "Why have you come up against us?" They said, "We have come up to bind Samson, to do to him as he did to us."'

An occupying army camps inside Judah, and Judah's response is to ask a polite question.

Not to muster, not to send to the other tribes, not to cry to the LORD as their fathers had done five times in this book. They ask what the trouble is. And when they are told, they organise the arrest.

'Then 3,000 men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam, and said to Samson, "Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? What then is this that you have done to us?"'

Three thousand men. Look at that number before anything else.

Judah can put three thousand fighting men into the field within days. Ehud had no army at all. Gideon beat Midian with three hundred. Shamgar killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad. Three thousand armed men of Judah went out that week, in force, and marched in the wrong direction.

Then the sentence that explains the whole Samson cycle: do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us?

Chapter 13 began this cycle without the clause the book always uses. Every previous oppression produced a cry to the LORD; forty years of Philistine rule produced none. Here is why. Judah is not in anguish. Judah has looked at the occupation, judged it liveable, and is angry with the one man who will not leave it alone. What then is this that you have done to us? — as if the trouble in the land were Samson.

Consider who is talking. This is Judah, the tribe God named when Israel asked who should go up first against the Canaanites (1:1-2). The tribe of the lion, of the sceptre, of David, and at long last of Christ. That tribe is out here as the occupier's police force, arresting the deliverer God sent them.

Nothing in the chapter is more uncomfortable than this, and it has nothing to do with foxes. Samson's sins are loud and obvious; you can see every one of them coming. Judah's sin is quiet, sensible, and shared by three thousand men who all thought they were being reasonable. They had made their peace with the thing God had sent a man to destroy, and their only complaint was that he was making life difficult.

'And he said to them, "As they did to me, so have I done to them."'

His whole defence is one sentence of arithmetic, and it is the same accounting as verse 3.

'And they said to him, "We have come down to bind you, that we may give you into the hands of the Philistines." And Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves." They said to him, "No; we will only bind you and give you into their hands. We will surely not kill you." So they bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.'

He surrenders, and asks for one guarantee.

Not that they let him go. Not that they join him — three thousand of them, against the raiding party at Lehi. Simply that they will not kill him themselves. That is the extent of what he expects from his own people, and they give him exactly that and nothing more.

Then they tie him with two new ropes and hand him over.

Do not hurry past this. The man God raised up to begin saving Israel from the Philistines is delivered to the Philistines, bound, by his own countrymen, who are afraid of what the rulers will do if they do not. Centuries later, at another handing-over, the words will be: we have no king but Caesar (John 19:15). The pattern of a people surrendering their deliverer to the occupying power to keep the peace is older than Pilate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — Heaps upon Heaps, and Then a Drink
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Lehi the Spirit of the LORD rushes on him, the new ropes burn off like scorched flax, and with a fresh donkey's jawbone he strikes down a thousand men (vv. 14-15). His victory song is a pun on the word for donkey and the word for heaps, and it mentions the jawbone, and himself, and nobody else (vv. 16-17). Then he is thirsty, and prays for the first time in his life — and the prayer says you have granted this great salvation by the hand of your servant (v. 18). God splits open the ground and water comes out (vv. 19-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The song and the prayer are four verses apart and say opposite things. In the song the victory belongs to a jawbone and the man holding it. In the prayer it is God's salvation and Samson is his servant. Thirst taught him in an afternoon what a thousand dead men had not.
verseByVerse.examples: The spring is named En-hakkore, the spring of him who called. Not the spring of the deserving. Samson had just handled a corpse in breach of his vow, sung a song with no God in it, and killed a thousand men in a private feud — and when he called, God split a rock for him.

verseByVerse.quote: When he came to Lehi, the Philistines came shouting to meet him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that has caught fire, and his bonds melted off his hands. And he found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, and put out his hand and took it, and with it he struck 1,000 men. And Samson said, "With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps, with the jawbone of a donkey have I struck down a thousand men." As soon as he had finished speaking, he threw away the jawbone out of his hand. And that place was called Ramath-lehi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When he came to Lehi, the Philistines came shouting to meet him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that has caught fire, and his bonds melted off his hands.'

They came shouting, which means they thought it was over.

Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed on him, and the image the writer chooses is exact: flax that has caught fire. Two new ropes, strong enough that three thousand men were satisfied with them, going the way a bundle of dry linen fibre goes when a spark touches it. Not snapped — melted off his hands.

'And he found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, and put out his hand and took it, and with it he struck 1,000 men.'

A fresh jawbone, which is the word the narrator wants us to have.

Fresh means recently dead; an old sun-dried bone would have shattered. So the animal has not long been a carcass, and it is a donkey, an unclean animal, and Samson picks it up in his hand without a moment's hesitation.

He is a Nazirite. He may not go near a dead body at all, not for his mother or his father (Num. 6:6-7). He has now handled a corpse to get honey, and a corpse to get a weapon, and in between he has hosted a seven-day drinking feast and walked the vineyards of Timnah. Two of the three strands of his vow are in ribbons, and the extraordinary thing is that the strength keeps coming anyway.

Sit with that. God went on using him. The power did not depend on Samson's faithfulness, and it never had — it was the Spirit of the LORD, rushing upon a man who was in no condition to deserve it. Which is a mercy, and also a trap, because a man who keeps succeeding while disobeying will conclude that the disobedience does not matter. Chapter 16 is what happens when he finds out.

'And Samson said, "With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps, with the jawbone of a donkey have I struck down a thousand men."'

His victory song is a pun, and it has no God in it.

The Hebrew plays on two words that sound almost identical — the word for donkey and the word for heap — so the line runs something like: with the jaw of an ass, I have assed them in heaps. It is clever. It is also two lines long, and its subject is a jawbone and the man swinging it.

Set it beside the other victory song in this book. Deborah and Barak sang for thirty-one verses and the song begins bless the LORD, and it is about him from end to end — his marching from Seir, his stars fighting from heaven, his people offering themselves willingly (5:2-5, 20). Samson sings two lines about his weapon.

'As soon as he had finished speaking, he threw away the jawbone out of his hand. And that place was called Ramath-lehi.'

He finishes the song and drops the bone, and the place is named after it: the height of the jawbone.

The map now carries the memory of the weapon. And the next four verses will put another name on the same ground, and that one will remember something else entirely.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was very thirsty, and he called upon the LORD and said, "You have granted this great salvation by the hand of your servant, and shall I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?" And God split open the hollow place that is at Lehi, and water came out from it. And when he drank, his spirit returned, and he revived. Therefore the name of it was called En-hakkore; it is at Lehi to this day. And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And he was very thirsty, and he called upon the LORD and said, "You have granted this great salvation by the hand of your servant, and shall I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?"'

A thousand men are dead on the ground and Samson is beaten by thirst.

Here is the man who tore a lion, snapped new ropes like burnt string, and killed a thousand Philistines with a bone, and he cannot get through the afternoon. The body that God had made irresistible still needed a drink of water. It is the first thing in his life he has not been able to do for himself, and it is what finally puts him on his knees.

This is also the first prayer Samson has ever prayed.

Everything until now has been demand, riddle, insult, threat and song. Not one word addressed to God since the day he was born. Then he gets thirsty, and he calls on the LORD.

Look at what he says, because it is better theology than anything else he has said.

You have granted this great salvation. Not I have struck down a thousand men — which is what he sang four verses ago. Now the victory is God's grant. And by the hand of your servant — the first humble word out of his mouth in three chapters. Not the strong man, not the son-in-law of the Timnite. The servant.

Thirst taught him in one afternoon what a thousand corpses had not.

Be honest about the rest of it, though. The second half of the prayer is a complaint with an edge: shall I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised? There is concern for his own dignity in it, and a hint that this would reflect badly on the arrangement. It is not a model prayer. It is a real one, from a man who has just discovered he is not self-sufficient and is not sure he likes it.

'And God split open the hollow place that is at Lehi, and water came out from it. And when he drank, his spirit returned, and he revived. Therefore the name of it was called En-hakkore; it is at Lehi to this day.'

God does not lecture him. God splits a rock.

There is no rebuke in the answer, no interrogation about the vineyards or the carcasses or the song. He asked for water and water came, immediately, out of the ground where he was standing. His spirit returned, and he revived — the phrase is used of a man coming back from the point of collapse.

The place gets a second name. Verse 17 called it Ramath-lehi, the height of the jawbone, after his weapon. Verse 19 calls this spot En-hakkore — the spring of him who called.

Not the spring of the deserving. Not the spring of the faithful Nazirite. The spring of the man who called — and the man who called had that same day broken his vow on a corpse, taken a thousand lives in a private feud, and sung a song in which God did not appear. He called, and God gave him water.

Israel had drunk from a split rock before, in the wilderness, and Paul says the Rock that followed them was Christ (Ex. 17:6; 1 Cor. 10:4).

One more thirst belongs beside this one. At Lehi a strong man cried out that he was dying of thirst, and God split open the ground and gave him water and he revived. At Calvary another man said I thirst, and no rock was split and no spring came. He was handed sour wine on a sponge, and he died (John 19:28-30).

Then a soldier put a spear into his side, and at once there came out blood and water (John 19:34). At Lehi God split a rock to save his servant. At Golgotha God let his Son be split open to save his enemies — and the water came out of him.

He had said what he intended to do with it: if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37).

'And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.'

Four words in that verse hold the whole assessment: in the days of the Philistines.

Twenty years of judging, and the Philistines are still the ones whose days these are. The oppression named in 13:1 has not lifted. Ehud gave the land eighty years of rest and Deborah forty; Samson's twenty years end with the enemy exactly where they were when he started.

That is precisely what the angel said would happen. He shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines (13:5). Begin, and no more. God announced the limit before the man was conceived, and the limit held.

16.title: Samson and Delilah
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Samson went to Gaza, and there he saw a prostitute, and he went in to her.<sup>2</sup>The Gazites were told, "Samson has come here." And they surrounded the place and set an ambush for him all night at the gate of the city. They kept quiet all night, saying, "Let us wait till the light of the morning; then we will kill him."<sup>3</sup>But Samson lay till midnight, and at midnight he arose and took hold of the doors of the gate of the city and the two posts, and pulled them up, bar and all, and put them on his shoulders and carried them to the top of the hill that is in front of Hebron.<sup>4</sup>After this he loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah.<sup>5</sup>And the lords of the Philistines came up to her and said to her, "Seduce him, and see where his great strength lies, and by what means we may overpower him, that we may bind him to humble him. And we will each give you 1,100 pieces of silver."<sup>6</sup>So Delilah said to Samson, "Please tell me where your great strength lies, and how you might be bound, that one could subdue you."<sup>7</sup>Samson said to her, "If they bind me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>8</sup>Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she bound him with them.<sup>9</sup>Now she had men lying in ambush in an inner chamber. And she said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he snapped the bowstrings, as a thread of flax snaps when it touches the fire. So the secret of his strength was not known.<sup>10</sup>Then Delilah said to Samson, "Behold, you have mocked me and told me lies. Please tell me how you might be bound."<sup>11</sup>And he said to her, "If they bind me with new ropes that have not been used, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>12</sup>So Delilah took new ropes and bound him with them and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And the men lying in ambush were in an inner chamber. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like a thread.<sup>13</sup>Then Delilah said to Samson, "Until now you have mocked me and told me lies. Tell me how you might be bound." And he said to her, "If you weave the seven locks of my head with the web and fasten it tight with the pin, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>14</sup>So while he slept, Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them into the web. And she made them tight with the pin and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he awoke from his sleep and pulled away the pin, the loom, and the web.<sup>15</sup>And she said to him, "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me? You have mocked me these three times, and you have not told me where your great strength lies."<sup>16</sup>And when she pressed him hard with her words day after day, and urged him, his soul was vexed to death.<sup>17</sup>And he told her all his heart, and said to her, "A razor has never come upon my head, for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. If my head is shaved, then my strength will leave me, and I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>18</sup>When Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart, she sent and called the lords of the Philistines, saying, "Come up again, for he has told me all his heart." Then the lords of the Philistines came up to her and brought the money in their hands.<sup>19</sup>She made him sleep on her knees. And she called a man and had him shave off the seven locks of his head. Then she began to torment him, and his strength left him.<sup>20</sup>And she said, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And he awoke from his sleep and said, "I will go out as at other times and shake myself free." But he did not know that the LORD had left him.<sup>21</sup>And the Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes and brought him down to Gaza and bound him with bronze shackles. And he ground at the mill in the prison.<sup>22</sup>But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.<sup>23</sup>Now the lords of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to rejoice, and they said, "Our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand."<sup>24</sup>And when the people saw him, they praised their god. For they said, "Our god has given our enemy into our hand, the ravager of our country, who has killed many of us."<sup>25</sup>And when their hearts were merry, they said, "Call Samson, that he may entertain us." So they called Samson out of the prison, and he entertained them. They made him stand between the pillars.<sup>26</sup>And Samson said to the young man who held him by the hand, "Let me feel the pillars on which the house rests, that I may lean against them."<sup>27</sup>Now the house was full of men and women. All the lords of the Philistines were there, and on the roof there were about 3,000 men and women, who looked on while Samson entertained.<sup>28</sup>Then Samson called to the LORD and said, "O Lord GOD, please remember me and please strengthen me only this once, O God, that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes."<sup>29</sup>And Samson grasped the two middle pillars on which the house rested, and he leaned his weight against them, his right hand on the one and his left hand on the other.<sup>30</sup>And Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines." Then he bowed with all his strength, and the house fell upon the lords and upon all the people who were in it. So the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed during his life.<sup>31</sup>Then his brothers and all his family came down and took him and brought him up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father. He had judged Israel twenty years.
16.overview:
Samson walks forty miles into Gaza, the chief Philistine city, to visit a prostitute, and leaves at midnight carrying the city gate — doors, both posts and the bar — thirty miles uphill to a hill facing Hebron, in the territory of the tribe that had bound him and handed him over one chapter earlier. Two things are absent from that feat: any mention of the Spirit, and any purpose beyond contempt.

Then Delilah, the only woman in his story who is given a name, and the first person he is ever said to love. Five Philistine lords offer her eleven hundred pieces of silver each. She asks him outright where his strength lies and how he could be subdued — no pretext, no disguise — and three times he lies, and three times she does exactly what he described and shouts the alarm with armed men in the next room. He is not deceived. He watches her try to kill him and comes back for the next round, and each false answer is nearer the truth than the last.

Worn down day after day until his soul was vexed to death, he tells her all his heart — and what he gives away is not a fact about hair but the vow: a Nazirite to God from his mother's womb. He wakes, expects to shake himself free as at other times, and did not know that the LORD had left him. They gouge out the eyes that had ruined him, take him back down to Gaza, and put him on the mill.

Then one word turns: but the hair of his head began to grow again. And when a temple full of Philistines credits Dagon with a victory over the God of Israel, a blind man asks to be remembered and strengthened once more, and brings the house down.
16.theology:
He did not know (v. 20). The heart of the whole cycle. The strength was never in the hair — every display of it is credited to the Spirit rushing upon him (14:6, 14:19, 15:14) — and the hair was the sign of a vow. What he lost was the LORD, and he lost him without noticing, because he had been functioning for years while the vow came apart: the vineyards, the carcass, the drinking feast, the jawbone. Every unpunished breach taught him the vow was decorative. A man may lose the presence of God and go on preaching, leading, being admired for his gift, because the gift is not the presence and can outlive it for a long time. You cannot measure your standing with God by whether things are still working.

He was not deceived. Delilah states her purpose to his face and then carries it out in front of him, twice, before he gives anything away. This is not a trap sprung on an innocent; it is a man who has survived so much that he no longer believes in consequences, and every escape teaches him the wrong lesson. Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Cor. 10:12). And the three lies move steadily inward — bowstrings, ropes, hair — which is the shape of every gradual fall. Nobody gives away the centre in one movement.

Shortened to death (v. 16). The idiom is the one used of God at 10:16, whose soul was shortened over the misery of Israel. The same worn-out endurance, running in God towards mercy for people who deserved nothing, and in Samson towards a millstone.

Why the last scene happens. Not because Samson has earned anything. From v. 23 the assembled rulers of a nation are crediting Dagon with a victory over the LORD, and God acts for the sake of his own name (Num. 14:13-16; Ezek. 36:22-23). The hair growing back in v. 22 is a sign restored where nobody is watching, on a man who can ask for nothing — which is the sort of place God begins again.

The prayer, both halves. Remember me... only this once... for my two eyes (v. 28) has not a word in it about Israel, and God answers it. The motive is mixed and the calling is real, and heaven does not require him to pray better before it listens. That is why Hebrews lists him among those made strong out of weakness (Heb. 11:32-34).

Where the parallel breaks. Another deliverer was seized, mocked for entertainment, blindfolded and struck, stretched out with his arms spread, and accomplished more by his death than by his life. The shapes match until the prayer. Samson said let me die with the Philistines and pulled the house down on his enemies. Jesus said Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34) and let it fall on himself. Samson killed more in his death than in his life; Christ saved more — and every one of them was on the roof.
16.examples:
Then: A man who had watched a woman attempt his murder three times went back a fourth, handed over the vow that had marked him for God since before he was born, woke expecting to be strong as usual, and found God had gone without telling him. He lost the eyes that had led him everywhere, ground grain in the dark, and prayed twice in his life — once for water and once for strength — and was heard both times.

Now: The warning is v. 20 and it is not mainly about lust. Ask whether anything is still running on momentum: the gift working, the reputation holding, the ministry going on, while the vow quietly comes apart in private. Success is not an audit, and God's generosity is not his approval. The comfort is v. 22, and it is for people who have already fallen: the hair grew back where nobody could see it, on a man who could not have asked for it, and God was not finished with him. If you can still say remember me, you are not past the point Samson prayed from.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samson walks into the chief city of the Philistines, sees a prostitute and goes in to her (v. 1). The Gazites lock the city and set an ambush at the gate for the morning (v. 2). At midnight he gets up, takes hold of the doors of the city gate and both posts, tears them out bar and all, puts them on his shoulders and carries them to the top of the hill in front of Hebron (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The gate was a city's strength, its law court and its front door. Samson leaves Gaza standing open and undefended, and does it as a joke on his way home from a brothel.
verseByVerse.examples: Two things are missing from verse 3, and both matter. There is no mention of the Spirit of the LORD, which the writer has been careful to record every other time (14:6, 14:19, 15:14). And the hill he chooses faces Hebron — in Judah, the tribe that had bound him with new ropes and handed him to these same Philistines one chapter earlier.

verseByVerse.quote: Samson went to Gaza, and there he saw a prostitute, and he went in to her. The Gazites were told, "Samson has come here." And they surrounded the place and set an ambush for him all night at the gate of the city. They kept quiet all night, saying, "Let us wait till the light of the morning; then we will kill him." But Samson lay till midnight, and at midnight he arose and took hold of the doors of the gate of the city and the two posts, and pulled them up, bar and all, and put them on his shoulders and carried them to the top of the hill that is in front of Hebron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Samson went to Gaza, and there he saw a prostitute, and he went in to her.'

He walks about forty miles into enemy country, to their chief city, for this.

Gaza is the greatest of the five Philistine capitals, and the judge of Israel goes there alone, for one reason, and the verb is the one that has run through his whole story: he saw. He saw the woman at Timnah; he sees this one. Twenty years of judging have not touched the eyes.

There is no attempt in the text to make anything of it. No Spirit rushing, no divine occasion sought, no mitigating clause. Just a man, a city, and a purchase.

'The Gazites were told, "Samson has come here." And they surrounded the place and set an ambush for him all night at the gate of the city. They kept quiet all night, saying, "Let us wait till the light of the morning; then we will kill him."'

The whole city knows within the hour, and they are perfectly sensible about it.

They do not attack him in the dark; they lock the only way out and wait for daylight, when they can see what they are fighting. It is good planning against a man they have every reason to fear.

'But Samson lay till midnight, and at midnight he arose and took hold of the doors of the gate of the city and the two posts, and pulled them up, bar and all, and put them on his shoulders and carried them to the top of the hill that is in front of Hebron.'

He does not break out. He takes the door with him.

Consider what a city gate was. It was the strongest thing the town possessed — massive doors, hung on posts sunk into the wall, barred at night. It was also the place where the elders sat, where cases were heard and business transacted; the gate was the city's authority in one structure. Boaz went to the gate to settle a legal matter (Ruth 4:1).

Samson pulls the whole assembly out of the wall — doors, both posts, and the bar still across them — hoists it onto his shoulders, and walks. And the hill in front of Hebron is not down the road. It is a climb of some thirty-odd miles, up out of the coastal plain into the hill country, carrying a gate.

Gaza wakes to find its front wall has a hole in it and no explanation.

Now note the two things the writer leaves out and puts in.

He leaves out the Spirit. Every other feat has the clause attached — the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him at the lion (14:6), at Ashkelon (14:19), at Lehi (15:14). Here, nothing. Samson is now doing this on his own account, for his own amusement, and the narrator declines to put God's name anywhere near it.

He puts in the destination: the hill that is in front of Hebron. Hebron is in Judah. Judah is the tribe that had just come down three thousand strong to tie him up and hand him to the Philistines (15:11-13). So the gates of the enemy capital are dumped on the doorstep of the men who would not fight for them.

It is a magnificent, pointless, contemptuous act, and it is the last free thing he does.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–14 — A Game He Thought He Could Win
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He loves a woman in the Valley of Sorek named Delilah — the first time love is said of him, and the only woman in his story who is named (v. 4). The five Philistine lords offer her eleven hundred pieces of silver apiece to find the secret of his strength (v. 5). She asks him outright, with no disguise: tell me where your strength lies and how you might be bound (v. 6). Three times he gives a false answer — fresh bowstrings, new ropes, his hair woven into a loom — and three times she does exactly what he described and shouts the Philistines are upon you, with men waiting in the next room (vv. 7-14).
verseByVerse.theology: He is not deceived. She tells him what she is doing before she does it, and then does it, and he comes back for the next round. This is not a man being tricked; it is a man playing a game he is sure he cannot lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch the answers move. Bowstrings, then ropes, then — for the first time — his hair (v. 13). Each lie is closer to the truth than the one before it. That is the movement of every appetite that is being managed rather than killed.

verseByVerse.quote: After this he loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah. And the lords of the Philistines came up to her and said to her, "Seduce him, and see where his great strength lies, and by what means we may overpower him, that we may bind him to humble him. And we will each give you 1,100 pieces of silver."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'After this he loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah.'

Two firsts in one verse.

This is the first time the book says Samson loved anyone. Of the girl at Timnah it said only that she was right in his eyes. Here the verb is loved, and the narrator uses it without comment.

Delilah is also the only woman in Samson's story who is given a name. His mother is the woman. His wife is Samson's wife, and then the daughter of the Timnite, and then ash. The prostitute in Gaza is a prostitute. The one who is named is the one who destroys him.

The Valley of Sorek runs down from the hills to the plain, past Zorah where he was born. He has not gone far. He is in the borderland he grew up in, and so is she.
