'And the lords of the Philistines came up to her and said to her, "Seduce him, and see where his great strength lies, and by what means we may overpower him, that we may bind him to humble him. And we will each give you 1,100 pieces of silver."'

All five lords come in person, which tells you what he is worth to them.

The Philistine confederation had five cities — Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath — and each had its lord. All five make the journey to a woman's house in a border valley because one Israelite is beyond their army.

Eleven hundred pieces of silver each. Five and a half thousand shekels for a man's life. There is no way to make that figure ordinary: it is a fortune several times over, and it was offered to a woman who evidently did not have to think about it very long.

Read their brief carefully, because she follows it to the letter and he watches her do it. Find where the strength lies. Find how we can overpower him. So that we may bind him — to humble him. They do not say to kill him. They want him brought low, and in the end they get exactly that: blind, shackled, grinding grain, and brought out to be laughed at.

Money has bought a man's betrayal before and since, and the price is never the point. Judas took thirty pieces of silver for the Son of God, which is a fraction of what Delilah was paid, and the smallness of that sum is part of its horror (Matt. 26:15). What Delilah's price shows is something else: the Philistines had learned, over twenty years, exactly what Samson could not be beaten by, and exactly what he could.

verseByVerse.quote: So Delilah said to Samson, "Please tell me where your great strength lies, and how you might be bound, that one could subdue you." Samson said to her, "If they bind me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, then I shall become weak and be like any other man." Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she bound him with them. Now she had men lying in ambush in an inner chamber. And she said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he snapped the bowstrings, as a thread of flax snaps when it touches the fire. So the secret of his strength was not known. Then Delilah said to Samson, "Behold, you have mocked me and told me lies. Please tell me how you might be bound." And he said to her, "If they bind me with new ropes that have not been used, then I shall become weak and be like any other man." So Delilah took new ropes and bound him with them and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And the men lying in ambush were in an inner chamber. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like a thread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So Delilah said to Samson, "Please tell me where your great strength lies, and how you might be bound, that one could subdue you."'

She does not disguise it in the slightest.

Read her question again. Where does your strength lie? How could you be bound? How could somebody subdue you? There is no story attached, no pretext, no clever indirection. It is the lords' brief, repeated to his face almost word for word, and it means precisely what it appears to mean.

He knows what she is asking, and he answers.

'Samson said to her, "If they bind me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."'

Note who appears in his answer: if they bind me. He has not been told there is a they. He has worked it out, and says so, and plays on.

'Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she bound him with them. Now she had men lying in ambush in an inner chamber. And she said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he snapped the bowstrings, as a thread of flax snaps when it touches the fire. So the secret of his strength was not known.'

So now he has seen it done.

She got the materials from somewhere, which means she is in contact with them. She tied him up while he lay there and let her. There were armed men behind the door. And she shouted the alarm that was meant to be the last thing he ever heard.

He snapped the strings and stayed.

'Then Delilah said to Samson, "Behold, you have mocked me and told me lies. Please tell me how you might be bound."'

Her complaint is that he lied to her.

There is a kind of brazenness here that is almost admirable. She has just attempted his murder and her grievance is his dishonesty. She reproaches him for not cooperating in his own destruction, and he accepts the reproach as reasonable.

'And he said to her, "If they bind me with new ropes that have not been used, then I shall become weak and be like any other man." So Delilah took new ropes and bound him with them and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And the men lying in ambush were in an inner chamber. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like a thread.'

New ropes. The same thing Judah used on him at the rock of Etam (15:13), and they came off at Lehi like flax in a fire.

He is now naming methods that have already failed in living memory. He is not even trying to be plausible; he is enjoying it.

Stop here and be clear about what is going on, because the usual account of this chapter is wrong. Samson is not seduced into an unwitting slip. He is not tricked. He has been told her purpose, has watched her carry it out twice, has heard the alarm shouted twice with men waiting in the next room — and he goes back for a third round.

This is a man who believes he can hold something lethal and put it down whenever he chooses. He has survived so much for so long that he has stopped believing in consequences. Every previous escape has taught him the wrong lesson.

That is precisely how sin destroys people who are strong. It does not usually take them by surprise. It waits while they prove to themselves, over and over, that they can handle it — and the proof is the trap. Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Cor. 10:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Delilah said to Samson, "Until now you have mocked me and told me lies. Tell me how you might be bound." And he said to her, "If you weave the seven locks of my head with the web and fasten it tight with the pin, then I shall become weak and be like any other man." So while he slept, Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them into the web. And she made them tight with the pin and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he awoke from his sleep and pulled away the pin, the loom, and the web.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Delilah said to Samson, "Until now you have mocked me and told me lies. Tell me how you might be bound." And he said to her, "If you weave the seven locks of my head with the web and fasten it tight with the pin, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."'

The third answer brings his hair into it, and that is new.

Look at the sequence. Bowstrings: nothing to do with him. New ropes: nothing to do with him. And now the seven locks of his head, woven into a loom — still a lie, but a lie built out of the truth. He has moved from things that have no connection to his vow to the one thing that does.

She now knows the hair is somewhere in this. He has handed her the field.

'So while he slept, Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them into the web. And she made them tight with the pin and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he awoke from his sleep and pulled away the pin, the loom, and the web.'

He was asleep in her house, for the third time, with his hair in her hands.

Hold the picture: the strongest man alive lying unconscious while a woman who has twice tried to have him killed works on the sign of his consecration with a weaving pin.

Take this out of the two verses, because it is the shape of every gradual fall. Each lie is nearer the truth than the last. He is not being dragged; he is drifting inward, one concession at a time, and every concession feels small because it is only slightly worse than the one before.

Nobody gives away the centre in one movement. He gives away the outer things first, discovers he survived, and moves in.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How can you say, "I love you," when your heart is not with me? — and she presses him day after day until his soul was vexed to death, and he tells her all his heart: the razor, and the Nazirite vow from the womb (vv. 15-17). She shaves him asleep on her knees, and his strength leaves him (vv. 18-19). He wakes saying he will shake himself free as at other times — but he did not know that the LORD had left him (v. 20). They gouge out his eyes, take him down to Gaza and put him to the mill (v. 21). And then one word turns: but the hair of his head began to grow again (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 20 is the heart of the whole Samson story. He did not lose his strength when the razor touched him; he had been losing God for twenty years, and had gone on functioning so well that he never noticed. The hair was the sign. The power was always the Spirit.
verseByVerse.examples: The idiom in v. 16 — his soul was shortened to death — is the one used of God himself at 10:16, whose soul was shortened over the misery of Israel. In God it ran out towards mercy. In Samson it runs out towards a millstone.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said to him, "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me? You have mocked me these three times, and you have not told me where your great strength lies." And when she pressed him hard with her words day after day, and urged him, his soul was vexed to death. And he told her all his heart, and said to her, "A razor has never come upon my head, for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. If my head is shaved, then my strength will leave me, and I shall become weak and be like any other man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And she said to him, "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me? You have mocked me these three times, and you have not told me where your great strength lies."'

Now go back and read 14:16.

You only hate me; you do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, and you have not told me what it is.

That was his bride at Timnah, twenty years earlier. The same accusation about love, the same complaint about a secret withheld, the same aim. He knows this speech. He has heard it before, in almost these words, from a woman in the pay of the same people — and thirty men in Ashkelon died the last time he gave in to it.

'And when she pressed him hard with her words day after day, and urged him, his soul was vexed to death.'

Day after day. It is not a moment of weakness; it is a siege.

Take the Hebrew of the last clause exactly: his soul was shortened to death. It is the idiom for an endurance that has come to its end — a man worn down to the point where he will pay anything to make it stop.

That same idiom has appeared once before in this book, at 10:16. There it is used of God: when Israel put away their foreign gods, his soul was shortened over the misery of Israel — he could bear it no longer.

The same phrase, and the two ends of the book's whole meaning. God's patience runs out, and what comes out of it is mercy for people who deserved nothing. Samson's endurance runs out, and what comes out of it is a shaved head and a millstone. It is one thing to be worn down by love for someone else's misery. It is another to be worn down by a woman who is being paid to do it.

'And he told her all his heart, and said to her, "A razor has never come upon my head, for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. If my head is shaved, then my strength will leave me, and I shall become weak and be like any other man."'

All his heart. The narrator says it here and says it again in the next verse, because it is the point.

Weigh what the secret actually is. It is not a fact about hair. It is a vow: I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. The one thing in Samson's life that had been about God, kept since before he was conceived, guarded by a mother who went without wine to carry him — and he hands it to a woman on the Philistine payroll to buy an hour's peace.

He has been giving away pieces of that vow for twenty years: the vineyards of Timnah, the honey out of the carcass, the seven-day drinking feast, the jawbone in his hand. The razor was all that was left of it. Now he gives that away too, and he gives it away in words — not overpowered, not drugged, not deceived. He told her.

verseByVerse.quote: When Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart, she sent and called the lords of the Philistines, saying, "Come up again, for he has told me all his heart." Then the lords of the Philistines came up to her and brought the money in their hands. She made him sleep on her knees. And she called a man and had him shave off the seven locks of his head. Then she began to torment him, and his strength left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart, she sent and called the lords of the Philistines, saying, "Come up again, for he has told me all his heart." Then the lords of the Philistines came up to her and brought the money in their hands.'

She knew immediately that this time it was true.

How? Because the first three answers were about equipment and this one was about God. A man does not invent a childhood vow and a mother's abstinence to get a woman off his back. She heard the difference at once, and sent for the lords.

They came with the money in their hands. Five men, five purses, a fortune carried up a valley path. That is what the picture of this house is: a man asleep inside, and outside the door his price being counted.

'She made him sleep on her knees. And she called a man and had him shave off the seven locks of his head. Then she began to torment him, and his strength left him.'

She made him sleep on her knees.

No sentence in the chapter is more terrible, and it contains no violence at all. The posture is trust. His head is in her lap, and he is asleep — the deepest thing a strong man can offer — and that is the position from which she calls in the barber.

Note that the shaving is not her own hand. She calls a man, so that the work is done carefully while Samson lies still. Twenty years of Philistine warfare ended by a professional with a razor and a steady hand.

Then she began to torment him — testing, before she raises the alarm, and this time there is no snapping of anything.

Here the narrator writes the clause the whole chapter has been moving towards: his strength left him. Not the hair was gone, therefore he was weak. Something left him. The next verse will say who.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And he awoke from his sleep and said, "I will go out as at other times and shake myself free." But he did not know that the LORD had left him. And the Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes and brought him down to Gaza and bound him with bronze shackles. And he ground at the mill in the prison. But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And she said, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And he awoke from his sleep and said, "I will go out as at other times and shake myself free."'

The fourth time she shouts it, he expects it to go like the first three.

As at other times. That is a man's whole life in three words. It has always worked before; it will work now. He stands up out of her lap, shakes himself, and reaches for what has never once failed him.

'But he did not know that the LORD had left him.'

There is not a sadder sentence in the Old Testament.

Take it apart slowly, because everything in these four chapters has been driving at it.

First: the LORD had left him. Not his hair, not his strength, not his luck. The LORD. The strength was never in the head of hair — the writer has told us plainly every time it came, and it was always the same thing: the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him (14:6, 14:19, 15:14). The hair was the visible token of a vow; the power was a Person, and the Person has gone.

Second: he did not know. He had lost God and could not tell. He got up and expected to perform, because he had been performing for years while the vow came apart in pieces — the carcass, the feast, the jawbone, and now the razor — and nothing had ever visibly changed. Every unpunished breach had taught him that the vow was decorative.

So the departure was not sudden. What was sudden was the discovery.

Sit with that, because it is the reason this chapter is in the Bible and it applies to people who will never go near a Delilah. A man can lose the presence of God and go on preaching, leading the family prayers, running the meeting, being admired for his gift — because the gift is not the presence, and the gift can outlive it for a long time. The Spirit gave Samson victories in a year when he was breaking his vow on a corpse. God is generous like that, and his generosity is not an audit.

The one thing you cannot do is measure your standing with God by whether things are still working. Samson's things were still working right up to the morning they were not.

'And the Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes and brought him down to Gaza and bound him with bronze shackles. And he ground at the mill in the prison.'

Four verbs, and they are the exact shape of what sin does.

They seized him, who had never been held. They gouged out his eyes — and consider which organ they took. It was seeing that ruined him: he saw a woman at Timnah, he saw a prostitute in Gaza, and everything was right in his own eyes. He is now blind, and the punishment is a picture of the sin.

They brought him down to Gaza — back to the city where this chapter began, back to the scene of his last free act, in chains. And he ground at the mill, which was the work of women and animals. The strongest man who ever lived, walking in a circle in the dark, turning a stone, on the same treadmill until he dies.

That is what it offers everyone in the end. It shows you what you want, takes what you see with, brings you back where you started, and puts you to work going round in circles.

'But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.'

One word turns this chapter, and the word is but.

Be careful how the sentence is read. It is not saying that the power was in the hair after all and is regrowing with it, like a battery on charge. God is not bound by follicles, and the writer has never once said the strength was in the hair.

What is growing back is the sign — the visible mark of a man set apart to God from his mother's womb, coming back on a head that is blind, shaved, shackled and grinding. The vow is being restored on a man in no position to restore anything.

Nobody in Gaza is watching a prisoner's hair. It happens where only God can see it, on a man who has nothing, can do nothing and can ask for nothing.

That is exactly the sort of place God begins again. He is not finished with people who are finished with themselves — and the proof of it, in this chapter, is a quiet biological fact noticed by no one and written down forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — Let Me Die with the Philistines
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lords gather to sacrifice to Dagon, crediting him with the victory: our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand (vv. 23-24). They bring the blind man out to entertain them and stand him between the pillars, with three thousand watching from the roof (vv. 25-27). He asks a boy to let him feel the pillars, and prays the second prayer of his life: remember me, strengthen me only this once, that I may be avenged for my two eyes (vv. 26-28). Then he bows with all his strength and the house falls (vv. 29-30). His family come and bury him between Zorah and Eshtaol, in his father's tomb (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: From verse 23 onwards the question is no longer what Samson deserves. A pagan temple is full of people crediting Dagon with a victory over the LORD, and that is a matter God answers on his own account.
verseByVerse.examples: The prayer is honestly recorded and honestly self-interested — not a word about Israel, only his two eyes — and God answers it. Hebrews names him among those who were made strong out of weakness (Heb. 11:32-34). A blind man in an enemy temple asked the God of Israel for strength one last time and staked his life on the answer, and that is faith, whatever else it was mixed with.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the lords of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to rejoice, and they said, "Our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand." And when the people saw him, they praised their god. For they said, "Our god has given our enemy into our hand, the ravager of our country, who has killed many of us." And when their hearts were merry, they said, "Call Samson, that he may entertain us." So they called Samson out of the prison, and he entertained them. They made him stand between the pillars.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now the lords of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to rejoice, and they said, "Our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand."'

With that sentence the whole matter changes, because it is no longer about Samson.

Read what they are saying. Not we caught him, not Delilah earned her money. Our god has given Samson into our hand. Dagon is being publicly credited with a victory over the God of Israel, at a great sacrifice, by the assembled rulers of a nation.

Nothing in the Old Testament is older or more serious than that issue. When Israel is beaten, the watching nations do not conclude that Israel was unfaithful; they conclude that Israel's God is weak. Moses argued with God on exactly that ground — what will the Egyptians say? — and God himself says he acts for the sake of my name, so that the nations shall know he is the LORD (Num. 14:13-16; Ezek. 36:22-23).

So the reason the last scene of this chapter happens is not that Samson has earned another chance. It is that a temple full of people is giving God's glory to a fish god, and God will not have it.

'And when the people saw him, they praised their god. For they said, "Our god has given our enemy into our hand, the ravager of our country, who has killed many of us."'

They have a point about him, and honesty requires admitting it.

The ravager of our country, who has killed many of us. That is a fair description from where they stand. He burned their harvest at harvest time and their olive groves with it. He killed thirty men in Ashkelon over a bet and a thousand at Lehi. From a Philistine farmer's side of the line, Samson is a terrorist, and the relief in this room is genuine.

'And when their hearts were merry, they said, "Call Samson, that he may entertain us." So they called Samson out of the prison, and he entertained them. They made him stand between the pillars.'

They send for him as the after-dinner amusement.

The word covers making sport of him — whatever a blind, shaved strongman could be prodded into doing to make a hall laugh. The man who tore a lion is now the act, and he is led out by the hand for it.

This is what the lords commissioned at the beginning: bind him to humble him (v. 5). They have got everything they paid for.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samson said to the young man who held him by the hand, "Let me feel the pillars on which the house rests, that I may lean against them." Now the house was full of men and women. All the lords of the Philistines were there, and on the roof there were about 3,000 men and women, who looked on while Samson entertained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Samson said to the young man who held him by the hand, "Let me feel the pillars on which the house rests, that I may lean against them."'

A boy is leading him, and he asks the boy for a favour.

The whole position is in that one image. The strongest man in the world is holding a child's hand, because he cannot cross a room alone, and has to ask permission to lean on something. And his request is the request of a tired old man: let me lean.

The boy does it. There is no reason not to. The prisoner has been safe for months.

'Now the house was full of men and women. All the lords of the Philistines were there, and on the roof there were about 3,000 men and women, who looked on while Samson entertained.'

The narrator stops and counts the house before anything happens.

Every one of the five lords is inside — the entire ruling class of Philistia in one building. The floor is full. And on the flat roof, three thousand more, pressed to the edges, looking down into the courtyard at the show.

So the weight of three thousand people is resting on the roof, and the roof is resting on those pillars, and the pillars are what a blind man has just been allowed to put his hands on.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samson called to the LORD and said, "O Lord GOD, please remember me and please strengthen me only this once, O God, that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes." And Samson grasped the two middle pillars on which the house rested, and he leaned his weight against them, his right hand on the one and his left hand on the other. And Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines." Then he bowed with all his strength, and the house fell upon the lords and upon all the people who were in it. So the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed during his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then Samson called to the LORD and said, "O Lord GOD, please remember me and please strengthen me only this once, O God, that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes."'

The second and last prayer of his life, and he uses three names for God in one breath.

O Lord GOD... O God. Sovereign Lord, the covenant name, and the name of the Almighty. A man who has hardly spoken to God in twenty years is suddenly formal, and it reads like someone reaching for every handle he can find.

Please remember me. That is the prayer of a man who has every reason to think he has been forgotten and would deserve it. It is the dying thief's prayer, centuries early: Jesus, remember me (Luke 23:42).

Only this once. He is not asking for restoration or a career. One more time, and then nothing.

Now be honest about the last clause, because the chapter is: that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes.

Not a word about Israel is in it. Not a word about the forty years of oppression, or the commission given before he was born, or the God whose name is being handed to Dagon in that very room. He wants to be avenged, and he wants it for his eyes. To the end, the account he is settling is his own.

God answers him.

Hold both of those together and do not tidy either one. The prayer is self-interested, and the prayer is real; the motive is mixed, and the man is genuinely calling on the LORD; and the God who had left him in verse 20 does not say no in verse 28. Samson prays like what he is — a ruined, blinded man with nothing left and no illusions about his own record — and heaven does not require him to pray better before it listens.

That is why Hebrews can put his name in the roll of faith (Heb. 11:32). Look at how the list describes what such men did: they were made strong out of weakness (Heb. 11:34). It is an exact description of a blind prisoner asking the God of Israel for strength one last time and staking his life on the answer.

'And Samson grasped the two middle pillars on which the house rested, and he leaned his weight against them, his right hand on the one and his left hand on the other. And Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines." Then he bowed with all his strength, and the house fell upon the lords and upon all the people who were in it.'

What he is asking for, he knows, and says out loud.

Let me die with the Philistines. This is not despair, and it is not suicide in the ordinary sense; it is a soldier choosing to go down with the objective. He is between the two pillars, with three thousand on the roof, and there is no version of this where he walks out.

'So the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed during his life.'

That is the narrator's verdict on Samson: his death accomplished more than his life.

The sentence is sad and true, and it is meant to be uncomfortable. Twenty years of judging, and the greatest blow struck for Israel was struck by a blind man in a heathen temple in the last thirty seconds he had.

Now set that sentence beside another death, because the Bible invites the comparison and then breaks it in the right place.

There is another deliverer who was seized by his enemies, mocked as entertainment, blindfolded and struck and told to prophesy, stretched out between two pieces of wood with his arms spread — and who accomplished more by dying than by living. So far the shapes match.

Here is where they part. Samson prayed let me die with the Philistines, and pulled the house down on the heads of his enemies. Jesus prayed Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34), and let the house fall on himself instead.

Samson killed more in his death than in his life; Christ saved more in his death than in his life — and every one of those saved was on the roof.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his brothers and all his family came down and took him and brought him up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father. He had judged Israel twenty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then his brothers and all his family came down and took him and brought him up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father. He had judged Israel twenty years.'

His family come for the body. Nobody else does.

No national mourning is recorded, no Israel gathering to honour a deliverer, no song like Deborah's. His brothers and his father's household walk down to Gaza, dig him out of the rubble of a Philistine temple, and carry him home.

They lay him between Zorah and Eshtaol.

Turn back three chapters. And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol (13:25).

Exactly the same ground. That is where the Spirit first made a young man restless, and it is where they put him in the earth. Everything in between — the girl at Timnah, the lion, the riddle, the foxes, the jawbone, the gates of Gaza, the lap, the razor, the mill, the pillars — happened between those two villages and came back to them.

He is buried in the tomb of Manoah his father: the man who prayed teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born, and was told to keep the vow and wait.

He had judged Israel twenty years. And the Philistines are still there. Chapter 13 said he would only begin, and he only began; the war he opened is not finished until David (2 Sam. 5:17-25; 8:1).

So the last word on Samson is not a triumph, and the book is not embarrassed about it. He is the deliverer who did what was right in his own eyes and destroyed himself doing it; who was given more raw power than any man in Scripture and used most of it on private quarrels; who lost God and did not notice; and who at the very end, blind and shaved and mocked, called on the LORD and was heard.

His hair grew back where nobody was looking. He asked to be remembered, and he was. And the God who left him in verse 20 answered him in verse 28 — not because the man had improved, but because a temple full of people were crediting Dagon with a victory over the living God, and the living God had one servant left in the building.

17.title: Micah's Idol
17.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a man of the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Micah.<sup>2</sup>And he said to his mother, "The 1,100 pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse, and also spoke it in my ears, behold, the silver is with me; I took it." And his mother said, "Blessed be my son by the LORD."<sup>3</sup>And he restored the 1,100 pieces of silver to his mother. And his mother said, "I dedicate the silver to the LORD from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image. Now therefore I will restore it to you."<sup>4</sup>So when he restored the money to his mother, his mother took 200 pieces of silver and gave it to the silversmith, who made it into a carved image and a metal image. And it was in the house of Micah.<sup>5</sup>And the man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and household gods, and ordained one of his sons, who became his priest.<sup>6</sup>In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.<sup>7</sup>Now there was a young man of Bethlehem in Judah, of the family of Judah, who was a Levite, and he sojourned there.<sup>8</sup>And the man departed from the town of Bethlehem in Judah to sojourn where he could find a place. And as he journeyed, he came to the hill country of Ephraim to the house of Micah.<sup>9</sup>And Micah said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I am a Levite of Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to sojourn where I may find a place."<sup>10</sup>And Micah said to him, "Stay with me, and be to me a father and a priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year and a suit of clothes and your living." And the Levite went in.<sup>11</sup>And the Levite was content to dwell with the man, and the young man became to him like one of his sons.<sup>12</sup>And Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest, and was in the house of Micah.<sup>13</sup>Then Micah said, "Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest."
17.overview:
A man of Ephraim named Micah admits to his mother that he stole the eleven hundred pieces of silver she cursed the thief for taking — and he admits it because he is under the curse, not because he is sorry. She cancels the curse with a blessing in the LORD's name, and then dedicates the money to the LORD to have a carved image and a metal image made. That sentence is the whole chapter: the covenant name and a breach of the second commandment in one breath. Of the eleven hundred she declared dedicated, two hundred reaches the silversmith.

Micah then assembles a complete religion in his own house — a shrine, an ephod, household gods, and one of his own sons ordained as priest. Every item is homemade. And the narrator states the thesis of the book's last five chapters: in those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes. It is Samson's own phrase from 14:3, now laid over the whole nation.

Then a young Levite comes past, away from the cities his tribe was given, looking for a place to land. Micah hires him for ten pieces of silver a year, a suit of clothes and his keep, and the Levite is content. Micah's conclusion: now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest.
17.theology:
Not apostasy — devotion done wrong. Nobody in this house has abandoned the LORD. They use his name constantly, and the mother intends the images as an act of piety on her son's behalf. That is what makes it more dangerous than open idolatry: a family worshipping the true God in a manner he explicitly forbade (Ex. 20:4), and feeling generous about the cost.

Words as mechanisms. She curses; he confesses to escape the curse; she blesses in the LORD's name to cancel it. Nothing in the exchange is addressed to God, and God's name is in every line of it.

Right in his own eyes (v. 6). Not what was wrong in his own eyes. These are people who have each become the final authority on what is good, and every one of them is satisfied. Ask Micah and he would say he was a religious man doing his best. The phrase is Samson's (14:3), and the writer has taken it from the deliverer's mouth and made it the nation's epitaph: Samson was not the exception, he was the specimen.

You cannot hire a father (v. 10). The moment a salary is attached, the man whose job is to tell you the truth is the man whose keep depends on you. Micah wants a priest's authority and a servant's compliance, and his budget says what he thinks he is buying: eleven hundred pieces for the images, ten a year for the clergyman.

The word 'because' (v. 13). Now I know the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest is superstition in flawless orthodox vocabulary. Every element of it is a true and good thing; the relationship is upside down. God has become the reliable output of a correctly configured system standing in a man's own house. The test is not whether a person believes right things but whether he is using them — and chapter 18 is the answer, because a mechanism you can build is a mechanism six hundred men can carry away.

The priest nobody hires. No one takes this honour for himself, but only when called by God (Heb. 5:4-5). Christ holds his priesthood permanently because he continues forever, and so saves to the uttermost, always living to intercede (Heb. 7:24-25). He cannot be bought for ten pieces a year and cannot be taken off you by six hundred men.
17.examples:
Then: A man returned stolen money to escape a curse, his mother dedicated it to the LORD to have an idol cast, he built a chapel in his front room and ordained his own son, and then hired a wandering Levite on a small annual salary and concluded that his prospects were now secure.

Now: The chapter's question is not whether you believe the right things — Micah's vocabulary was faultless — but whether you are using them. Listen for his word: because. I know it will go well for me because I read, pray, attend, give, serve. That sentence feels like faith and works like machinery, and the difference shows the day the machinery is taken away. And check the mother's arithmetic against your own: she pledged eleven hundred out loud and spent two hundred, and nobody ever audited the gap.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Eleven Hundred Pieces of Silver
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man of Ephraim named Micah confesses to his mother that he stole the eleven hundred pieces of silver she had cursed the thief for taking (vv. 1-2). She blesses him in the LORD's name, and then dedicates the money to the LORD for the making of a carved image and a metal image (v. 3). Of the eleven hundred she hands two hundred to the silversmith, and the images stand in Micah's house (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The figure is the one every Philistine lord offered Delilah for Samson (16:5). The money that bought a deliverer's betrayal is the money that pays for this shrine, and the writer puts the two chapters side by side.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 is the whole chapter in one sentence: the covenant name and a breach of the second commandment in the same breath (Ex. 20:4). And she promised eleven hundred and spent two hundred. Even the devotion is eighteen per cent.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a man of the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Micah. And he said to his mother, "The 1,100 pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse, and also spoke it in my ears, behold, the silver is with me; I took it." And his mother said, "Blessed be my son by the LORD." And he restored the 1,100 pieces of silver to his mother. And his mother said, "I dedicate the silver to the LORD from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image. Now therefore I will restore it to you." So when he restored the money to his mother, his mother took 200 pieces of silver and gave it to the silversmith, who made it into a carved image and a metal image. And it was in the house of Micah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'There was a man of the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Micah. And he said to his mother, "The 1,100 pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse, and also spoke it in my ears, behold, the silver is with me; I took it."'

Note the figure, because the writer has just used it.

Eleven hundred pieces of silver is what each of the five Philistine lords offered Delilah for the secret of Samson's strength (16:5). It is a distinctive sum, it appears twice in adjoining chapters, and both times it buys something that should never have been for sale.

Now notice why Micah confesses. Not because he has been caught, and not because he is sorry. His mother uttered a curse over the thief and spoke it in my ears — he was standing there when she cursed him, and he has been living under it ever since.

He is not repenting. He is trying to get out from under a curse.

'And his mother said, "Blessed be my son by the LORD."'

Her reply is not forgiveness either. It is a countermeasure.

She had put a curse into the air; she now puts a blessing into the air on top of it, using the covenant name, to cancel the first. Mother and son are both handling words as though they were mechanisms. Something has been said that might damage him, so something must be said to undo it.

Nothing here is about God at all, and both of them are talking about him constantly.

'And he restored the 1,100 pieces of silver to his mother. And his mother said, "I dedicate the silver to the LORD from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image."'

Read that sentence twice, because the whole chapter is in it.

I dedicate the silver to the LORD... to make a carved image and a metal image. The covenant name of the God of Israel, and the direct breach of his second commandment, in one breath, with no sense of any difficulty.

The commandment could hardly be plainer: you shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath (Ex. 20:4). She is not turning to Baal. She is not renouncing the LORD. She intends this as an act of piety, in his honour, funded by recovered money, on behalf of her son.

That is what makes it so much more dangerous than open apostasy. Nobody in this house has decided to abandon God. They have decided to worship him in a way he forbade, and to feel good about the expense.

'So when he restored the money to his mother, his mother took 200 pieces of silver and gave it to the silversmith, who made it into a carved image and a metal image. And it was in the house of Micah.'

She said eleven hundred. She spent two hundred.

The arithmetic is right there and the narrator does not comment on it, which is his way. She had declared the whole sum dedicated to the LORD from my hand, and then she took less than a fifth of it to the silversmith and kept the rest.

Eighteen per cent, and a speech about dedication.

There is a kind of religion that is generous in its language and careful with its money, and the question to ask is whether anyone has ever seen the gap between what was pledged out loud and what actually went. Nobody audited this woman. The silver simply stayed where it was.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Micah has a shrine of his own, makes an ephod and household gods, and ordains one of his sons as priest (v. 5). Then the sentence the last five chapters of this book are built on: in those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything in his religion is homemade — the building, the images, the ephod, and the priest. Nothing was received, nothing was commanded, and nothing came from outside his own household.
verseByVerse.examples: The phrase is Samson's. She is right in my eyes, he told his parents when they quoted the law at him (14:3), and now the writer says the whole nation had been living there. The strong man was not the exception. He was the sample.

verseByVerse.quote: And the man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and household gods, and ordained one of his sons, who became his priest. In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And the man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and household gods, and ordained one of his sons, who became his priest.'

Everything in this verse is homemade.

Go through the list. The building — his own house of gods, not the tabernacle. The ephod — the priestly garment used for seeking God's guidance, and the exact thing Gideon made out of the Midianite gold, which became a snare to him and his household (8:27). The household gods — teraphim, the family figurines Rachel stole from Laban. And the priest — his own son, ordained by his own father, from the tribe of Ephraim.

The Hebrew for ordaining is filled the hand of, which is the technical term for installing a priest. Micah uses the correct word for something he has no right whatever to do.

Not one item on that list was received. Every piece of it was commissioned, built, bought or appointed by the man himself, and the whole assembly is in his own front room, where he can get at it.

'In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.'

Now the sentence the last five chapters of this book are built on.

It will be said twice more before the end (21:25 in full, and shorter at 18:1 and 19:1), and it is the writer's verdict on everything from here to the last verse.

Take the two halves separately. There was no king in Israel — no central authority, no one to enforce the covenant, no one over the tribes. The book is arguing for a monarchy, and it is doing so honestly: what follows in these five chapters is what happens without one.

But the second half is the deeper diagnosis, because a king would not have cured it. Every man did what was right in his own eyes. Not what was wrong in his own eyes — what was right. This is not a nation of people knowingly doing evil. It is a nation of people each of whom has become his own final authority on what is good, and every one of them is satisfied.

Micah is a case in point. He has restored stolen money, honoured his mother, built a place of worship, made provision for the LORD's service and installed a priest. If you asked him, he would tell you he was a religious man doing his best, and he would be sincere.

Now put the phrase where it belongs, because you have met it three chapters ago. She is right in my eyes — Samson, to his parents, when they quoted the law to him about marrying a Philistine (14:3). Identical words. And the writer has now taken that private sentence from the mouth of the deliverer and laid it over the whole nation as its epitaph.

Samson was not the exception to his generation. He was the specimen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — A Priest for Ten Pieces a Year
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah leaves home to sojourn where he could find a place and arrives at Micah's door by chance (vv. 7-9). Micah offers him ten pieces of silver a year, clothing and his keep, to be a father and a priest — and the Levite takes it, and is treated like one of the sons (vv. 10-12). Micah's conclusion: now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: A Levite had forty-eight cities assigned to him and work to do in them (Josh. 21). This one is looking for a position, and takes the first one offered, in a private chapel, serving images.
verseByVerse.examples: Ten pieces of silver a year for the priest; eleven hundred set aside for the gods. And verse 13 gives away what the whole apparatus is for. Micah is not worshipping; he is installing a mechanism. He has the right vocabulary and the wrong God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a young man of Bethlehem in Judah, of the family of Judah, who was a Levite, and he sojourned there. And the man departed from the town of Bethlehem in Judah to sojourn where he could find a place. And as he journeyed, he came to the hill country of Ephraim to the house of Micah. And Micah said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I am a Levite of Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to sojourn where I may find a place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Now there was a young man of Bethlehem in Judah, of the family of Judah, who was a Levite, and he sojourned there.'

A Levite living in Bethlehem, which is the first thing wrong.

The tribe of Levi had no territory of its own. That was deliberate: the LORD himself was to be their inheritance, and in place of land they were given forty-eight cities scattered through every other tribe, so that the whole nation would have men among them who knew the law and could teach it (Num. 18:20; Josh. 21). Bethlehem was not one of the forty-eight.

So this young man is away from his post before the story starts.

'And the man departed from the town of Bethlehem in Judah to sojourn where he could find a place. And as he journeyed, he came to the hill country of Ephraim to the house of Micah.'

To sojourn where he could find a place.

That is the whole of his ambition, stated by the narrator without comment: somewhere to land, somewhere to be kept. He is not going anywhere in particular. He is a young clergyman looking for a position, walking north with no destination, and he arrives at Micah's door because that is the door he happened to reach.

'And Micah said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I am a Levite of Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to sojourn where I may find a place."'

Asked who he is, he leads with his qualification.

I am a Levite — and then, in the same sentence, that he is available. He has told a complete stranger, within a minute of meeting him, both what he is certified to do and that nobody currently employs him.

Micah, whose priest at present is one of his own sons, is listening very carefully.

verseByVerse.quote: And Micah said to him, "Stay with me, and be to me a father and a priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year and a suit of clothes and your living." And the Levite went in. And the Levite was content to dwell with the man, and the young man became to him like one of his sons. And Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest, and was in the house of Micah. Then Micah said, "Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'And Micah said to him, "Stay with me, and be to me a father and a priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year and a suit of clothes and your living."'

Here is the offer, and the two halves of it do not belong in the same sentence.

Be to me a father — a title of respect for a spiritual guide, someone whose counsel you submit to. And then the terms of employment: ten pieces of silver a year, one suit of clothes, and board.

A father cannot be hired. The moment a salary is attached, the man who is supposed to tell you the truth is the man whose keep depends on you, and everyone in the arrangement knows it. Micah wants the authority of a priest and the compliance of a servant, and he thinks the two can be bought together.

Compare the two sums in this chapter while they are in front of you. Eleven hundred pieces of silver were set aside for the images. Ten pieces a year is what the priest is worth. Micah's budget tells you exactly what he thinks he is buying.

'And the Levite went in. And the Levite was content to dwell with the man, and the young man became to him like one of his sons.'

Content is the writer's word, and it is the most damning thing said about him.

He does not argue about the images. He does not ask whose shrine this is, or point out that a carved image in a private house in Ephraim is not what Levites were scattered through Israel to maintain. He has been trained in the law of Moses, and he settles down.

He came looking for a place to sojourn and he has found one. That was his only criterion, and it has been met.

'And Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest, and was in the house of Micah.'

Micah filled his hand — the technical phrase again — and the Levite lets him.

An Ephraimite householder has now installed a priest by his own authority, which belonged to nobody but God, and the priest so installed had every reason to know it and said nothing.

'Then Micah said, "Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest."'

There is what all of it was for.

Weigh the shape of the sentence. Now I know — certainty, at last. That the LORD will prosper me — the desired outcome. Because I have a Levite as priest — the reason, the lever, the thing that makes the outcome follow.

Micah has assembled a machine. Shrine, ephod, images, and now a genuine Levite to work the controls, and with that last component fitted he is confident of results. God has become the predictable output of a correctly configured system, and the system stands in his house where he can maintain it.

This is superstition speaking perfect orthodox vocabulary, and that is precisely why it needs stopping over. Everything in Micah's sentence is a true and good thing in itself. The LORD is the God of Israel. Levites really were set apart. Priests really were appointed. He has got the words right and the whole relationship upside down.

The danger is a live one for anyone who takes religion seriously, in a way that open idolatry never is. The question is not whether a person believes the right things. It is whether he is using them. Do I read, pray, attend, give and serve because God is God, or because the practices are the mechanism by which I expect life to come out well? The second one feels like faith and behaves like machinery, and the tell is the word because. Now I know it will go well for me, because I have got the arrangement right.

The next chapter is God's answer to Micah's sentence. Six hundred armed men will walk into his house, take the images, take the ephod, take the household gods and take the Levite, and leave him standing in the road with nothing. It turns out that a mechanism you can build is a mechanism somebody else can carry away.

Set beside it the priest nobody hires. No one takes this honour for himself, but only when called by God — and Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest; his Father appointed him (Heb. 5:4-5). He holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever, and therefore he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:24-25).

He cannot be bought for ten pieces of silver a year, and he cannot be taken off you by six hundred men.

18.title: The Danites Steal the Idol
18.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days there was no king in Israel. And in those days the tribe of the people of Dan was seeking for itself an inheritance to dwell in, for until then no inheritance among the tribes of Israel had fallen to them.<sup>2</sup>So the people of Dan sent five able men from the whole number of their tribe, from Zorah and from Eshtaol, to spy out the land and to explore it. And they said to them, "Go and explore the land." And they came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and lodged there.<sup>3</sup>When they were by the house of Micah, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. And they turned aside and said to him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What is your business here?"<sup>4</sup>And he said to them, "This is how Micah dealt with me: he has hired me, and I have become his priest."<sup>5</sup>And they said to him, "Inquire of God, please, that we may know whether the journey on which we are setting out will succeed."<sup>6</sup>And the priest said to them, "Go in peace. The journey on which you go is under the eye of the LORD."<sup>7</sup>Then the five men departed and came to Laish and saw the people who were there, how they lived in security, after the manner of the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting, lacking nothing that is in the earth and possessing wealth, and how they were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone.<sup>8</sup>And when they came to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol, their brothers said to them, "What do you report?"<sup>9</sup>They said, "Arise, and let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and behold, it is very good. And will you do nothing? Do not be slow to go, to enter in and possess the land.<sup>10</sup>As soon as you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people. The land is spacious, for God has given it into your hands, a place where there is no lack of anything that is in the earth."<sup>11</sup>So 600 men of the tribe of Dan, armed with weapons of war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol,<sup>12</sup>and went up and encamped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. On this account that place is called Mahaneh-dan to this day; behold, it is west of Kiriath-jearim.<sup>13</sup>And they passed on from there to the hill country of Ephraim, and came to the house of Micah.<sup>14</sup>Then the five men who had gone to scout out the country of Laish said to their brothers, "Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, household gods, a carved image, and a metal image? Now therefore consider what you will do."<sup>15</sup>And they turned aside there and came to the house of the young Levite, at the home of Micah, and asked him about his welfare.<sup>16</sup>Now the 600 men of the Danites, armed with their weapons of war, stood by the entrance of the gate.<sup>17</sup>And the five men who had gone to scout out the land went up and entered and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, while the priest stood by the entrance of the gate with the 600 men armed with weapons of war.<sup>18</sup>And when these went into Micah's house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, the priest said to them, "What are you doing?"<sup>19</sup>And they said to him, "Keep quiet; put your hand on your mouth and come with us and be to us a father and a priest. Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and clan in Israel?"<sup>20</sup>And the priest's heart was glad. He took the ephod and the household gods and the carved image and went along with the people.<sup>21</sup>So they turned and departed, putting the little ones and the livestock and the goods in front of them.<sup>22</sup>When they had gone a distance from the home of Micah, the men who were in the houses near Micah's house were called out, and they overtook the people of Dan.<sup>23</sup>And they shouted to the people of Dan, who turned around and said to Micah, "What is the matter with you, that you come with such a company?"<sup>24</sup>And he said, "You take my gods that I made and the priest, and go away, and what have I left? How then do you ask me, 'What is the matter with you?'"<sup>25</sup>And the people of Dan said to him, "Do not let your voice be heard among us, lest angry fellows fall upon you, and you lose your life with the lives of your household."<sup>26</sup>Then the people of Dan went their way. And when Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back to his home.<sup>27</sup>But the people of Dan took what Micah had made, and the priest who belonged to him, and they came to Laish, to a people quiet and unsuspecting, and struck them with the edge of the sword and burned the city with fire.<sup>28</sup>And there was no deliverer because it was far from Sidon, and they had no dealings with anyone. It was in the valley that belongs to Beth-rehob. Then they rebuilt the city and lived in it.<sup>29</sup>And they named the city Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor, who was born to Israel; but the name of the city was Laish at the first.<sup>30</sup>And the people of Dan set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan the son of Gershom, son of Moses, and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day of the captivity of the land.<sup>31</sup>So they set up Micah's carved image that he made, as long as the house of God was at Shiloh.
18.overview:
Dan is looking for somewhere to live, for until then no inheritance had fallen to them — which is not the whole truth. Joshua 19 names their territory town by town; 1:34 says the Amorites pressed them back into the hills and they never took it. The failure has been rewritten as a shortage, and the shortage justifies what follows.

Five scouts lodge at Micah's house, recognise the young Levite by his southern accent, and ask him to enquire of God. He consults nothing — there is an ephod in the house and he does not fetch it — and answers instantly with a blessing that cannot be tested: go in peace. At Laish they find a prosperous, peaceable, isolated town with no allies, and every line of their report is about defencelessness. Then they tell the tribe God has given it into your hands, which is Joshua's conquest formula laid over a soft target.

Six hundred armed men march north, stop at Micah's house, and strip the shrine while the priest stands at the gate with the soldiers. He is offered a promotion in Micah's own words — a father and a priest, but to a tribe rather than one house — and his heart is glad, and he carries the stolen gods out himself. Micah pursues, is told to keep his voice down, and says the truest thing in the story: you take my gods that I made... and what have I left?

Laish is put to the sword and burned, and there was no deliverer. The city is renamed Dan, the image is set up there, the priest is named as Jonathan son of Gershom son of Moses, and the shrine runs until the captivity. And the last line: all this while the house of God was at Shiloh.
18.theology:
A grievance edited into a shortage (v. 1). Not we would not fight for what God gave us but nothing fell to us. The thing that was refused becomes the thing that was never offered, and the rewritten history licenses the raid.

The hired oracle (v. 6). No ephod, no waiting, no enquiry, and an answer that is soothing and unfalsifiable. A man whose keep depends on his hearers will find over time that the word of the LORD agrees with them, and will never experience it as dishonesty — he will simply never have anything uncomfortable to say. Paul names the market and says who drives it: people accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their passions (2 Tim. 4:3). And the journey did succeed, which proves nothing — Moses had already ruled that a sign coming true does not authenticate a man who leads you elsewhere (Deut. 13:1-3).

Providence read backwards (v. 10). You will come to an unsuspecting people... for God has given it into your hands. The reason for the confidence is stated first, and it is not God; it is that the victims will not see them coming. The test on any such claim is simple: would you still call it God's will if it were hard, costly, or if they could fight back?

My gods that I made (v. 24). Micah gives the complete case against idolatry in five words and uses it as an argument. Isaiah watches the same thing being evacuated by mule — they cannot save the burden (Isa. 46:1-2) — and the psalm says those who make them become like them (Ps. 115:4-8). Ask it of whatever you rely on: if six hundred men took it, what would be left? That answer names your actual god.

The hired hand (v. 20). Content when he found a post (17:11), glad when a bigger one arrived, and he carries the stolen images out with his own hands. Not one word the narrator gives him is about God. He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep (John 10:12-13).

Three generations from Sinai (v. 30). The priest is Moses' own great-grandson. Ancient scribes suspended a letter so the name could be read Manasseh and spare the lawgiver; the text was preserved anyway. And the shrine outlasts everyone in the chapter, down to the captivity — and Jeroboam later sets a golden calf on that same ground (1 Kings 12:28-30).

And the house of God was at Shiloh (v. 31). The real tabernacle, with the ark and the appointed priesthood, stood a few miles away the entire time. The spies walked past it; the six hundred marched past it; the Levite lived in its shadow. Nobody went. They preferred a shrine they could carry, a priest they could pay and an oracle that agreed with them — and the real thing was near, free, and impossible to manage, which is exactly why they left it alone.
18.examples:
Then: A tribe that would not fight for the land God gave it marched north instead, chose a town for the sole reason that it could not defend itself, called that God's gift, robbed a private chapel on the way, bought the chaplain with a bigger job, and founded a shrine that lasted until the exile — all within a morning's walk of the tabernacle.

Now: Three tests. First, the Danites': am I calling something God's will because it is right, or because it is easy? Ask whether you would still say it if the thing were costly. Second, Micah's: if it could be taken from me by force, it was never God. What have I left is the question that finds out what you were actually trusting. Third, the one the chapter ends on: Shiloh was four hours away. The genuine thing is usually nearer than the substitute, and the reason people prefer the substitute is not that it is closer but that it can be managed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A Tribe Looking for Somewhere Easier
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In those days there was no king in Israel, and Dan was seeking for itself an inheritance, because none had fallen to them (v. 1). Five men are sent from Zorah and Eshtaol to scout, and lodge at Micah's house on the way, where they recognise the young Levite's voice (vv. 2-4). They ask him to enquire of God whether their journey will succeed, and he answers at once: go in peace. The journey on which you go is under the eye of the LORD (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Dan did have an inheritance. Joshua 19:40-48 assigns it, and 1:34 says what happened: the Amorites pressed them back into the hills and they never took it. The grievance in v. 1 is worded as though God had left them out.
verseByVerse.examples: The priest consults nothing. No ephod, no waiting, no enquiry of any kind — he produces the answer his questioners came for, in one breath, and puts the LORD's name on it. That is what a hired oracle is for.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days there was no king in Israel. And in those days the tribe of the people of Dan was seeking for itself an inheritance to dwell in, for until then no inheritance among the tribes of Israel had fallen to them. So the people of Dan sent five able men from the whole number of their tribe, from Zorah and from Eshtaol, to spy out the land and to explore it. And they said to them, "Go and explore the land." And they came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and lodged there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In those days there was no king in Israel. And in those days the tribe of the people of Dan was seeking for itself an inheritance to dwell in, for until then no inheritance among the tribes of Israel had fallen to them.'

The refrain again, and then a claim that is not quite true.

No inheritance among the tribes of Israel had fallen to them. Read on its own, that sounds as though Dan had been overlooked in the division of the land — as though the lot came round and there was nothing left for them.

Turn to Joshua 19. Dan was allotted a territory, and it is named town by town: Zorah, Eshtaol, Aijalon, Timnah, Ekron, Joppa and more — good country on the coastal plain, some of the best in the land. It fell to them exactly as the others did.

What happened is recorded in the first chapter of this book. The Amorites pressed the people of Dan back into the hill country, for they did not allow them to come down to the plain (1:34). They had the deed and never took possession. It was too hard, and the enemy was too settled, and they gave up and stayed in the hills.

So the grievance in verse 1 is a piece of careful editing. Not we would not fight for what God gave us, but nothing had fallen to us. The failure has been rewritten as a shortage, and the shortage justifies what they are about to do.

People do this with their own histories. The thing that was refused becomes the thing that was never offered.

'So the people of Dan sent five able men from the whole number of their tribe, from Zorah and from Eshtaol, to spy out the land and to explore it. And they said to them, "Go and explore the land." And they came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and lodged there.'

From Zorah and from Eshtaol.

Those are Samson's two villages. He was born between them, the Spirit first stirred him between them, and his brothers buried him between them two chapters ago (13:2, 13:25, 16:31). This scouting party sets out from the ground where God's deliverer for this tribe is lying in his father's tomb.

They are going the other way. Samson went down to the Philistine plain to begin taking what Dan had abandoned; his tribe now sends five men north, to look for somewhere easier.

verseByVerse.quote: When they were by the house of Micah, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. And they turned aside and said to him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What is your business here?" And he said to them, "This is how Micah dealt with me: he has hired me, and I have become his priest." And they said to him, "Inquire of God, please, that we may know whether the journey on which we are setting out will succeed." And the priest said to them, "Go in peace. The journey on which you go is under the eye of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'When they were by the house of Micah, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. And they turned aside and said to him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What is your business here?"'

They knew him by his accent.

The Levite is from Bethlehem in Judah and they are men of Dan, and the moment he speaks they place him — a southern voice a long way north, in a private house in Ephraim. This book has already shown what an accent could do at a river crossing (12:6). Here it simply makes a stranger recognisable.

Their three questions are the right ones. Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What is your business here? A Levite belongs in one of the forty-eight cities given to his tribe, teaching the law. He is a long way from any of them and everyone can see it.

'And he said to them, "This is how Micah dealt with me: he has hired me, and I have become his priest."'

He answers with the terms of his employment, and hears nothing wrong in the answer.

He has hired me. The word is exact and the young man volunteers it. Asked what his business is, he describes a transaction: a man engaged him, and consequently he is a priest. That is the whole account of his calling.

'And they said to him, "Inquire of God, please, that we may know whether the journey on which we are setting out will succeed."'

Having established that he is for hire, they ask him for an oracle.

The request is polite and the theology behind it is old and good: before a campaign, ask God. Israel asked at the start of this very book — who shall go up first for us against the Canaanites? — and got an answer (1:1-2). Joshua's disaster at Ai came from not asking.

'And the priest said to them, "Go in peace. The journey on which you go is under the eye of the LORD."'

He answers immediately, and he consults nothing.

Look at what is missing. There is an ephod in the house — the very instrument used for enquiring of God — and he does not go and get it. He does not withdraw, or wait, or pray, or say he will have an answer in the morning. There is no pause of any kind between the question and the reply.

What he gives them is a blessing with no content: go in peace, the journey is under the eye of the LORD. It is soothing, it is unfalsifiable, and it is precisely what five armed men on their way to look for a soft target wanted to hear.

That is what a hired oracle is for, and it is why the arrangement in chapter 17 was rotten from the first day. A man whose keep depends on the goodwill of his hearers will discover, over time, that the word of the LORD tends to agree with them. He will not experience it as dishonesty. He will simply never find himself with anything uncomfortable to say.

Paul saw the same market and named it: the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions (2 Tim. 4:3). Note who is doing the accumulating. The demand comes first; the supply always arrives.

The Danites will get a hundred miles up the country on the strength of that sentence, and it will turn out to have been true — the journey succeeds. That is the last thing to notice here, and the most sobering. A false prophet's word coming true proves nothing at all. Moses had already said so: even if the sign comes to pass, if he leads you after other gods, do not listen (Deut. 13:1-3).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The five reach Laish, far north, and report what they saw: a people living in security, quiet and unsuspecting, wanting for nothing, and isolated — far from Sidon and with no dealings with anyone (v. 7). Their report to the tribe is a call to arms: the land is very good, do not be slow, God has given it into your hands (vv. 8-10). Six hundred armed men set out and camp at Mahaneh-dan (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Every detail in the scouting report is about defencelessness. Not that the land is theirs by promise, not that God has commanded it — that these people are peaceable, prosperous and would have no help if attacked.
verseByVerse.examples: And then God has given it into your hands, which is Joshua's language for the conquest, laid over a target chosen because it was soft. It is the most religious sentence in the chapter and there is nothing in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the five men departed and came to Laish and saw the people who were there, how they lived in security, after the manner of the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting, lacking nothing that is in the earth and possessing wealth, and how they were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone. And when they came to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol, their brothers said to them, "What do you report?" They said, "Arise, and let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and behold, it is very good. And will you do nothing? Do not be slow to go, to enter in and possess the land. As soon as you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people. The land is spacious, for God has given it into your hands, a place where there is no lack of anything that is in the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Then the five men departed and came to Laish and saw the people who were there, how they lived in security, after the manner of the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting, lacking nothing that is in the earth and possessing wealth, and how they were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone.'

Every detail in that report is about how easy it would be.

Go through it as an intelligence assessment, because that is what it is. They live in security — no defences worth the name. Quiet and unsuspecting — no watch, no expectation of attack. Lacking nothing... possessing wealth — worth taking. Far from the Sidonians — their nearest kin are too far off to come. No dealings with anyone — no allies, no treaties, nobody who owes them anything.

Not one word about whether the land was promised to Israel. Not one word about the people's wickedness, which is the ground on which Canaan was to be dispossessed (Gen. 15:16; Deut. 9:4-5). The five men have found a prosperous, peaceable, isolated town that cannot defend itself, and that is the entire case.

'And when they came to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol, their brothers said to them, "What do you report?" They said, "Arise, and let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and behold, it is very good. And will you do nothing? Do not be slow to go, to enter in and possess the land."'

The speech is stirring, and every phrase in it is borrowed.

Arise... the land is very good... do not be slow... go in and possess the land. That is the vocabulary of Caleb and Joshua at Kadesh, urging a frightened nation into the country God had sworn to their fathers (Num. 13:30; 14:7-9). It is the language of faith, used here to recruit a raiding party.

'"As soon as you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people. The land is spacious, for God has given it into your hands, a place where there is no lack of anything that is in the earth."'

There it is: God has given it into your hands.

That sentence is the conquest formula. It is what the LORD said to Joshua about Jericho and Ai, and it means that God has determined an outcome and Israel is to act on his word. Here it is being used of a town nobody asked God about, chosen for the single reason that it could not fight back.

Weigh the sentence structure, because the two halves give the game away. You will come to an unsuspecting people — and then, in the very next breath, for God has given it into your hands. The reason for the confidence is stated first, and it is not God. It is that the victims will not see them coming.

This is the chapter's most religious sentence and there is nothing whatever in it. Providence is being read backwards off an opportunity: the thing is easy, therefore God must intend it. Men have justified a great deal that way, and the test is simple enough — would you still call it God's will if it were hard, or costly, or if the people concerned could defend themselves?

verseByVerse.quote: So 600 men of the tribe of Dan, armed with weapons of war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol, and went up and encamped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. On this account that place is called Mahaneh-dan to this day; behold, it is west of Kiriath-jearim. And they passed on from there to the hill country of Ephraim, and came to the house of Micah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So 600 men of the tribe of Dan, armed with weapons of war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol, and went up and encamped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. On this account that place is called Mahaneh-dan to this day; behold, it is west of Kiriath-jearim.'

The writer counts them, and will count them twice more before the chapter ends.

He keeps counting them — six hundred here, six hundred at the gate in verse 16, six hundred again in verse 17 — because the number is the argument. Everything that happens from now on happens because six hundred men with weapons want it to.

Then the place name. Mahaneh-dan, the camp of Dan.

That is where the Spirit of the LORD began to stir Samson (13:25). The writer names it here without comment, and the two uses could hardly be further apart: at the first, God moving on one man to begin saving Israel; at the second, six hundred of that man's own tribe camped on the road north, leaving the fight behind them.

'And they passed on from there to the hill country of Ephraim, and came to the house of Micah.'

They stop at Micah's house, which the five had told them about.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — Is It Better to Serve One House or a Tribe?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The five tell the six hundred that Micah's house holds an ephod, household gods, and a carved and a metal image (v. 14). While the priest stands at the gate with the armed men, they walk in and strip the shrine (vv. 15-18). He asks what they are doing and is told: keep quiet, put your hand on your mouth, and come and be a father and a priest to us — is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and clan in Israel?
